Where an Adams County deed gets recorded

Land records for the county are kept in West Union. Bring a deed or mortgage to 110 West Main Street, Room 133, West Union, OH 45693. Two phone lines are posted on the county's recorder page, 937-544-5051 and 937-544-2513. Weekday service ends at 4 in the afternoon.

You can also look up filed documents on the Adams County public access portal. Make an account first, since the portal wants a username and password. It also sells an alert service for new filings against a parcel, which some owners use to catch fraud early.

Most sellers never carry the deed themselves, since the closing agent usually does. Still, knowing the route helps you read the charges on your settlement statement.

Recording fees in Ohio

The legislature, not the county, fixes what the recorder may charge. Section 317.32 pairs every base fee with an equal housing trust fund fee. For a standard instrument the first two pages cost $17 plus $17. Every further sheet, legal size or any part of one and counting the caption page, adds $4 plus $4.

A preservation surcharge, capped at $5 an instrument, may be added on top and is kept by the county. Ohio law sets a cap only, so call the recorder for Adams County's actual figure before you bring a check.

Other recorder charges under Ohio Revised Code 317.32
ServiceBase feeHousing trust fund fee
Certified copy, per page$1$1
Recorder's seal on a certification50 cents50 cents
Marginal reference or index entry, each$2$2
Local fax or electronic transmission, per page$1$1

Payment is due at the counter when the paper is handed in. Electronic filers can settle later by bank transfer. Count the pages in your deed before you go, since every page past the second adds to the bill.

Stop at the auditor first

In Ohio, the auditor sees a deed before the recorder does. Under section 319.202, the person receiving title, or someone acting for that person, files a statement of value. That can be done online or on three paper copies. Next the auditor marks the deed with the fee taken and a notation that the filing was made. Then it moves to the recorder.

Two charges can land on the seller here:

  • The conveyance fee under section 319.54(G)(3): $1 or ten cents per hundred dollars of value, whichever is larger, with a partial hundred rounded up.
  • A county real property transfer tax, which applies only if the commissioners adopted one under section 322.02. It tops out at thirty cents per hundred dollars and falls on the grantor.

Ask the auditor, at 937-544-2364, if the optional tax is in force here. Numbers for other offices: treasurer 937-544-2317, commissioners 937-544-3286, clerk of courts title department 937-544-2345.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Adams County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Transfers exempt from the conveyance fee

The auditor's fee has carve-outs, and many involve family. A gift between spouses qualifies, and so does a gift from a parent to a child or the child's spouse. Heirs or devisees of one estate who trade property without paying for it are covered too. So is a deed placing land into a trust that the maker can revoke at will, and a deed whose only job is to correct or confirm an earlier recorded one. Transfers made solely to secure a debt, or to release that security, are also excused, as are transactions with no money or other value changing hands that are not gifts, and any interest worth $100 or less.

If your transfer qualifies, the filing must give the reason. The recorder's own charges still apply to an exempt deed, so budget for them.

Tax reductions and the statement of value

This filing connects the sale to the tax bill. The buyer either affirms that the seller reported no reduction of the prior or current year's taxes under section 323.152, or attaches a sworn instrument showing the estimated reduction. A parcel with farm-use valuation needs a similar affirmation about the current agricultural use value and any recoupment charge.

Find out what reductions your parcel carries before closing. The auditor's office can tell you, and the same 937-544-2364 number takes questions about CAUV farm valuation.

Selling fast or selling an inherited house

A cash sale follows the standard sequence. The deed is signed, the auditor receives the statement of value, and the recorder files the deed in West Union. Title companies normally handle the runs between offices. If you are handling it alone, phone the auditor first about the conveyance fee and any county tax, then phone the recorder about page rates and the surcharge.

An inherited house adds steps, because whoever signs needs authority over the estate. Heirs should talk to the court handling the estate before they sign, and ask the title agent which proof the recorder wants attached.

For a seller the order runs like this: contract, title search, drafted deed, signing at closing, auditor's stamp, then filing at the recorder. Fees at the auditor and the recorder are normally settled out of the closing funds, so check the settlement statement for each line before you sign.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Adams County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What to bring to West Union

Pack your folder before you leave. It should hold the signed deed, with the legal description copied word for word from your own prior deed, plus the statement of value and a way to pay at each window. If you are recording for an estate, add whatever papers show who has authority to sign. Phone ahead about the surcharge so the check is right the first time.

Plan the trip in the right order: auditor first, recorder second. A deed with no auditor's stamp gets turned away at the recorder's window, and you lose a trip. If a title company is closing the sale, hand it the same list and let it confirm each step.

Adams County at a glance

Home values here are modest. The typical owner-occupied house is worth $164,200, rent is about $732 a month, and 71.7 percent of homes are lived in by their owners (2020 to 2024 figures). The county holds 12,808 housing units and about 27,865 people as of July 2025. Median household income is $50,264. West Union is the seat and the largest village.

A river-view lot and a village house can price very differently, so rely on recent nearby sales when you set an asking price.

Frequently asked questions

How do I reach the Adams County recorder by phone?

Dial 937-544-5051 or 937-544-2513. Staff are at 110 West Main Street, Room 133, in West Union, weekdays from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.

What will the Adams County recorder charge to file a deed?

Expect $17 plus an equal housing trust fund fee for pages one and two, and $4 plus an equal fee for each page after. A surcharge of up to $5 may sit on top, so ask the recorder for the total.

Is there a county transfer tax on an Adams County sale?

Most sales pay the state-authorized conveyance fee. A county tax is extra and exists only if the commissioners voted for one. Ask the auditor at 937-544-2364.

Who files the statement of value on an Adams County sale?

The buyer or the buyer's representative, at the auditor's office, online or in three paper copies. The seller pays the conveyance fee and any county tax then.

Is a deed from parent to child exempt from the conveyance fee in Adams County?

Usually, yes. Such a gift is on the auditor's exempt list, but you must state the reason on the filing, and recording fees are still due.

Recorder's office location and hours

Deeds in Allen County are recorded at 237 N. Main St., Suite 132, Lima, OH 45801, in the Allen Government Center next to the courthouse. The phone is (419) 223-8517. Mail goes to P.O. Box 1243, Lima, OH 45802. The counter is open Monday to Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:15 p.m., and shuts from 11:00 a.m. to noon for lunch.

Plan around that midday break if you are carrying a deed in yourself, and aim for a morning or mid-afternoon visit so a short line does not push you past 4:15 p.m. Mailed documents follow a separate rule, covered below.

Records the office keeps

The recorder is the county's permanent keeper of land records and indexes each document so a title examiner can trace who owned a parcel and when. The holdings are broader than most sellers expect:

  • Deeds and mortgages, plus a daily register of both that anyone may read during business hours.
  • Liens against property for delinquent taxes.
  • Maps, plats of town lots and other land divisions, and the recorded property lines.
  • Powers of attorney.
  • Military service discharges, recorded without a fee.

A certified copy of any record is available on request for a fee that depends on page count. The office also notes that a recorder can be sued on the official bond for failing to record a document or for damaging a record.

Mailing or e-recording a deed

Mail works only under one condition: the Allen County Auditor's conveyance stamp must already be on the deed. A deed that skips the auditor goes nowhere, so visit the auditor before you buy postage.

Electronic recording takes setup first:

  • Open an escrow account with the recorder.
  • Complete the e-Recording agreement, which can be downloaded from the recorder's page and mailed to the Main Street address.
  • Be ready for a possible extra fee from the e-recording vendor on top of the county's charge.

One screen applies on every route. Under ORC 317.082, a document with a Social Security number on it is refused unless an affidavit is attached or the law excludes that document. Black out the number before you bring a deed in.

What recording costs

Fees for each kind of document are set by law, in section 317.32. For an ordinary instrument, the first two pages cost a $17 base fee plus a $17 housing trust fund fee. Each further page adds $4 and $4. A preservation surcharge of up to $5 may also apply, and it goes to the county general fund.

Two smaller items matter to sellers. A certified copy costs $1 plus $1 per page, and filing an instrument that notes a marginal reference costs $2 plus $2 per reference. For the exact total on your papers, use the recorder's printable fee schedule.

Auditor charges before the deed is recorded

This is the step sellers forget. The auditor's conveyance fee is $3.00 per thousand of the purchase price, and the transfer charge is $.50 per parcel. Write checks for these to the Allen County Auditor. A conveyance form from another Ohio county is fine as long as it has four parts.

The auditor's side also settles what a buyer inherits. In Allen County, taxes follow ownership and the auditor does not prorate them, so the split belongs on the closing statement. A parcel is billed as it stood on January 1, so request a tax split if you are dividing land.

Offices a seller visits

Three desks handle most of a sale, all near each other in Lima.

Allen County offices a home seller usually contacts
OfficeRole in a saleAddress, phone and hours
RecorderRecords the deed and mortgage payoff releases237 N. Main St., Suite 132; (419) 223-8517; weekdays 8:00 to 4:15, closed 11:00 to noon

TreasurerCollects real estate tax and sewer bills237 N Main St, Suite 123; (419) 223-8515; weekdays 8:00 to 4:30

The auditor's site also has a property search, a tax calculator, a property sales lookup and maps. Ask the auditor whether a county transfer tax applies to your deed. That tax depends on a commissioners' resolution under section 322.02, which caps it at 30 cents per $100.

How a deed moves from signing to the record

The path has four stops. First the deed is signed and prepared, with any Social Security number removed. Second it goes to the Allen County Auditor, who stamps the conveyance and collects the conveyance fee and the transfer charge. Third the stamped deed goes to the recorder, in person, by mail or electronically. Fourth the recorder indexes it, which puts the new owner into the chain of title.

If a mortgage is being paid off, the lender's release is recorded too, and it follows the same route. Title companies handle this routinely, and most sellers never visit the counter. If you are selling on your own, call the recorder at (419) 223-8517 before you go and confirm the hours, because the lunch closing catches people out.

What to bring to the counter

  • The signed deed with the auditor's conveyance stamp on it.
  • A check for the recording fee. The page count drives the total, so ask for the fee schedule if you are unsure.
  • Any mortgage release or other document that has to be filed along with the deed.
  • The e-Recording agreement and escrow account details, if you plan to file electronically.

Ask for a certified copy once the deed is recorded if you want proof for your own files. The fee for a certified copy is $1 plus $1 per page.

Allen County market snapshot

Allen County had 100,881 residents in July 2025. It has 44,946 housing units, and 67.7 percent were owner-occupied in 2020 to 2024. The median value of an owner-occupied home is $165,300. Lima is the county seat and largest city, so most sellers deal with the Lima offices listed above. If the market is slow, a clean title and paid-up taxes are what keep a sale from stalling at the recorder's desk.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Steps before you sell

Work in this order. Confirm who is on title, call the treasurer about any balance, get the auditor's stamp, then record. A closing agent normally handles the last two steps. If you do them yourself, bring a deed with no Social Security number on it.

If you inherited the house, ask the probate court which papers support a deed. Open repairs or a tenant in the house do not change the recording steps, although a mortgage payoff adds a release for the recorder to file. A cash sale skips the lender's payoff, but the stamp, the fees and the recording still happen the same way.

Frequently asked questions

Does the Allen County recorder close for lunch?

Yes. The office is open Monday to Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:15 p.m., and closed from 11:00 a.m. to noon.

Can I mail a deed to the Allen County recorder?

Yes, but only with the Allen County Auditor's conveyance stamp already on it. Without the stamp, a mailed conveyance is refused.

Does Allen County accept electronic recording?

Yes, for filers who set up an escrow account and file a completed e-Recording agreement. The e-recording vendor may charge its own fee.

Are military discharge records free to record in Allen County?

Yes. There is no fee to record military service discharges.

Why was my deed refused for a Social Security number?

Ohio Revised Code 317.082 bars the recorder from taking a document with one unless an affidavit is attached or the law excludes the document. Black the number out of the copy you submit, or ask the closing agent how to handle it.

What the Athens County Recorder handles

The recorder keeps the public land records. If a paper transfers any interest in land, it is recorded here, as are DD214 military discharge papers and financing statements that create a lien on real property. The office opens at eight on weekdays, closes at four, and is shut on weekends.

Real property records run from 1790 to the present, with alphabetical indices covering the same span. Staff can direct you to records, though they do not perform title searches. Ownership history is on the AvaWeb portal, free to view and print.

Recording fees

Basic recording is $34.00 for pages one and two, $8.00 for every printed page after that, and $4.00 per marginal notation. Those totals come from ORC 317.32, which splits each into halves: a $17 base fee plus a $17 housing trust fund fee on the first two pages, and $4 plus $4 on each later page.

Athens County Recorder fees
ServiceFee

A county may also add a document preservation surcharge, capped at $5 by statute. Ask the recorder whether it applies before you send payment.

Why a deed may be rejected or surcharged

Ohio House Bill 525, effective July 1, 2009, set standardization rules that nearly all recorded documents must meet. Papers that fall short are still accepted, for an extra $20.00. Documents also have to be drafted and signed as Ohio law requires, so use a preparer who knows the state's rules.

  • Count your pages before mailing a check, because pages set the fee.
  • If you are unsure of the total, phone the office. Its own fee list controls.
  • Direct formatting questions to the recorder. A template is on the Ohio Recorders' Association site.

Transfer tax and the auditor

The recorder does not collect the transfer charge. That belongs to the auditor. ORC 319.202 has the buyer file a statement of value before the auditor endorses the deed, and ORC 319.54(G)(3) sets the charge at a $1 floor or 10 cents per $100 of value (or fraction), whichever is higher. The seller pays it, plus any Chapter 322 county transfer tax.

Certain transfers owe nothing, among them gifts between spouses, gifts from parent to child, delinquent-tax sales and transfers to the trustee of a revocable trust. Call the Athens County auditor at 740-592-3223 to learn whether one fits your deed.

Documents in a typical house sale

A typical sale involves a deed and, if the seller had a loan, a mortgage release. Occasionally a power of attorney or an affidavit about a deceased owner joins them. Every one is recorded separately and priced by page.

  • The deed moving title from seller to buyer, either warranty or fiduciary.
  • A mortgage release, filed once the lender is paid at closing.
  • An affidavit or court certificate if an estate is the seller.

Condition, tenants or probate history do not stop an as-is sale, and the title steps are unchanged. Title companies confirm the chain of ownership in the recorder's index.

Which office does what

One sale involves several offices, and visiting the wrong one costs a trip. The recorder gets deeds and mortgage releases. At the auditor you file the statement of value and pay the conveyance fee, and the homestead and owner-occupancy records live there. The treasurer handles tax payments and payoffs.

  • Recorder: records the deed, charges per page, and holds the index from 1790.
  • Auditor: endorses the conveyance and files the statement of value required by ORC 319.202.
  • Treasurer: tax bills, payments and payment plans.

Only UCC filings tied to real estate have gone to the county since July 1, 2001. Other personal property filings go to the Ohio Secretary of State, so a lien on equipment or inventory will not appear in the county index.

Other recorder fees under ORC 317.32

The statute is the ceiling for what every Ohio recorder charges, and Athens County's figures follow it. Certifying a copy runs $1 base plus $1 housing trust fund per page, with 50 cents plus 50 cents when the seal is required. A marginal reference made by separate instrument is $2 plus $2.

Local fax or electronic transmission is one dollar plus one dollar per page, and long-distance fax is two dollars plus two dollars per page. Instruments filed by a county land reutilization corporation are exempt. The county quotes its own totals for copies, so treat its listing as the number that controls and call to confirm.

A few more charges matter to lenders and title agents. A UCC termination is $12.00, and a search costs $20.00 plus $2.00 for each page of copies requested. If a closing depends on an exact total, confirm by phone.

Look up your records before you sell

Open AvaWeb, the free online land record search, and print the latest deed on file. The auditor's website shows current parcel data, and recorder staff can name the right index volume for older records. Plain copies run $2.00 a page, and certified copies add a $1.00 certification.

Check that the name on the deed matches the name you will sign with, and that any old mortgage shows a release. Clearing a gap now is cheaper than clearing it at closing, and a cash buyer will run the same title search a lender would.

Recording a deed step by step

Have the deed prepared to Ohio's formatting standards, and count its pages so you know the fee. Take it to the auditor for the statement of value and endorsement, and pay the conveyance fee there. Then bring the endorsed deed to the recorder with payment, for example $34.00 for a two-page deed. If the seller had a mortgage, the lender's release goes in as its own recording. The recorder indexes everything, and that index is what the next title search will read.

Most sellers never do this personally, because the title company or closing agent files the paperwork. If you are handling it yourself, phone the recorder first, confirm the current fees, and ask whether anything about your document looks nonstandard.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

What a cash sale changes

A cash buyer removes the lender, so there is no new mortgage to record and the closing can move faster. The seller's side stays the same. Any old mortgage still needs its release recorded, the auditor still takes the statement of value, and the treasurer still supplies a tax payoff. The deed is recorded at the same page-based fee. If you want the deal done quickly, getting the payoff and the deed formatting right in advance is what saves the time.

Athens County at a glance

Athens County had 62,431 people in 2020, with a 2025 estimate of 63,197. About 54.4% of occupied homes are owner-occupied and 45.6% are rented, so many deeds in the county involve rental property.

Frequently asked questions

What are the Athens County Recorder's hours?

Weekdays only, eight to four.

What fees apply when Athens County records my deed?

The county charges $34.00 for the first two pages and $8.00 for each page added. A nonstandard document can be recorded for $20.00 more.

Can I search Athens County land records online?

Yes, through AvaWeb, where documents can be viewed and printed free. Records reach back to 1790.

Does the recorder bill the conveyance fee?

No, the county auditor does. The conveyance fee is $1 or 10 cents per $100 of value or fraction, whichever is higher, plus any Chapter 322 county tax.

How much is a certified copy?

The county charges $2.00 per page plus $1.00 for certification. Plain copies cost $2.00 a page.

Recorder's office address and hours

You will find the recorder at 209 S. Blackhoof St., Suite 103, Wapakoneta, Ohio 45895. Staff are in from eight to half past four on weekdays. The phone is 419-739-6735 and the fax is 419-739-6736.

The treasurer shares the street address, at 419-739-6745, so a single visit can handle the deed filing and the tax payoff together.

What the recorder keeps

Whatever passes title to land here, or puts a burden on it, lands in the recorder's permanent files. Property records start in 1848, the county's founding year, and the books are preserved in archival form for public use.

  • The recorder's work is governed by over 1,000 Ohio Revised Code sections.
  • The recorder sits on the records commission, the body that sets how long county records are kept.
  • The office runs the county microfilming department.
  • Money taken in at the counter is paid into the county general fund.
  • Commissioners and township trustees get a yearly reminder from the office to file zoning resolutions, maps and amendments.

A fee schedule is posted on the recorder's page, and it is the place to find the amount to send with a deed.

Recording fees under Ohio law

Statewide fees come from ORC 317.32, and the local schedule operates inside that law.

Recording fees under ORC 317.32
ServiceBase feeHousing trust fund fee
Recording and indexing, first two pages$17$17
Each subsequent page$4$4
Marginal reference by separate instrument$2$2
Certified copy, per page$1$1
Local fax or electronic transmission, per page$1$1

Auglaize and other counties may add a preservation charge, no more than $5, credited to the general fund. Ask the recorder whether it applies here.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Auglaize County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Deed transfer fee and the auditor

The recorder leaves transfer fees to the auditor, whose office is separate. That office also keeps the records of deed transfers, homestead exemptions, oil and gas wells, special assessments and all real property, exempt parcels included. A statement of value comes first, which ORC 319.202 requires from the buyer.

ORC 319.54(G)(3) charges the seller $1 or 10 cents per $100 of value or fraction, whichever comes out higher. The commissioners can add a Chapter 322 transfer tax as well, so find out from the auditor whether it applies. Exempt transfers fall in three groups: security for a debt that is only given or released, court-ordered moves that are not sales, and fixes to a deed already recorded.

Valuation and complaints

Valuation is the auditor's job as chief assessor, reappraising every six years and updating every three. Value complaints go to a Board of Revision of three: the auditor, the treasurer and one commissioner.

Under ORC 5715.19(A)(1) you may file until the later of two dates: March 31 following the tax year, or the day first-half collection ends. Mail is dated by Postal Service postmark rather than a private meter. If unpaid land tax could be on your parcel, ask the treasurer before listing.

Housing in Auglaize County

The 2020 count showed 19,873 housing units, 6.4% of them empty, and 75.6% of occupied homes lived in by their owners. Wapakoneta, the county seat, is the biggest town. Because owners dominate, most sales are plain house-to-house deeds. Selling a parent's house or leaving the state does not change the recording steps, and as-is sales work the same.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Auglaize County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Treasurer and auditor duties in a sale

Voters elect the treasurer for four years, and the office serves as the county's banker. The office collects real property and personal taxes, plus taxes on manufactured homes, hotel-motel stays and special assessments, and holds the money collected for schools, cities, townships and villages until it is distributed. The staff is small, two full-time employees, so call ahead for a payoff figure instead of showing up on closing day.

The auditor does the assessing. Beyond reappraisals, the auditor registers manufactured homes and assesses their value, then passes the proceeds to municipalities, townships and school districts in proportion. The auditor also sits with the treasurer and the prosecuting attorney on the budget commission, which oversees the tax rates other subdivisions set.

  • Payoff and delinquent balances: treasurer, 419-739-6745.
  • Statement of value, homestead and parcel records: auditor.
  • Deed and mortgage recording: recorder, 419-739-6735.

Typical documents and who files them

A normal house sale generates a deed and, when the seller has a loan, a release of the mortgage. If the seller has died, an affidavit or court papers may also be needed to show who can sign. Each document is its own recording, and the page count drives the fee in the table above. Title companies bundle these filings and send them in together, which is why many sellers never meet the recorder in person.

If you are selling on your own, the practical risk is a rejected packet. A missing auditor endorsement, a legal description that differs from the last deed, or a wrong payment amount will send you back to start. One call to the recorder before you leave prevents all three problems.

Why recording matters to a seller

Recording is what puts the sale on the public record, and the recorder's index is where the next buyer's title search will find it. A deed that is signed but never recorded leaves the record showing the old owner, which leaves the buyer without a clean record of ownership. Ask the closing agent for confirmation that the deed was filed.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Phone numbers to keep handy

  • Recorder, 419-739-6735, with a fax line at 419-739-6736.
  • Treasurer, 419-739-6745, for tax payoffs and delinquent balances.
  • Auditor, for the statement of value, homestead records and the transfer fee.

Call the recorder to confirm the fee total, the treasurer for a payoff before the closing date, and the auditor before you carry the deed over. Taking the calls in that order keeps the paperwork moving in the order the county needs it, and it saves a second drive to Wapakoneta. People selling a house they inherited or one they are leaving from out of state can do most of this by phone and mail, as long as the auditor's endorsement is already on the deed.

What to bring to record a deed

Take the signed, acknowledged deed, the auditor-endorsed value statement and payment matching the county schedule. Mailing it? Phone 419-739-6735 first and confirm the total. Hold on to the last recorded deed so you can match the legal description.

Save the recorded deed and value statement with your closing papers. A title company running the closing usually sends the deed in for you, after which the index lists the new owner.

One workable order: obtain a payoff from the treasurer, prepare the deed, visit the auditor for the endorsement, then record. A cash purchase drops the lender's paperwork but not these visits or fees.

Frequently asked questions

What are the Auglaize County Recorder's hours?

Eight to half past four, Monday through Friday, at 209 S. Blackhoof St., Suite 103, Wapakoneta. The phone is 419-739-6735.

How far back do Auglaize County property records go?

To 1848. The books are kept permanently in archival form.

What fees does Auglaize County add for a deed?

State law sets $17 plus a $17 housing trust fund fee for pages one and two, then $4 plus $4 per added page. The posted county schedule shows local totals.

Which office collects the conveyance fee?

The auditor does. Sellers pay $1 or 10 cents per $100 of value or fraction, if higher, and any Chapter 322 county tax.

Where do I contest my property value?

File with the auditor, for the Board of Revision, by March 31 or the close of first-half collection, whichever is later.

Belmont County, OH Recorder of Deeds: Recording a Deed, Fees and Transfer Tax

Who records a deed in Belmont County

Deeds, mortgages and related papers go to the Belmont County recorder, whose office is in the St. Clairsville courthouse at 101 West Main Street. The job is keeping the county's land records accurate, indexed and open to the public, and more than 220 years of them are on hand. Staff can explain how the records are arranged. A title search is something you arrange separately.

Indexing is the part sellers rarely notice. Each document is indexed so a searcher can build a chain of title, showing every owner and every debt attached to the land. That is what lets a title company find a deed, a lien or a release years later. The files include farm deeds, home mortgages, oil and gas leases and military discharge papers.

Recording fees

The recorder's online calculator follows Ohio Revised Code 317.32. Belmont County does not add the optional $5 document preservation fee that the statute lets a county charge.

Belmont County Recorder fee structure
ServiceFee
First two pages of a document$34
Each additional page$8
Each indexed marginal notation (reference)$4
Document that misses the layout standard$20 extra

In the statute, the first two pages carry a $17 base fee and a second $17 for the housing trust fund. Each added page carries a $4 base and a $4 trust fund share. The trust fund share is collected under section 317.36. Other services have their own statutory rates:

  • Certified copy: a $1 base fee and a $1 trust fund fee per page, plus 50 cents and 50 cents when the recorder's seal is needed.
  • Photocopy at the counter: $1 and $1 per page.
  • Each marginal reference: $2 and $2, which matches the $4 in the table.
  • Living will or health care power of attorney: a base fee of $17 to $20 plus a matching trust fund fee.

Payment is due when the paper is handed in, except that electronic filers may settle by funds transfer or ACH afterward. Use the calculator to price a deed with several pages of legal description.

Layout rules for a deed

Documents must meet the standards in section 317.114, which the recorder summarizes on its document standards page. A document that falls short is still recorded, with a $20 surcharge.

  • Text set in at least 10-point type.
  • Sheets between letter size (8 1/2 by 11) and legal size (8 1/2 by 14).
  • Ink in black or blue, with highlighter left off the page.
  • Three inches of blank space above the text on page one, then an inch and a half on each page after.
  • One inch free along both sides and the bottom edge.

The rules do not apply to papers from a court or taxing authority, plats, exhibits, DD-214 discharge papers, state or federal documents, or any document signed before the law took effect in July 2009.

What the recorder files

Section 317.08 lists what goes into the official records, which is why more than deeds pass through the counter. Items most relevant to a house sale include:

  • Deeds and other instruments that convey land outright.
  • Mortgages, with their amendments, modifications and extensions.
  • Executory installment contracts for land that run more than a year.
  • Options to purchase, which must state a specific day and year of expiration.
  • Powers of attorney and memoranda of trust.
  • Declarations and bylaws for condominiums under Chapter 5311.
  • Easements, environmental covenants and conservation easements under the listed statutes.

A recorded mortgage, option or contract stays in the public record until a release or other instrument is recorded against it. Ask a title company to check for a paid-off mortgage whose release was never recorded.

The auditor comes first

The auditor's office sits in the same courthouse and acts on the deed before the recorder does. Under section 319.202, the auditor does not endorse a deed until the grantee or a representative submits a statement declaring the value of the property, or a statement of the reason for exemption. The deed transfer desk takes calls at 740-699-2136, and the real estate desk at 740-699-2132.

A common order in Ohio counties, which the Belmont County offices can confirm, runs like this:

  1. Draft the deed with the legal description and parcel number.
  2. Take the deed and value statement to the auditor, pay the conveyance fee and get the endorsement.
  3. Present the endorsed deed to the recorder with the fee.
  4. Receive the recorded original or a return by mail.

Ask the deed transfer desk for the current conveyance rate, since counties set their own transfer tax within the statutory limit. Ask the recorder's staff whether the recorded deed can be returned by mail.

Recording checklist for sellers

Before anything is filed, confirm that the legal description and parcel number on the new deed match the last recorded deed. Check that the seller's original signature and the notary acknowledgement are in place. Print on the right paper in the right ink, with the margins above, so the $20 surcharge does not apply. Pay the auditor first, then the recorder, and keep the receipts with your closing papers.

If you are paying off a mortgage, make sure the lender's release gets recorded after closing. The county's records will show the old loan as open until it is. Title companies usually file the release for you, but it is worth asking for confirmation. For an inherited house, bring whatever papers the title company or probate court says support the deed, since the recorder cannot repair a gap in the chain.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Belmont County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What the local market means for a seller

The typical owned home in Belmont County is valued at $154,900, and 73.6 percent of homes are lived in by their owners. Some 90.9 percent of residents were in the same house a year earlier, so title often sits unchanged for years and older deeds are common. The 2020 count was 31,618 housing units, 13.6 percent of them vacant. Owners spend a median $1,215 a month with a mortgage and $489 without one.

Population slipped 3.1 percent from April 2020 to July 2025. A house near Piedmont Lake, Belmont Lake or Barkcamp State Park is sold on the same recorded title as one in town.

If a deed has gaps, such as a missing heir or a lien never released, the recorder cannot fix it. Clear it up through a title company or attorney before a new deed goes on record. A cash buyer will want the same clean title a lender would, so the cleanup does not get skipped on a cash sale.

Frequently asked questions

What is the price of recording a deed in Belmont County?

The first two pages run $34 and every page after costs $8. A $4 fee applies to each indexed reference, and a document that misses the layout standard costs $20 more. The county does not add the optional $5 preservation fee.

Where is the Belmont County Recorder's office?

Inside the St. Clairsville courthouse, 101 West Main Street, Ohio 43950, under the same roof as the auditor and treasurer. Deed transfers start at the auditor's desk, 740-699-2136.

What paper size and ink does the recorder require?

Letter or legal paper in black or blue ink, 10 point or larger, with no highlighter. Leave 3 inches at the top of page one, 1 1/2 inches after that, and 1 inch at the sides and bottom. Missing these standards costs $20 more.

Does the recorder search my title?

No. Staff will explain how the records are arranged but will not perform title searches. Hire a title company or attorney, and expect a lender or buyer to ask for the result before closing.

Do I need the auditor before I record a Belmont County deed?

Yes, start with the auditor. The endorsement under section 319.202 depends on a statement of value or a statement giving the reason for an exemption. Ask the recorder's staff how to deliver the endorsed deed.

Recorder's location

The county sits on Ohio's southern edge, across the Ohio River from Kentucky. Deeds are recorded in Georgetown, the seat, at the Administration Building, 800 Mt. Orab Pike, Suite 151, Georgetown, Ohio 45121. Two other offices you will need share the building: the auditor in Suite 181 and the treasurer in Suite 171.

Brown County counted 43,676 residents in 2020 and is estimated at 44,397 for July 2025. Of its 19,965 housing units, 77.2 percent are owner-occupied, and the median owned home is worth $196,200.

What recording costs

Recording charges are fixed by state law. Each is split evenly between a basic fee and a contribution to the Ohio Housing Trust Fund (sections 317.32 and 317.36), and most common documents share a single price.

Deed checklist

Make sure the deed carries all nine of these before it goes anywhere:

  • The Tax Map office stamp of approval for the transfer.
  • The auditor's transfer endorsement.
  • The seller's name.
  • The buyer's name and mailing address.
  • The seller's original signature and the date, with the name typed or printed beneath.
  • A notary acknowledgement.
  • A legal description giving the county, the township or village, and the acreage.
  • The parcel identification number.
  • A preparation statement.

The recorder's staff cannot draw up documents, sell forms or give legal advice, so most sellers use a title company or attorney for the draft.

Every transfer needs a conveyance or exemption form, and every deed needs a parcel number. To avoid the non-standard fee, use type of 10 points or more on letter or legal paper in black or blue ink, no highlighting, with 1-inch margins at the sides and bottom and 3 inches clear at the top of page one.

What the recorder accepts

Several kinds of paper reach this counter in a house sale. Deeds come in many forms, among them warranty, survivorship, quit claim and sheriff's deeds, plus certificates of transfer. Mortgages arrive with their releases, assignments, assumptions, subordinations and amendments. Land contracts, affidavits, easements and leases are also recorded, along with plats and condominium drawings, powers of attorney, trusts and bills of sale. Liens fit in too: mechanic's liens, federal tax liens and homeowner association liens, plus notices of commencement.

Military service discharges, zoning resolutions with maps, annexations and street name changes are filed here as well. If something that touches your house is in the public record, from an old mortgage to a lien, it came through this counter. Whoever buys will have a title company read all of it, so an unfiled mortgage release is a loose end worth tying up before you list.

Which office first

Whether you walk in or mail it, the deed has to clear the auditor and the county's Tax Map department.

  • In person. Begin with the recorder, who checks the document against the office's requirements and fees. Then step over to the auditor's office to complete the conveyance. The Tax Map department then picks up the deed at the Engineer Building in Georgetown.
  • By mail. Mail the deed to the recorder at Suite 151 with a cover note and phone number, a check made out to Brown County Recorder, every auditor fee and form, and a self-addressed stamped envelope.

Tax Map works through documents in the order they arrive, so nobody can hurry a deed through. It checks legal descriptions, so phone the department about its requirements. After Tax Map and the auditor stamp the deed, it goes back to the recorder for recording. The auditor can answer questions at 937-378-6398.

Transfer fee and conveyance tax

Locally, the auditor charges $4.00 of transfer fee and conveyance tax per $1,000 of purchase price, plus fifty cents for each parcel number. Every transfer also needs a conveyance or exemption form.

Two laws stand behind it. The auditor's statement-of-value fee is covered by section 319.54(G)(3). A county may also levy a deed transfer tax under section 322.02, no higher than 30 cents per $100. The grantor listed on the deed owes it, and it is settled with the auditor before the deed is recorded. Exempt transfers such as family gifts use an exemption statement instead of a value statement.

If you think your transfer is exempt, ask the auditor which box to check before you sign.

Taxes owed at sale

Property tax goes to the county treasurer, 937-378-6705, and the counter is open weekdays 8:00 to 4:00. Deadlines are not fixed from year to year. Ohio House Bill 186 created an inflation cap credit on certain school district levies and pushed the latest second-half deadline later, so phone the treasurer for the current schedule.

Owners who fall behind can ask the treasurer for a payment plan, and a monthly escrow program lets owners pay ahead of the bill in smaller pieces. Paying online adds convenience fees, among them $1.50 for an electronic check. The auditor's site lists 35,315 parcels in the county and notes that the homestead exemption is the relief available to seniors, disabled owners and qualifying disabled service members.

Your title company should request the parcel's balance from the treasurer ahead of closing. Cash deals need it as well, though they can wrap up sooner with no lender in the loop.

Why the Tax Map stop matters

Many sellers expect the recorder to be the last word on a deed, but in Brown County the Tax Map department checks the legal description first. If the description is wrong or fails to fit your parcel, the deed stalls there and nothing gets recorded. That is why the recorder suggests calling the department about its requirements before you submit. Because Tax Map takes documents in the order they arrive, a deed submitted the week of closing can sit in line, so build some slack into your timeline.

For a quick sale, the practical step is to get the legal description and parcel number right in the draft, line up the auditor's forms, and submit early. Cash buyers often want a short closing, and the office stamps are the part you cannot rush.

Putting it together as a seller

The right sequence saves trips. A title company or attorney drafts the deed, legal description and parcel number included, and the seller signs before a notary. The recorder checks it and the fee, the auditor endorses it, and Tax Map stamps it. Then it returns to the recorder to go on record. Mailing it in means enclosing every auditor fee and form with the check.

Count pages before paying: $39.00 covers up to two, each added page or attachment is $8.00, and non-standard formatting adds $20.00. After recording, a certified copy gives you proof, priced at $2.00 per page plus $1.00 for the seal.

Up to two pages costs $39.00, then $8.00 for each extra page or attachment, and $20.00 more if the paper is non-standard. State law, section 317.32, is the basis.

Where do I mail a deed in Brown County?

Address it to the Brown County Recorder, 800 Mt. Orab Pike, Suite 151, Georgetown, OH 45121, and enclose a cover note with your phone number, a check payable to the recorder, the auditor's fees and forms, and a stamped return envelope.

How is the Brown County conveyance charge figured?

The rate is $4.00 for each $1,000 of price, plus fifty cents per parcel number to the auditor. Questions go to the auditor, 937-378-6398.

Will the recorder's staff write my deed?

No. The office will not draft documents, sell forms or answer legal questions. Have a lawyer or title company prepare it, then get Tax Map and auditor stamps before the recorder.

Where to record a Butler County deed

Butler County runs one recorder's office, at 130 High Street, Hamilton, OH 45011. The front desk answers at 513-887-3192, email goes to recorder@bcohio.gov, and conveyance or transfer questions go to 513-887-3154.

Sellers from Middletown, Fairfield, Oxford, Monroe, Trenton and Sharonville all file in that same building. The office promises 24 hour turnaround if you include a self addressed stamped return envelope. Its website offers a record search going back to 1987. Because recorded papers are generally public, strangers can read whatever is on your deed, so skip any personal detail the form does not call for.

Recording fees

The current schedule took effect January 1, 2025. A deed, mortgage or lease of two pages or fewer is $39.00, which includes the $5.00 preservation surcharge, and $8.00 more is charged for each further page. Section 317.32 explains the total: $17, plus $17 for the housing trust fund, on the first two pages, and up to $5 more at the county's option. Schedules get revised, so request the latest copy before you write a check.

Recorder's fees effective January 1, 2025
Document or serviceFee
Deed, mortgage, lease, up to two pages$39.00, surcharge included
Each added page$8.00
Non-standard document (ORC 317.114)$20.00 per document
Satisfaction, release, assignment or amendment$4.00 per reference
Copy of recorded document$2.00 per page

Why the auditor comes first

A deed that skipped the auditor gets turned away at the recorder. The buyer files a statement of value under section 319.202, and the auditor then notes the fee on the deed. Take a conveyance or exemption form and all parcel numbers with you.

Two laws sit behind the one rate printed on the schedule:

  • A state-set auditor fee, section 319.54(G)(3), for handling the value statement: one dollar minimum, or ten cents per $100 or part of $100.
  • An optional county charge, section 322.02, capped at thirty cents per $100, which the grantor pays the auditor.
  • What the schedule actually says: $3.00 per $1,000 of price, check to the Butler County Auditor, and 50 cents for each parcel number on the deed.

With several parcels on one deed the parcel charge multiplies, so phone 513-887-3154 before you file.

Exempt deeds

Some deeds escape the auditor's fee under section 319.54(G)(3), but you still must state the exemption reason on the filing. Family and estate sales often involve:

  • Gifts between spouses, or from a parent to a child.
  • Corrective deeds that repair a mistake in an earlier deed.
  • Deeds that only secure or release a debt.
  • Court-ordered transfers, though not a sale carried out under the order.
  • Transfers where nothing at all is paid and no gift is involved.
  • A grantee who is not a dealer and takes title only to resell soon after.

The statute lists many more, from government transfers to deeds worth $100 or less. Check with the auditor on which exemption form belongs with the deed.

Layout rules and rejected deeds

Section 317.114 covers papers prepared after June 30, 2009, and a document that violates the layout rules costs an extra $20.00. Court papers, plats, DD214s and state or federal documents do not have to follow them. The standards are:

  • Paper from 8.5 by 11 up to 8.5 by 14 inches, with text of at least 10 point.
  • Black or blue ink only, and no highlighter.
  • A one inch margin on both sides and at the bottom.
  • Page one keeps its top three inches empty for the recorder, auditor and engineer stamps.
  • Later pages need a one and a half inch top margin.

Content rules apply too. Every document needs a legal description, affidavits must name the current owner, and papers notarized in Ohio need a prepared by statement. Blanket assignments and blanket satisfactions are refused, so a lender that paid off several loans must prepare a separate release for each.

E-recording and Property Alert

You can skip the counter. Simplifile, CSC and the eRecording Partners Network all deliver deeds electronically, whichever the closing office prefers. The county's free Property Alert will email you when a paper is recorded under a name or legal description you sign up with. Landlords, owners of empty houses and heirs can catch a fraudulent filing that way.

Two fee notices are posted on the home page: the 2025 increases and an older 2022 notice on the reference fee. Packets printed before those dates may carry outdated amounts.

Recording a sale step by step

The title agent or an attorney drafts the deed, using the full legal description and parcel number. You sign in front of a notary. Someone checks the deed against the layout rules above. It goes to the auditor with the conveyance form and a check for the transfer fee, then on to the recorder for the page fee and recording. The original returns in your envelope, or the closing office gets a confirmation for an electronic filing. If you cannot make it to the counter, the title company can do all of this for you.

The county and the local market

Butler County, in southwestern Ohio, had 390,357 people in 2020 and an estimate of 400,128 for 2025, with Hamilton as seat and largest city. About 69.9 percent of homes are owner-occupied, the median value is $258,500 and median household income is $81,590. Most of the county lies in the Great Miami and Little Miami river valleys. The 1913 flood hit Hamilton and Middletown hard, with 46 percent of Hamilton under water, so ask about flood history when a house sits near the Great Miami.

Selling quickly

Selling for cash changes nothing about the route: deed, then auditor, then recorder, usually carried by the closing agent. A seller who drafts the deed personally should phone the auditor about the transfer charge and the recorder about page count before signing. Skipping a mortgage lender means no lender-driven delays, but the county steps stay. Ask the closing agent early which exemption form, if any, applies, and confirm the fee amounts the same week you close.

For an inherited house, the signer needs authority from the estate, and the title agent can say which probate documents must be attached. A seller with an old mortgage should confirm that the lender recorded its release, because an unreleased lien blocks clean title. What phone number reaches the Butler County recorder?

The main desk is 513-887-3192, or write recorder@bcohio.gov. For transfer and conveyance questions use 513-887-3154. Visit 130 High Street in Hamilton.

What does a two-page deed cost in Butler County?

$39.00 under the schedule effective January 1, 2025, with the $5.00 preservation surcharge built in. Extra pages are $8.00 each. Ask the office for its newest sheet before filing.

Whose name goes on the Butler County transfer fee check?

The Butler County Auditor. The rate is $3.00 per $1,000 of purchase price, with 50 cents more per parcel number on a deed.

Can a Butler County deed be filed electronically?

Yes, through Simplifile, CSC or the eRecording Partners Network. Your closing office picks whichever it already uses.

Will Butler County accept a deed with no legal description?

No. A legal description is required on every document, and deeds also need parcel identification numbers, or the filing is refused.

Clark County, OH Recorder of Deeds: Recording a Deed, Fees and Transfer Tax

Where to file a Clark County deed

The Clark County recorder is located in the A.B. Graham Building at 31 North Limestone Street in Springfield, OH 45502. Phone 937-521-1705 to reach the office, or send a fax to 937-328-4620. Bring the deed, the parcel numbers and a way to pay for the fees listed below.

Because the auditor and treasurer share the building, a single visit can cover the value statement, any tax payoff and the recording. Owners in New Carlisle, the villages and the townships use the same counter. The county's public records page links to a Recorder's Office Title Search and a Land Records and Property Alerts page, which lets you review any recorded deed or lien before listing or signing.

Recording fees under Ohio law

Ohio fixes recording costs in section 317.32. Every charge has two equal halves, a base fee kept by the recorder and a housing trust fund fee. A county is also allowed a preservation surcharge, up to $5 on each instrument. The statute says "up to," so find out the exact local amount and ask for the current sheet.

Clark County recording charges set by state statute
Recorder serviceBase portionTrust fund portion
Recording and indexing, pages one and two$17$17
Every added page or fraction of a page$4$4
Certified copy per page$1$1
Seal on a certification50 cents50 cents
Marginal reference (separate instrument)$2$2
Photocopy at the counter, per page$1$1

Pages are sized 8.5 by 14 inches, with the caption page counted, so a third page raises the bill.

What the auditor does before recording

Before recording, the deed goes to the auditor (section 319.202). The buyer or the buyer's agent files a value statement, either electronically or as three paper copies, and the auditor stamps the fee onto the deed. The auditor is at 31 N. Limestone Street, phone 937-521-1860. Charges that may apply:

  • The statement fee, from section 319.54(G)(3): $1, or ten cents per $100 of value (counting any part of $100), whichever is higher.
  • An optional transfer tax under section 322.02. It tops out at thirty cents per $100 and requires two public hearings before a county adopts it. The auditor can say whether Clark County has done so.
  • The recorder's own fees, shown in the table, which you pay separately at that counter.

Sellers cover the auditor's fee and any transfer tax, so look for both on your closing statement. When the property is a residential rental, the endorsement adds a reminder that the buyer owes the auditor landlord information under section 5323.02. If you are a landlord selling, tell the buyer about this early, since it becomes the new owner's task during closing.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Clark County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Tax questions on the value statement

The value statement also works as a tax checkpoint. The buyer records the seller's answer under section 323.152: either no reduction applies to this year's or last year's taxes, or a sworn estimate of the reduction. Homestead and owner-occupancy credits are typical.

A second question covers land valued for farm use. If the parcel was enrolled, the buyer must acknowledge a possible recoupment charge once it stops qualifying. Roughly a quarter of residents live in rural areas. If you own acreage, ask the auditor about enrollment ahead of signing.

Deeds exempt from the auditor's fee

Certain transfers owe no fee under section 319.54(G)(3). The filer writes the reason on the filing. A Clark County owner might meet one of these:

  • Government deals: any deed going to or coming from a federal, state or local body.
  • Tax or assessment sales for delinquency.
  • Deeds written only to secure a debt or to release one.
  • Property worth $100 or less.
  • A handover where no money or other tangible value changes hands and it is not a gift.
  • Leases, except one renewable forever.

More cases exist beyond these. For an exempt deed, the auditor supplies the exemption form that replaces the value statement.

Record searches and fraud alerts

The public records page leads to a recorder title search and to a land records site with property alerts. Sign an alert up for a name or parcel and you get a notice when a paper is filed against it. This helps most with rentals, estate houses and vacant houses, where no one may be around to see a suspicious filing.

Title companies run that same search ahead of closing. When an old mortgage was paid but the lender never recorded a release, the release must be filed first and costs its own recording fee.

Recording a sale step by step

Someone, usually the title agent or an attorney, drafts the deed with the legal description and each parcel number. You sign in front of a notary. Then the buyer's side finishes the value statement and takes it, with the deed, to the auditor. The auditor endorses the deed, and the grantor pays the fee and any transfer tax. After that the deed goes to the recorder, who counts the pages, collects the base and trust fund fees and any surcharge, and records it. Hold on to a copy of the recorded deed and the receipt, since the title company may ask for either later, and check that the recording date matches your closing date. If a lender is paid off in the same closing, confirm that its release is recorded too.

Clark County in brief

Clark County covers 403 square miles of west central Ohio. It has two cities, Springfield and New Carlisle, and Springfield sits roughly 45 miles west of Columbus and 25 miles northeast of Dayton. Population was 135,340 in July 2025, down 0.5 percent from April 2020. There are 61,550 housing units, and owners occupy 69.4 percent of homes. The median owner-occupied value is $169,900 and median monthly rent is $872. Most city residents attend Springfield City Schools, though parts of the north go to Northeastern Local or Northwestern Local and parts of the west and south to Clark-Shawnee Local.

Getting ready for a quick sale

A cash closing still goes through the auditor, then the recorder. The title agent normally carries the papers, but you can walk them over yourself. For a house that came through an estate, confirm that the person signing has authority from the probate court. Clear liens and back taxes before closing so the recording goes smoothly.

Three questions are worth settling before the signing date. Is there a county transfer tax? What will the recorder charge for the page count of your deed? Does any old mortgage still lack a recorded release? A cash sale skips lender underwriting, so these county steps are usually the only ones that set the timeline.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Which building houses the Clark County recorder?

The A.B. Graham Building, 31 North Limestone Street, Springfield, OH 45502. The office phone is 937-521-1705.

What does Ohio charge to record the first two pages of a Clark County deed?

The state charges $17 as a base fee and another $17 for the housing trust fund. On top of that a county may add as much as $5, so ask the Clark County recorder what applies.

Does Clark County levy a real property transfer tax?

A county may adopt one, up to thirty cents per $100 of value. Whether Clark County has is a question for the auditor. The seller pays it with the auditor's fee.

Are Clark County deeds searchable online?

Yes. Use the Recorder's Office Title Search or the Land Records and Property Alerts page, both linked from the county's public records page. Alerts tell you when something is filed under your name or parcel.

Do I go to the auditor or the recorder first with a deed?

Start at the auditor. That is where the buyer's value statement is filed, and the auditor endorses the deed before the recorder sees it.

What the Clermont County recorder does

The recorder files deeds, mortgages and mortgage releases and keeps them as the permanent land record. Unlike a car title, a deed is not held by the office or the bank while a loan is outstanding. The original goes back to whoever submitted it, and the recorder keeps an imaged copy.

The office is at 101 East Main Street, Batavia, Ohio 45103, open weekdays from eight in the morning to four in the afternoon. The main line is 513-732-7236. A title company normally handles recording for both sides of a sale. A seller without one can still walk the deed through three counters in Batavia, and each checks something different: the tax map office checks the legal description, the auditor checks the fee and the transfer, and the recorder checks the format of the document.

Adding a spouse, removing a former owner or fixing a spelling takes a newly drafted deed, so see an attorney first. The office records what it is handed and does not draft.

Ways to record a deed

You can e-file through an approved partner, mail the packet, or bring it in. E-filing is fastest: e-filed documents are typically recorded the same day and show online within 24 hours. Partner companies are listed on the recorder's e-filing page, and fees are paid by ACH.

  • E-file: submissions are processed from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. on business days. Anything arriving later is worked the next business day. Plats and DD214 discharge papers must come in on paper.
  • Mail: send the prepared document, a check payable to the Clermont County Treasurer, the auditor's conveyance forms, a cover letter naming a contact, and a return envelope with postage already on it. The office will not pay to send your document back.
  • In person: start at the Tax Map Office for a legal description stamp, go to the Auditor for the transfer stamp, and only then go to the recorder's counter.

Expect 1 to 14 days to finish recording, depending on how the packet arrives. Auditor fees need their own check, also made out to the county treasurer, when they travel with the deed.

Recording fees

The recorder's schedule prints a basic charge of $34.00 for the first two sides and $8.00 for each added side on 8 1/2 by 14 inch paper. Statewide base fees changed in October 2024 under Senate Bill 94, so call 513-732-7236 to confirm the figure before you write the check.

Clermont County Recorder fees as printed on the schedule
Document or serviceFee
Basic recording of deeds and mortgages$34.00 for two sides, $8.00 each added side
Marginal notation on a standard document$4 for each document referenced
Document that misses margin and font rules of ORC 317.114$20.00 extra
Large plat (24 by 36 inches)$86.40
Small plat (22 by 34 inches)$74.80
Photocopies$2.00 per page
Certified copies$2.00 per page plus $1.00 for certification

A short payment sends the paper back unrecorded. Card payments carry a 2.5% convenience charge with a $2.00 floor.

Auditor fees before recording

Transfers pass through the auditor first. The conveyance fee is $4.00 for each $1,000 of consideration, rounded up to the nearest hundred dollars, and the transfer fee is $0.50 for each parcel. Those standards were adopted under Revised Code 319.203 and took effect January 1, 2024.

Each deed travels with a state conveyance form: DTE 100 for a priced sale, or DTE 100EX where the seller claims the fee does not apply. A seller who held the Homestead reduction for the preceding or current tax year adds DTE 101, and a seller with farmland under current agricultural use valuation adds DTE 102. The auditor is at the same Batavia address and keeps weekday hours until 4:30 p.m., a half hour past the recorder's closing for new filings.

Why deeds get rejected

Four problems explain most returned deeds, and each can push a closing back by days.

  • The check is short, or it names the wrong payee.
  • The document has no legal description, or the image is too poor to read.
  • A Social Security number is printed anywhere on the instrument.
  • The deed arrives without the tax map and auditor stamps.

A paper that fails the margin and font rules in Revised Code 317.114 can still be recorded, but the $20 surcharge applies. The recorder holds plats of condominiums, subdivisions and city lots only. If the land is acreage with no lot number, the tax map survey sits with the County Engineer, and the auditor's property search shows the same surveys online.

Searching records and preventing deed fraud

Recorded documents from 1980 forward can be searched on the recorder's website. Printing from the computer at the counter costs 10 cents a page, and pulling a paper book costs $0.25 a page. A copy ordered by mail runs $2.00 a page plus a prepaid return envelope.

The recorder also runs FraudSleuth, a free account that sends an email alert when a document is recorded in a name you enter. Set up a separate profile for each spelling, such as first and last, or first, middle initial and last, with no commas or periods. An alert does not prove fraud, since another person may share the name, but it gives an owner a reason to phone 513-732-7236.

The recorder, the probate judge and the clerk of the common pleas court also promote a Good Deeds Program, aimed at helping owners lower or avoid probate court costs. An heir who inherited a Clermont County house should ask the recorder about it before listing.

Once a loan is retired, the lender sends a release, and the recorder cross-references it to the original mortgage. The clerk of courts, 513-732-7560, files foreclosure suits, and the sheriff, 513-732-7087, lists auctions.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Clermont County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Clermont County housing and taxes

The county has 91,743 housing units and 84,955 households, and about 89.3% of residents had not moved within the prior year. Median monthly owner costs run $1,677 with a mortgage and $646 without. Ask your lender how long it takes to send the release after a payoff, since the recorder indexes that paper only after it arrives.

Property tax belongs to the treasurer, whose line is 513-732-7254. The recorder will not accept tax payments and refers callers there.

Selling fast with a cash buyer

A cash sale still needs the deed recorded, so the steps above stay the same. The title company usually gathers the stamps, the conveyance form and the checks, and e-filing lets the deed record the same day in most cases. Before you sign, make sure no Social Security number appears on the deed, confirm the payee name on each check, and ask the title agent whether a mortgage release is still waiting to be recorded.

Frequently asked questions

Which office takes a Clermont County deed for recording?

The Clermont County Recorder, 101 East Main Street, Batavia, or an approved e-filing partner. In-person deeds first get stamps from the Tax Map Office and the Auditor.

How long does Clermont County take to record a deed?

The office quotes 1 to 14 days depending on the submission method. E-filed documents are typically recorded the same day and appear online within 24 hours.

What is the Clermont County conveyance fee?

The auditor charges $4.00 per $1,000 of consideration, rounded up to the nearest hundred dollars, plus a transfer fee of $0.50 per parcel. These are paid to the auditor, separate from the recorder's check.

Can the recorder write or correct my deed?

No. The office records documents but does not prepare them. Adding or changing a name needs a new deed drawn up, so contact an attorney.

Does a Clermont County deed need a Homestead statement?

Yes, when the seller was entitled to the Homestead reduction for the preceding or current tax year. DTE 101 goes with the conveyance form.

Where a Columbiana County deed is filed

The Columbiana County Recorder files deeds at the courthouse in Lisbon, phone 330-424-9517. Section 5301.25 puts a deed on the record of the county where the land sits. An unrecorded deed is treated as fraudulent against a later buyer who knew nothing about it. Recording is therefore the closing step of your sale.

Beyond deeds, the office handles mortgages, easements and military discharge papers. A new filing is recorded and can be searched right away. After quality control, staff return the originals to whoever submitted them. You can also order copies of plats and old maps, from 8 by 11 up to 36 by 80, at $2 to $5 each depending on the paper.

Recording fees and charges

Costs come from three places: the recorder, the auditor and, if one exists, the county transfer tax. Every state recording charge is split evenly between the recorder and the Ohio Housing Trust Fund. A county can add its own preservation surcharge of up to $5, and the amount varies. Call the office for the Columbiana County number before closing day.

ChargeStatutory amount
Deed filing, pages one and two (section 317.32)$17 to the recorder plus $17 to the housing trust fund
Every further page (section 317.32)$4 to the recorder plus $4 to the housing trust fund
Preservation surcharge (section 317.32)Up to $5, county decides
Auditor's conveyance fee (section 319.54)$1 or 10 cents per $100 of value, whichever is more
Auditor's entry fee (section 319.54)50 cents per transfer
County transfer tax, if levied (section 322.02)Capped at 30 cents per $100 of value

Ask the Columbiana County Auditor whether the commissioners levy the county transfer tax. The figure above is a statutory ceiling, so it may not apply here.

Why the auditor goes first

Ahead of the recorder, the auditor transfers the parcel to the buyer on the tax list and endorses the deed. Section 319.202 puts the value statement on the buyer and the conveyance fee on the seller. Any mortgage balance staying with the property counts toward value.

Two questions on the form fit a county of town lots and farms. Did the property get an owner-occupancy or homestead tax reduction? Was the land in the agricultural use valuation program, and how will a recoupment charge be handled if it leaves? Sellers of acreage in the northern townships should expect that second question.

Some transfers owe no conveyance fee. Common ones:

  • A gift between spouses, or from a parent to a child
  • A division among heirs where no money changes hands
  • A corrective deed repairing an earlier deed
  • A trust's maker moving property into or out of a revocable trust

Put the exemption reason on the value statement, and settle on the wording before you go to the auditor in Lisbon. If you are unsure which exemption fits a family transfer, the auditor's office can tell you before you sign, which is cheaper than refiling a deed that was marked wrong.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Columbiana County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What a deed must show

The seller signs the deed and acknowledges it before an official listed in section 5301.01: a judge, court clerk, county auditor, county engineer, notary or mayor. Your bank or title company probably has a notary. Section 319.20 has the auditor look for three more things:

  • A mailing address for at least one buyer
  • The volume and page, or other marker, of the seller's own deed
  • A legal description that lines up with the tax list

When only part of a parcel changes hands, the auditor divides the tax value between the piece sold and the piece kept. Any back taxes on the original parcel are then shared out by value if the buyer or the remaining owner asks.

How recording works from start to finish

The title agent or an attorney prepares the deed, and you sign before a notary. The deed and the completed value statement go to the auditor, who checks the legal description against the tax list, takes the conveyance fee and endorses the deed. From there it moves to the recorder, who charges the filing fee for the pages and any preservation surcharge, then records it. The record is searchable right away, and the original returns to whoever submitted it. If an old loan is being paid off, its release is recorded separately, so confirm with the lender that it has been sent. Keeping these steps in order avoids a bounced deed and a delayed closing. Ask the auditor and the recorder at the counter how each wants its payment handed in, and bring a second form of payment in case one office refuses a check.

The county and its housing

The county sits along Ohio's eastern border. Pennsylvania lies to the east, Mahoning County to the north, and the Ohio River runs about 20 miles along the south. Its 534 square miles hold 18 townships. Level, fertile farmland covers the north, while the south is hilly, with limestone soils that suit pasture, orchards and timber. After Salem, the largest cities are East Liverpool and Columbiana.

The July 2025 population estimate is 99,377, which is 2.5% under the April 2020 base. Counted housing units total 46,220 and households 41,459, with 72.7% of homes owner-occupied. Median home value is $151,600, median monthly rent is $756 and median household income is $58,180. A house on a village street in Lisbon and a farmhouse in Madison Township will sit far apart, so use a written offer or local appraisal for the real number on your own property.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Columbiana County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Preparing before you go to Lisbon

Each item here takes about one phone call, and doing them a few days ahead keeps the closing on schedule:

  • Get the amount owed on the parcel from the county treasurer, so the title company can pay it from the proceeds
  • Have any lender record the release of an old mortgage
  • If the owner has died, ask the probate court which papers allow a sale and who signs
  • Match the legal description on your deed to the tax record
  • Agree on who covers any farm-use recoupment or open assessment

The same route applies when a house is sold as-is for cash. The deed still passes through the auditor first and the recorder second. Salem, East Liverpool, Columbiana and the villages all file in the same Lisbon office, so a seller in Wellsville or Leetonia does not need a separate local filing. Bring the signed deed, the completed value statement and a way to pay each office, and ask at the counter how the recorder and the auditor want the payments handed in.

Frequently asked questions

Can I reach the Columbiana County Recorder by phone?

Yes, at 330-424-9517. The office is at the courthouse in Lisbon.

What is the preservation surcharge on a deed filed in Columbiana County?

State law lets a county charge up to $5 per document, and the amount varies by county. Ask the office for the current Columbiana County charge.

Does the buyer or the seller pay the conveyance fee?

The seller pays it under section 319.202, while the buyer files the statement of value. If the county levies a transfer tax, the seller pays that as well.

Can relatives transfer a house without the conveyance fee?

Often, yes. Section 319.54 exempts gifts between spouses or between a parent and child, and splits among heirs when no money is paid. The reason must be stated on the value statement.

What if the deed is signed but never filed?

The deed is still a signed document, but section 5301.25 treats it as fraudulent against a later purchaser with no knowledge of it. Filing with the recorder closes that gap.
