Where a Crawford County deed is recorded

The Crawford County Recorder's office in Bucyrus, the county seat, records every deed in the county. It serves as the official land records office for all real estate here, and its number is 419-562-6961. Staff follow sections 317.11 and 317.112 of the Ohio Revised Code, which control how a document must look before it is accepted.

One local step catches sellers off guard. A document that transfers real estate must be approved before it is filed, and that approval begins at the Crawford County Engineer's office, not at the recorder. Staff there cannot offer legal advice, which is why an attorney or title agency should draft the deed. Fill-in-the-blank forms exist, but whoever submits one is responsible for meeting every legal requirement.

Recording fees for a deed

Senate Bill 94 added $5 to recording costs starting January 1, 2025. Today a standard deed costs $39 for pages one and two, then $8 for every further page, and a printed side is one page. Reference fees of $4 and the office's formatting standards still apply on top.

Pages in the deedRecorder's fee
1 or 2$39.00
3$47.00
4$55.00
5$63.00
6$71.00
10$103.00

A few other charges can turn up in a sale. Recording the release of a lien costs $4, a federal tax lien filing costs $5, and each marginal notation on a document adds $4 to the regular fee. Plats and condominium drawings are charged by size: $0.10 per square inch, minimum $40 a page. When you go in, bring separate checks for the recorder, the auditor and the treasurer.

What the recorder wants to see on a deed

The recorder publishes an eleven-point checklist. Sellers most often trip on these:

  • An original document, signed and notarized
  • A prepared-by statement on any deed drawn up in Ohio
  • The complete legal description, which the office uses to index the deed by location
  • Book and page references to earlier recordings, in any later document
  • Clear labels on every exhibit and schedule
  • The preparer's name and address, a return address and a phone number for minor corrections
  • A self-addressed stamped envelope, so the original comes back without postage charges

Pages must be legible enough to scan, and that is the filer's responsibility. Check the work again before you go, fees especially, since a miscount is a common reason for rejection.

The office indexes by legal description, not street address. If all you have is a house number, find the owner name and transfer date on the Crawford County Auditor's search page first, then bring that to the recorder.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Crawford County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What the Crawford County Auditor adds to a sale

The auditor decides the value your tax bill is based on and receives the conveyance paperwork. Property is revalued every three years under Ohio Department of Taxation rules, and tax is figured on 35% of market value. Crawford County has 54 taxing districts, each with its own rate. An owner pays no more than 10 mills of unvoted levies, and the voted portion depends on local elections.

At a sale, the buyer files a value statement under section 319.202, and the seller pays the conveyance fee plus any transfer tax the commissioners have levied under section 322.02. The conveyance fee in section 319.54 is $1 or 10 cents per $100, whichever is greater. State law caps any county transfer tax at 30 cents per $100, and the auditor can tell you the local rate.

Other auditor rules a seller may run into:

  • A value complaint goes to the Board of Revision, with the filing window running January 1 to March 31.
  • New construction or an improvement over $2,000 has to be reported, and skipping that can bring a 50% penalty on the owner's taxes.
  • Building permits come from the cities of Bucyrus and Galion, Jackson, Jefferson and Polk townships, and the villages of Crestline, New Washington, North Robinson and Chatfield.
  • Farmland in the current agricultural use program pays a one-time $25 enrollment fee.
  • A manufactured home buyer has 30 days to register with the auditor or face a $100 penalty.

Crawford County housing and population

North central Ohio's Crawford County has two cities, Bucyrus (the largest) and Galion. Population was 42,025 in 2020 and is estimated at 41,896 for July 2025. In 2020, 65.9% of residents lived in urban areas and 34.1% in rural ones, which helps explain why a Bucyrus lot and a township farmhouse can be priced so differently.

The typical owner-occupied home is worth $136,700 on the 2020 to 2024 figures, with 73.1% of homes lived in by their owners. Median gross rent is $794. Just 3 building permits were counted in 2025, which means buyers mostly shop among existing houses. A written cash offer or a local appraisal prices a specific house better than a countywide median. Sellers in Galion, Crestline, Bucyrus and the townships all record at the same Bucyrus office.

What is the order of steps for a seller?

The trip has three stops. First comes the Crawford County Engineer's office, where the transfer is approved. Second comes the auditor, who receives the buyer's value statement and the seller's conveyance fee. Last comes the recorder, who accepts the finished deed, collects the page-based fee and indexes the document by its legal description.

Because each office wants a separate payment, carrying three checks saves a second trip. If the deed is going by mail, include the stamped return envelope and a contact number so staff can phone about a small fix instead of rejecting the package. Questions about which stop comes next can go to the recorder at 419-562-6961, though staff will not draft documents or advise on legal wording.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Crawford County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Settling liens and taxes before you go

The recorder records liens but does not release them. Property tax matters belong to the Treasurer, and court filings belong to the Clerk of Courts. Before the deed is filed, a seller should sort out the following with the right office:

  • Ask the County Treasurer for the unpaid tax figure, so the title company can pay it from the proceeds.
  • Ask the lender to file a release of any old mortgage, since the recorder only records it.
  • Check with the Clerk of Courts for judgments tied to the owner.
  • Ask the County Engineer's office about the transfer approval step.
  • Match the legal description to the one on your last deed.

The same steps apply when the buyer pays cash and takes the house as-is. A cash sale can close faster, but the title still has to be clear, and a missed release can hold up the filing.

Frequently asked questions

What is the phone number for the Crawford County Recorder?

The office number is 419-562-6961. The office is in Bucyrus.

How much does it cost to record a three-page deed in Crawford County?

The fee table shows $47.00 for three pages. That is $39 for the first two pages and $8 for the third, before any other charges the document triggers.

Does the recorder remove liens from my title?

No. The office records certain liens but does not release them. Property tax liens go through the County Treasurer, and court matters through the Clerk of Courts.

Where does the transfer process start in Crawford County?

At the County Engineer's office. A document that transfers real estate has to be approved there before it moves on.

Can I search records by street address at the recorder?

Not directly. The recorder indexes by legal description, so look up the owner name or transfer date on the County Auditor's search page if you only have an address.

Which office files a Darke County deed?

The Darke County Recorder does. The office is in the Greenville courthouse at 504 S. Broadway, answers at 937-547-7390, and keeps weekday hours of 8 to 4.

ORC Chapter 317 governs the office, which the county treats as its official keeper of records. Besides deeds and mortgages, the recorder takes mechanic liens, powers of attorney, recognizance bonds, IRS liens, corporate franchise liens and partnership papers. Its job is to record what you bring, so a deed drafted by you or your attorney has to be finished before it arrives.

What must be done to a deed before it is accepted

A deed needs the grantor's signature, an acknowledgment and the auditor's stamp before it goes to the recorder. ORC 5301.01 has the grantor acknowledge the signature in front of an authorized official (a judge or clerk of a court of record, county auditor, county engineer, notary public or mayor), who then certifies it.

The usual order in Darke County:

  1. Draft the deed using a legal description that fits the parcel. The county engineer keeps the tax maps and reviews deeds, land transfers and lot splits for proper boundary descriptions.
  2. Sign and acknowledge the deed.
  3. Take the deed and a conveyance fee statement to the Darke County Auditor on the courthouse first floor. The auditor's forms page lists DTE 100 for a standard conveyance, DTE 100EX for an exempt one, DTE 101 for homestead property and DTE 102 for farmland valued at its agricultural use.
  4. Pay the auditor the conveyance fee and any county transfer tax, get the stamp, and take the deed to the recorder.

Bring these to the auditor's counter:

  • The signed and acknowledged deed with its legal description
  • A completed conveyance fee statement on the right DTE form
  • Money for the conveyance fee and any county transfer tax

Splitting a lot off a larger parcel adds a step. Call the zoning inspector at 937-547-7381 with split questions. Building permits across the unincorporated area, Greenville and many villages go through the county building regulation office at 937-547-7379.

Darke County recording charges

The schedule comes from ORC 317.32. Through page two, a standard deed or mortgage costs $17 plus an equal $17 housing trust fund fee, and each later page costs $4 plus $4. A county can tack on a preservation surcharge of up to $5 a document, so ask the recorder whether Darke County collects it and how much.

StepOfficeWhat you leave with
Boundary checkCounty engineerSign-off on the legal description
Value statement and feesCounty auditorStamped deed
FilingCounty recorderRecorded instrument

The same statute prices copies. Per page, a certified copy runs a $1 base fee plus a $1 housing trust fund fee, a recorder's seal on the certification adds $0.50 and $0.50, and a marginal reference entered through a separate instrument costs $2 and $2. Charges fall due when the paper is presented, and each page, caption page included, counts at its 8.5 by 14 inch size or fraction of one.

Who pays the transfer costs?

The seller. ORC 319.202(D) puts the conveyance fee under section 319.54(G)(3) on the grantor, along with any transfer tax the commissioners adopted under Chapter 322. The ceiling on a county transfer tax is thirty cents per hundred dollars of value, payable to the auditor ahead of recording (ORC 322.02). Ask the Darke County auditor whether one is in place.

On a sale, value is the entire price paid or payable, including any mortgage or vendor's lien. For a gift it means the likely open-market price, and willful falsification is prohibited. The auditor's site has a calculator that takes a parcel count and a sale price and includes the parcel transfer fee, so run your numbers before closing.

What the auditor checks on a deed

The stamp tells the recorder the paperwork is complete. Under ORC 319.202 the buyer, or someone acting for the buyer, files the value statement. The auditor then marks the deed with the fee and compliance, keeps the original, and sends the tax commissioner a copy noting the latest assessed value.

Two sets of affirmations ride on that statement. One asks about a homestead or owner-occupancy reduction taken on this year's or last year's tax. The other covers agricultural valuation. If either answer is yes, both sides sign a sworn instrument accounting for the reduction or the recoupment charge. For residential rental property, the indorsement also reminds the buyer of landlord information due under ORC 5323.02.

A family transfer or other exempt deed only needs the reason for the exemption. Pick the exempt form (DTE 100EX) and state the reason plainly.

What to expect on filing day

If the paperwork is in order, the visit is short. The auditor reviews the statement, takes the conveyance fee and any county transfer tax, and stamps the deed. You then walk the stamped deed to the recorder, who charges the page-based fee and records the instrument. Ask whether the office wants cash, a check or both, since each office collects its own payment.

Mortgage releases follow a different path. The recorder only records a release, and the lender is the party that files it, so a seller with a paid-off loan should ask the lender to confirm it was recorded. When the deed comes back, store it with your sale file, because the recorded copy proves that title passed to the buyer.

Searching Darke County land records online

The recorder's online search of land records begins at May 1996, and the office has been extending the index back to January 1980. Call to ask how far back it runs now and how to view older books in person.

A free Property Fraud Alert subscription warns an owner when a document is recorded against the property, a useful safeguard for anyone with an empty house.

  • Parcel searches, the county map and the sales report live on the auditor's website, not at the recorder.
  • Questions about value or tax on a parcel go to the auditor. Questions about what is already of record go to the recorder.

Land in Darke County: what a seller should know

The 2020 count was 51,881 residents. Land that families have held for decades makes the legal description important, and the county engineer reviews deeds for proper boundary descriptions. Cities, villages and townships hold zoning authority for their own ground, and a house in an unzoned township answers to the township trustees, so confirm that before you list. The parcel record shows the school district for tax purposes.

A tidy deed package saves time. Before you go, compare the legal description with your last deed, get any tax payoff from the treasurer, and have your lender record a release of an old mortgage. A cash buyer can close quickly, but the stamp and the filing still follow the same order: engineer, auditor, then recorder.

Frequently asked questions

How do I reach the Darke County Recorder?

Call 937-547-7390 or go to the courthouse at 504 S. Broadway in Greenville. The office is open weekdays.

Is the Darke County filing charge based on page count?

Yes. Ohio sets one price for the first two pages and a lower price per added page, and a preservation surcharge of up to $5 may apply on top. ORC 317.32 has the list.

Which comes first in Darke County, auditor or recorder?

The auditor. The conveyance fee statement and fee earn the stamp, and the recorder then files the stamped deed.

Is a homemade deed acceptable in Darke County?

It can be brought in, but it needs a signature, an acknowledgment before an authorized official, a description the engineer's tax maps support and the auditor's stamp. A title company or attorney can prepare it.

Can older Darke County deeds be found online?

Online search starts with May 1996, and the office has been extending the index to January 1980. Ask what year it begins now.

What the Defiance County Recorder handles

Every paper that conveys or burdens land in Defiance County ends up in the recorder's permanent files. The office also accepts military discharge papers (DD214s), keeps them from public view, and issues free veteran ID cards to honorably discharged service members without an appointment.

Filing is the office's job. Staff do not run searches for the public, confirm for you that a mortgage was cancelled, or prepare liens. Anyone may come in and search the public records, and staff will help. An online document index lets a seller look for a recorded mortgage release before listing.

Landowners can also sign up for a free property fraud alert at propertyfraudalert.com, or through the hotline number printed on the recorder's page.

Defiance County recording charges

The office charges $34 for the first two pages of a document and $8 for each page after those. A $5 document preservation fee joined the schedule on January 1, 2025, after Ohio Senate Bill 94, which took effect October 24, 2024 and let counties charge up to that amount per document.

Papers that carry their own statutory fees skip the extra $5. The recorder names federal tax liens, state job and family services liens, plats, township zoning documents and UCCs. Recording is paid in cash or by check only. A page counts toward the fee if it has writing on it.

ChargeAmount
Pages one and two together$34
Every page after page two$8

Marginal notation on a release or assignment$4
Copies made by the public$0.25 per copy
Auditor's conveyance fee$4.00 per thousand
Auditor's transfer fee$0.50 per parcel

Which approvals does a Defiance County deed need first?

Sellers start at the auditor, because no deed reaches the recorder without the auditor's stamp. The sequence runs like this:

  1. The county engineer's office checks the legal description, locates the parcel on the tax maps and stamps its approval with a date and signature. The engineer's number is 419-782-4751.
  2. For certain splits or subdivisions of less than 20 acres, or with a leftover parcel under 20 acres, the Defiance County Planning Commission must also approve.
  3. A conveyance form travels with the deed. A sale for money pays $4.00 per $1000 at transfer unless an exemption applies, and any deed moving an interest, exempt or not, adds $0.50 for each parcel number.
  4. The auditor confirms that the grantor matches the tax duplicate and that the descriptions agree, then stamps the deed with the fee collected and the parcel count.
  5. The stamped deed goes to the recorder.

A land split adds a tax step. After the engineer approves it, the real estate assessors in the auditor's office work out the tax effect of the split, looking at items such as buildings being transferred and any current agricultural use recoupment charge that may apply to the land. Where a split would leave a parcel under 20 acres, expect the planning commission to be involved too.

Bring these on the day you record:

  • The stamped deed, with its fee paid at the auditor
  • Cash or a check for the recording charge
  • A self-addressed stamped envelope if you want the original mailed back

Call the auditor at 419-782-1926 about conveyance requirements before recording, and 419-784-3111 for property value, sales history and tax questions.

Page and margin rules for a deed

Check the paper against the recorder's list before you carry it in. A printed or typed name must sit beside each signature, and a "prepared by" line must appear (ORC 317.11). Notary seals must be present, the whole document must be in English or come with a certified translation, and pages must reproduce legibly.

  • Ink is black or blue, type is at least 10 point, and nothing is highlighted.
  • The first page keeps a three-inch blank band at the top, and later pages keep one and a half inches.
  • All pages keep one inch clear at the bottom and both sides.
  • Sheets run from 8.5 by 11 up to 8.5 by 14 inches.
  • A self-addressed stamped envelope goes in for the return.

The county engineer must approve some legal descriptions before recording, and releases and assignments need a legal description. Reference earlier recorded documents when a marginal notation is needed. The office lists a turnaround of three days.

How the county fees relate to the Ohio statute

The county's $34 and $8 figures are the sum of two statutory pieces. ORC 317.32 sets a base fee of $17 for the first two pages plus a $17 housing trust fund fee, and $4 plus $4 for each page after that. The office forwards the housing trust fund share quarterly and divides the rest between the general fund and the technology fund.

The statute also names smaller items a seller may meet. A certified copy costs a base fee of $1 plus a $1 housing trust fund fee per page, a recorder's seal on a certification adds $0.50 plus $0.50, and a marginal reference entered by a separate instrument costs $2 plus $2. Defiance County lists a flat $4 for marginal notations on a release or assignment, so ask which figure applies to a mortgage release you plan to record.

Recording is often done by mail, so the practical points are short. Send cash or a check, add a self-addressed stamped envelope, and allow the three days the office lists for turnaround. A call to the office confirms the total before you mail anything.

Defiance County housing snapshot

Defiance County sits in northwest Ohio along the Indiana line, and the city of Defiance is the county seat and largest city. The 2020 count showed 38,286 people and 16,539 housing units, with 6.4 percent vacant. Of occupied homes, 76.1 percent were owner-occupied and 23.9 percent rented. About 46.4 percent of residents lived in urban areas and 53.6 percent in rural ones, so a seller may hold a town lot or a house on acreage.

Sellers with long-owned parcels should confirm legal descriptions with the engineer before a deed goes to the auditor, since that office will not transfer a deed without the approval stamp. Cash buyers and financed buyers face the same stamp, fee and filing sequence.

Before you list, check the online document index for your mortgage release, collect the numbers for the engineer and the auditor, and decide who will carry the deed. If a title company is handling the sale, ask what it will submit for you and what you must sign in person. Doing this early shortens the gap between signing and recording.

Frequently asked questions

What will a Defiance County deed cost to file?

Expect $34 for the first two pages, $8 for each page beyond those, and the $5 preservation fee in force since January 1, 2025. Pay with cash or a check.

Does the auditor see a Defiance County deed first?

Yes. The engineer approves the legal description, then the auditor collects its fees and stamps the deed, and only then does the recorder file it.

What rate does the Defiance County auditor charge on a sale?

The conveyance fee is $4.00 per thousand and the transfer fee is $0.50 per parcel. An exempt deed skips the first but still carries the second.

Will the recorder's staff correct a flawed deed?

No. The office may not engage in the unauthorized practice of law, which rules out drafting papers or giving legal advice. An attorney or title company should prepare the deed.

Can I look up Defiance County records from home?

Yes, through the online document index in AVA Land Records. A seller can use it to see if a mortgage release was recorded, then visit the office for anything the index lacks.

What the Delaware County recorder does for a home seller

The recorder's office indexes all real estate and personal property records for Delaware County, collects the filing fees, and keeps military service discharge records. When a house sells, two papers land on its desk: the deed that gives the buyer title, and the satisfaction that shows the seller's lender has been paid.

Visit 145 N. Union St., Delaware, OH 43015, or call (740) 833-2460. Recordings are accepted on weekdays from 8:30 to 4:30, holidays excluded. The cutoff for submitting documents is 4:00 p.m., and an exam room is open to the public during the same hours. The recorder's site also offers a recorded document search, a military graves search and a property fraud page.

What does filing a two-page deed cost in Delaware County?

The fee page lists $39.00 for the first two pages of a deed, mortgage, lease, power of attorney, release or assignment on paper 8.5 by 14 inches or smaller, and $8.00 for every page after that. A footnote explains that the $39.00 already contains the $5.00 preservation surcharge permitted by ORC 317.32.

Document or serviceCharge
Basic instrument, first 2 pages$39.00, then $8.00 per added page

Behind these numbers is ORC 317.32, which splits the first-two-pages price into a $17 base fee and a $17 housing trust fund fee. Each added page carries $4 plus $4, and a county may add a preservation surcharge of up to $5. If you mail a document, enclose a postage-paid return envelope or enough cash to cover the postage.

The auditor comes before the recorder

When a county levies a real property transfer tax, ORC 322.02 makes the grantor named in the deed pay it to the county auditor at delivery of the deed, ahead of presenting the deed to the recorder. The buyer also files a statement of value with the auditor under ORC 319.202 before the deed is endorsed.

State law caps a county's transfer tax at thirty cents per hundred dollars of value. Because the commissioners set the rate by resolution, call the auditor at (740) 833-2900 close to the closing date to learn the one in force.

  • Auditor first: value statement, any transfer tax, and the endorsement on the deed.
  • Recorder second: the endorsed deed, the page-count fee, and a return envelope if the package is mailed.
  • Same building: both offices share 145 N. Union St., so a hand delivery needs only one trip.
  • Last stop: the online document search, to see that the deed shows against the right parcel.

Other papers the recorder files

The fee schedule reads like a map of what can cloud or clear a title. Federal tax liens cost $5.00 to record in original, corrected, refiled, partial release or subordination form, and a release costs $3.00. Uniform Commercial Code filings such as fixture filings and continuation statements cost $12.00 plus $4.00 for each name indexed, and a UCC search costs $20.00.

Other entries a homeowner may meet include zoning resolutions at a $50.00 flat fee, zoning amendments at $20.00, attested accounts that place liens on public funds, a motor vehicle bond lien at $10.00, and Bureau of Workers' Compensation releases, which are free. A bill of sale in a bulk sale carries no fee either.

Ask the title company which of these appear against your name before you list. A federal tax lien or a stale mortgage that was never released can slow down a buyer's lender, and the recorder's online search shows what is on file.

Warranty deeds and quitclaim deeds

The recorder's Real Estate Recording page borrows definitions from a real estate dictionary. A general warranty deed is one where the grantor agrees to protect the grantee against any other claim to title and adds further promises. A special warranty deed narrows that promise to anyone claiming by, from, through or under the grantor, with no warranty against title defects from before the grantor owned the land.

A quitclaim deed passes along only whatever rights the grantor has, without naming those rights and without warranties of ownership. Recording means entering an instrument in the public books, which gives notice to the world. The sale contract and the title agent decide which deed form a sale uses. The recorder's office does not pick it.

Where Delaware County deeds are recorded

Every parcel in the county records here, whichever town it sits in. The city of Delaware is the seat, and Powell, Sunbury and the Delaware County portions of Dublin and Westerville are also inside the county, along with the villages of Ashley, Galena, Ostrander and Shawnee Hills.

  • A deed for a Powell, Sunbury or Delaware house goes to the same recorder as one for a township farm.
  • Dublin and Westerville lie partly in other counties, so a mailing address in either one does not tell you which recorder applies. Check the parcel record first.
  • The auditor's GIS property search shows which parcel number to cite on the paperwork.
Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Delaware County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

A seller's checklist before recording

The deed is only the last step. Before it is filed, confirm that your old mortgage has a recorded satisfaction, since a lender's release is a separate paper from the deed. Gather the parcel number from the auditor's GIS search, ask the auditor what transfer tax applies, and decide who will carry the package. A title company usually handles all of this for a sale.

Cash sales skip the buyer's lender, but the deed still goes through the auditor and then the recorder, and the same fee schedule applies. When the package is accepted, use the online document search to confirm the deed appears against the right parcel, and keep a copy for your own files. If something looks wrong, such as a wrong parcel or a misspelled name, call the recorder at (740) 833-2460 before the closing date passes, because fixing an error later can mean a second filing and a second set of fees.

Households here have high ownership costs: median monthly owner costs are $2,493 with a mortgage and $986 without, and median gross rent is $1,492. Population grew from 174,214 in 2010 to 214,124 in 2020 and is estimated at 242,032 for 2025.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Delaware County recording fee for a three-page deed?

The schedule posts $39.00 for the first two pages and $8.00 for each page after that, so the third page is billed at the $8.00 rate. Marginal references on releases and assignments cost $4.00 each and are billed separately.

When must a document reach the Delaware County recorder?

The submission cutoff is 4:00 p.m., while the office itself works from 8:30 to 4:30 on weekdays. Holidays are excluded.

Does the Delaware County recorder charge for a veteran's discharge?

No. The fee schedule marks a veteran's discharge, and an expunged discharge, as no fee.

Who pays Delaware County's transfer tax at closing?

State law puts it on the grantor, meaning the seller named in the deed, and it goes to the auditor before recording. Ask the auditor's office at (740) 833-2900 what rate applies.

Can I look up Delaware County deeds from home?

Yes. The recorder's home page links a recorded document search. Use it to check that your deed or a mortgage release was recorded.

Erie County, OH Recorder of Deeds: Recording a Deed, Fees and Transfer Tax

  • Erie County, OH Recorder of Deeds: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Where the Erie County recorder is and what it handles

The Erie County Recorder's Office is in the Erie County Office Building at 247 Columbus Avenue, Suite 225, Sandusky, OH 44870, phone (419) 627-7686. The counter is open Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. and closes for the usual holidays, including Juneteenth, Columbus Day and the day after Thanksgiving. When a holiday lands on a Saturday the office closes the Friday before, and a Sunday holiday means closing the Monday after.

The office records deeds, mortgages, releases and similar papers, and it also takes military discharges. It is not a place to get paperwork drafted. Staff are not attorneys, keep no forms, run no lien or title searches, and cannot advise on how to prepare a legal document.

What does recording a deed cost in Erie County?

Recording costs the same in every Ohio county and is charged by page: $34 total for the first two printed pages, then $8 for each page after that. A sheet printed on both sides counts as two pages. A two-page document costs $34 and a three-page one $42.

Type of chargeAmount
First two printed pages$34 total
Each page after the first two$8
Marginal reference, such as an assignment or release$4 per document reference
Affidavit for transfer (successor trustee)No $4 marginal fee
Document that fails Ohio Revised Code standards$20 nonconformance fee
Copies not available free online$2 per page

Copy requests paid by card over the phone carry a processor charge, a $2 minimum and up to 2 or 3 percent of the total, and American Express is not taken. Every charge in the office is fixed by the Ohio Revised Code, so staff cannot waive or negotiate them.

What an Erie County deed must contain

The office publishes Basic Recording Requirements that spell out what gets a document turned away. Originals must be legible with original signatures, and photocopies are refused. Staff check a long list before they stamp anything.

  • A full legal description beginning "Situated in" the city or township, county and state, not the short description from the auditor's site or a tax bill.
  • A printed or typed name under every signature, and a full notary clause with the notary's stamp or printed name and the commission expiration date.
  • Both a first and last name for every party, with marital status. The office recommends that the spouse of a married grantor sign and be notarized, even only to release dower.
  • A "Prepared By" line naming whoever drafted the document, and every attached exhibit that the document mentions.
  • No Social Security numbers or tax ID numbers. The office redacts the number on an original death certificate itself, and the certificate must stay unmarked.
  • For a signer acting under a power of attorney, the Erie County recording number of the power, or the power recorded just ahead of the deed in the same package.

White-out is not allowed. The $20 nonconformance fee applies when a document misses these standards, which is why staff suggest stopping in first so they can look it over.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Erie County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Can I mail a deed or record it electronically?

A deed that transfers property cannot be mailed. Any document that transfers property, or a transfer on death designation or confirmation, must be stamped by the Transfer office and then carried in or recorded electronically, never sent by mail, UPS or FedEx. The office can e-record almost every document type, transfer deeds included, for filers with an account at one of its listed vendors: ePN-eRecording Partners Network, Simplifile or CSC.

Papers that do not need the Transfer stamp can come by mail with a self-addressed stamped envelope large enough for everything. Each document goes through recording, indexing and verification before it is mailed back, and the usual turnaround is one to two business days before it goes out in the mail.

Conveyance and transfer fees on an Erie County sale

The county auditor sets the conveyance fee at $4.00 per thousand dollars of the sale price, charged on real estate and on manufactured homes. A separate transfer fee is $0.50 per line. The rate history runs from $1 per $1,000 in May 1969 to March 1990, rising in steps to $4 per $1,000 since February 1994.

An exemption has to meet a qualification on the state's DTE 100EX form, and the auditor's site has a Conveyance Fee Calculator that asks for the number of properties and the sale amount. The auditor's office is at 247 Columbus Avenue, Room 210, phone (419) 627-7746. Ask the recorder's staff where to get the Transfer stamp before you walk a deed to Suite 225.

Finding a recorded deed or a mortgage release

Start with the free online search at the county's self-service site. Indexing and images go back to 1990, with older documents being added, and you can download or print images for free. Enter the last name first, then the first name, such as Smith Jane, in the Both Names box.

Two points help sellers. The recorder does not hold your deed: you receive the original recorded deed at purchase, and the office keeps copies only. A paid-off mortgage produces a separate release or satisfaction, so a seller who cannot find proof of a payoff should look for that recorded document.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Erie County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Erie County property tax and your deed

The county bills a year behind, and taxes follow the property, not the owner, so the balance on a parcel matters at closing. Real estate bills for 2027 are due February 19 and July 16. The treasurer's office is at 247 Columbus Avenue, Suite 115, phone (419) 627-7701.

The treasurer sorts the county's school districts by whether parcels may get the Inflation Cap Credit created by House Bill 186.

  • May receive it: Bellevue, Edison, Firelands, Huron, Monroeville, Vermilion and Western Reserve.
  • Will not receive it: Kelleys Island, Margaretta, Perkins and Sandusky.
  • Homestead: the auditor lists a $40,000 household income threshold for applicants who are 65 or older or disabled.
  • Overdue parcels: sold only at sheriff's sale.

Erie County housing snapshot

Erie County sits on the Lake Erie shore, and 374 of its 626 square miles are water, which leaves 252 square miles of land. Sandusky is the seat and largest city. The 2025 estimate is 73,296 people, down 3.1% from 2020, and owners occupy 71.9% of homes. A typical owner-occupied home is worth $199,700, and median gross rent is $933. Price a particular house with a written offer or a local appraisal instead of a countywide number.

Before you record, check the legal description, find your mortgage release, and decide whether you will walk the deed in or e-record it through a title company. A cash buyer does not change those steps.

Frequently asked questions

How much does the Erie County recorder charge for a two-page deed?

The charge is $34 for the first two printed pages. Each further page costs $8, and a document printed on both sides of one sheet counts as two pages.

Can I mail an Erie County deed to the recorder?

No, not if it transfers property. Those documents must be stamped by the Transfer office and delivered in person or recorded electronically through a listed vendor.

What is the Erie County conveyance fee?

The auditor charges $4.00 per thousand dollars of the sale price, plus a $0.50 per line transfer fee. Call the auditor at (419) 627-7746 to confirm figures for your closing.

Does the Erie County recorder keep my original deed?

No. The recorder keeps copies only, and you receive the original recorded deed when you buy. A mortgage payoff produces its own release document.

What time does the Erie County recorder open and close?

The office is open Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Closed days include Juneteenth, Columbus Day, Thanksgiving, the day after Thanksgiving and Christmas Day.

Recorder's office location and hours

The Recorder sits in the Administrative Courthouse at 210 East Main Street, Suite 205, in Lancaster. Weekday hours run 8:00 am to 4:00 pm, and you can call 740-652-7100. Everything that becomes part of the county's permanent public record lands here, including deeds, mortgages, leases, liens, plats, powers of attorney and military discharges.

The land records index goes back to 1800, and scanned documents can be searched online from January 1980 on. Employees will tell you which desk to visit. They will not do your searching, help write a document or give you recording forms, so the deed itself comes from a closing agent or an attorney.

  • Look up deeds and mortgages through the land records link on the Recorder page.
  • The same page has free sign-ups for a Property Fraud Alert and a Notary Fraud Alert.
  • Phone ahead before a trip. Short closures, such as a one-hour midday closing on a single day, get posted on that page.

The Auditor comes first

Take the deed to the County Auditor before the Recorder. The transfer is completed there, and the recording step comes afterward. Most sales need two papers at the Auditor: the deed, plus a conveyance fee statement on Ohio form DTE 100 (DTE 100EX if an exemption applies).

The Auditor's Map Room compares the legal description with county conveyance standards before accepting the deed. You can email a prepared deed to the Map Room for that approval, and the transfer cannot proceed without it. After approval, leave the deed and statement at the transfer desk, 108 N. High Street in Lancaster, or mail the set to the Auditor marked Attn: Conveyance.

Ohio puts the statement of value on the buyer or the buyer's representative, and the conveyance fee on the seller. Value is everything paid or promised for the property, and that includes the mortgage. A gift is valued at its estimated open market price. R.C. 319.202 prohibits knowingly writing a false value.

Transfer and recording costs

You will pay two separate bills. One is the Auditor's transfer and conveyance charges. The other is the Recorder's fee, which grows with the number of pages.

Fees on a Fairfield County deed
ChargeRatePaid to
Transfer fee$.50 per parcel, exempt and non-exempt transfers alikeCounty Auditor
Conveyance fee$4.00 per thousand of consideration when money changes handsCounty Auditor
Recording, first two pages$17 base fee plus $17 housing trust fund feeCounty Recorder
Recording, each added page$4 base fee plus $4 housing trust fund feeCounty Recorder
Document preservation surchargeUp to $5, if the county charges itCounty Recorder

The figures follow the Auditor's conveyance fact sheet and Ohio Revised Code 317.32. A fee schedule is linked from the Recorder page, and it is the place to check the surcharge and any other line item before writing a check. R.C. 322.02 also lets a county add a real property transfer tax of up to 30 cents per $100, paid by the grantor at the Auditor ahead of recording.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Fairfield County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Who can acknowledge a deed, and where it is filed

An Ohio deed needs the grantor's signature, acknowledged in front of an authorized officer (R.C. 5301.01). Acceptable officers are:

  • a judge or clerk of a court of record in Ohio
  • a county auditor or county engineer
  • a notary public
  • a mayor

Record in the county where the land lies. R.C. 5301.25 treats an unrecorded deed as fraudulent against a later good faith buyer with no knowledge of it. A house in Pickerington, Canal Winchester, Reynoldsburg or an unincorporated township is still recorded in Lancaster.

Each instrument is entered in the order presented, stamped with date and exact time. R.C. 317.13 gives the Recorder room to turn away anything materially false or fraudulent. A person who is refused may petition the Court of Common Pleas for an order to record.

Electronic recording

Yes. Simplifile is the e-filing route the Auditor's fact sheet names. Someone filing only once may find the account setup more trouble than it is worth and can simply file on paper.

State law pushed every county recorder, auditor and engineer toward electronic recording of conveyances, with recorders posting online indexes and images for instruments recorded since January 1, 1980. Fairfield's own online start in 1980 fits that. Logins are allowed for viewing, though no charge for a login is.

If you choose paper, ask your title company whether it would rather submit electronically for you. Many closing agents already hold a Simplifile account, which means the deed can be sent the same day it is signed and you avoid a trip to Lancaster altogether.

Paper still works. Deliver the deed to the Auditor, then pay the Recorder's fee. Phone 740-652-7100 to arrange return of the original.

Before you close on a Fairfield County sale

Lancaster is both seat and largest city of Fairfield County, which belongs to the Columbus metropolitan area and counted 158,921 residents in 2020. Franklin, Licking, Perry, Hocking and Pickaway counties border it. A neighboring county's mailing address does not move the recording location. Before you list, check with the city or township office for open permits on the house.

Three offices are involved, so keep a short closing checklist: approve the legal description, sign the conveyance fee statement, confirm taxes with the Treasurer, then record.

  • Legal description cleared by the Auditor's Map Room
  • Grantor's signature acknowledged by an authorized officer
  • Statement of value (DTE 100 or DTE 100EX) completed
  • Transfer and conveyance fees paid at the Auditor's transfer desk
  • Recording fee sent to the Recorder

Selling for cash removes the lender's paperwork, yet each item above still applies. Your title company normally sequences the stops. You bring your signature, a photo ID for the notary and your latest tax bill. If a mortgage is being paid off, expect the release to be recorded as well, and ask the title agent when that filing will be done.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Fairfield County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

If you suspect fraud on your property

Fraud on a house is rare, but it hurts most when the owner is away, the home is empty or the owner has died. Inherited houses waiting for a sale are a common target, so sign up before you list.

Start by enrolling in the Recorder's free alerts, which notify you of new documents recorded under your name or a notary's name. If something looks wrong, phone 740-652-7100 to ask what was filed, then talk to an attorney. Veteran ID cards are issued by this office as well, through the same number.

Keep your closing documents in one folder after the sale. A recorded deed and the matching release of any old mortgage are your proof that the title is clear, and you may be asked for them again.

Frequently asked questions

Which office files a deed for a Fairfield County house?

The Recorder, at 210 East Main Street, Suite 205 in Lancaster, once the County Auditor has processed the transfer. The Auditor is a separate stop at 108 N. High Street.

What does the Auditor charge to transfer a deed in Fairfield County?

A $.50 per parcel transfer fee, plus a conveyance fee of $4.00 per thousand of consideration when money changes hands. Have the transfer desk confirm the total before you bring payment.

Does Fairfield County have its own deed form?

No. Neither forms nor drafting help come from the Recorder. A title company or attorney writes the deed, and the Auditor's Map Room reviews the legal description.

Can I look up old Fairfield County deeds from home?

Partly. The index reaches back to 1800, but images are online only from January 1980 forward. Older documents are viewed at the office.

Who pays the conveyance fee when a house sells?

The seller, as grantor. The buyer files the statement of value with the Auditor.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Fayette County?

Recorder's office, hours and contact

Visit the Fayette County Recorder at 133 S. Main Street, Suite 305, Washington Court House. Doors are open weekdays from 8 am to 4 pm. The phone is 740-335-1770 and the fax is 740-333-3521. Real estate and personal property records for the whole county are kept here, such as:

  • deeds, mortgages and land contracts
  • IRS liens and mechanics liens
  • plats and zoning resolutions
  • military service discharges

The county seat, Washington Court House, is also the only city in the county. One office records every Fayette County deed, for in-town homes and township farms alike.

Recording fees

Pricing here is a set amount by length, and the first two pages cost the same.

Recording fee by document length
Pages in the documentRecording fee
1 page$39.00
2 pages$39.00
3 pages$47.00
4 pages$55.00
5 pages$63.00
10 pages$103.00

A $4.00 marginal fee may be added. The posted schedule ends at ten pages, so call for a quote on anything longer. Behind the numbers is Ohio Revised Code 317.32: each page carries a base fee and a housing trust fund fee, and a county may also add a document preservation surcharge of up to five dollars for its general fund.

Delivering a deed to the Recorder

Hand the deed in at Suite 305 or send it by mail. Payment is by cash or check, because cards of any kind are not accepted.

  • Papers arriving after 3:30 PM wait until the next day to be run, so a late afternoon drop misses that day's time stamp.
  • To get documents returned by mail, enclose a stamped envelope addressed to yourself.
  • Since June 22, 2026, the county offers e-recording through Simplifile for both conveyance and non-conveyance documents.

Time stamps count because instruments are filed in the order presented, with the exact time noted (R.C. 317.13). When two papers hit the same house, the earlier one has priority.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Fayette County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What the Auditor does before the deed is recorded

Go to the Auditor's real estate department before the Recorder. It handles deed transfers, new parcels, lot splits and homestead exemptions, and it is down the hall at 133 S. Main Street, Suite 303, phone 740-335-6461, on identical weekday hours.

Conveyance paperwork lives on the Auditor's forms page: the Real Property Conveyance form (DTE 100), the Exemption from Real Property Conveyance form (DTE 100EX), a statement for homestead property, another for property under current agricultural use valuation, and mobile home forms. Standards for legal descriptions are posted there too.

On the DTE 100 you list total consideration, then subtract what was paid for things that are not real property. The fee is figured on what remains. Questions follow about whether the seller reported senior or disabled homestead or farm use valuation, and whether the buyer will occupy the home by January 1 of the next year. Leaving out the owner-occupancy application holds back the 2.5 percent reduction until a timely, proper application is filed, so complete that section. The Auditor can quote the conveyance fee rate before closing.

Papers the Recorder can refuse

Ohio recorders can reject a paper that the law neither requires nor authorizes to be recorded, or one they reasonably believe is materially false or fraudulent. The remedy for a rejected filer is a request to the Court of Common Pleas for an order to record.

One refusal is not optional. R.C. 5301.94 directs the recorder to reject a right-to-list home sale agreement, so an owner pitched on recording one against the house should know the office will not accept it.

Nobody at the counter is obliged to inspect what you hand over. Legal description, names and signatures are the drafter's job to check.

Copies and small extras

Beyond the recording fee, R.C. 317.32 sets other charges, each split into a base fee and an equal housing trust fund fee:

  • Certified copy of a recorded document: $1 base plus $1 trust fund per page, with a further 50 cents plus 50 cents when the recorder's seal is required.
  • Photocopy outside the recording process: $1 plus $1 per page.
  • Marginal reference entered by a separate instrument: $2 plus $2 for each reference, which matches the $4.00 marginal fee Fayette posts.
  • Local fax or electronic transmission: $1 plus $1 per page.

A title company wants proof of how you took ownership, and the vesting deed shows it. If your own copy is lost, the Recorder can supply one for the per-page copy charge. Sellers most often need a certified copy of their vesting deed, since a title company will often ask for one. Order it a few days before closing so it is in hand when the title agent calls.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Fayette County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Values, tax bills and a sale

The Auditor doubles as chief fiscal officer and real property appraiser. Reappraisal comes every six years under Ohio direction, with an update in year three. The Auditor builds the yearly tax list, then splits what the Treasurer collects among townships, schools and other taxing bodies. Delinquent taxes are certified and published by the Auditor, and the Treasurer chases those accounts.

As secretary of the county Board of Revision, the Auditor also hosts the Board of Revision Property Complaint form on the forms page. A value dispute goes on that form, not to the Recorder. Spot an error in the Auditor's online data for your parcel and you can report it for correction.

When the deed is filed, the conveyance statement has to record whether the seller was asked about a homestead or owner-occupancy reduction and about farm use valuation. Ending farm use can trigger a recoupment charge, which buyer and seller sort out between themselves (R.C. 319.202). If you own farmed acreage, tell the title agent early.

Fayette County at a glance

The 2020 count was 28,951 residents, and the 2025 estimate is 28,552. Washington Court House anchors a micropolitan area in the Columbus-Marion-Zanesville region. Madison, Pickaway, Ross, Highland, Clinton and Greene counties touch its borders, and Good Hope and Pancoastburg are the named unincorporated places.

On a cash sale the order of stops is short. Start with the legal description and conveyance forms at the Auditor in Suite 303. Then take the signed deed to the Recorder in Suite 305 before 3:30 PM, with a check or cash for the fee. With no lender involved there is no loan package to deliver, so the deed is often the only document you carry in.

Before you drive over, phone both offices to confirm the fee total and that the legal description is acceptable. A rejected description sends you back to the start, and it is cheaper to catch a problem by phone than at the counter.

Frequently asked questions

How much is the Fayette County recording fee for a two page deed?

It costs $39.00, with a possible $4.00 marginal fee on top. One page is also $39.00, and three pages are $47.00.

Can I pay the Fayette County Recorder by card?

No. Only cash or a check will be taken.

Can I e-record a deed in Fayette County?

Yes, through Simplifile, for both conveyance and non-conveyance documents. You can still file on paper at Suite 305.

What time should I get a deed to the Fayette County Recorder?

Aim for before 3:30 PM. Later arrivals are held and run the next day.

Does the Fayette County Recorder or Auditor handle the conveyance form?

The Auditor does, in Suite 303 of the same building. Both the DTE 100 and the exemption form DTE 100EX are on the Auditor's forms page, and the Recorder files the deed afterward.

Recorder's office and what it records

The office records, preserves and retrieves real estate, personal property and other records so property interests are safeguarded and easy to find.

In this county the Auditor and the Recorder are separate offices. The Auditor handles ownership changes and the fees for the transfer, and the Recorder files the deed itself. Plan to visit or mail to both.

Steps to record a deed

The deed goes to the Auditor first and reaches the Recorder afterward. The sequence runs like this:

  • Prepare a new deed form. A template is available through the County Law Library under real estate forms.
  • Copy the legal description from the last deed on file, which the Recorder's website lets you search, and follow the county document standards.
  • Sign the deed in front of a notary.
  • File the deed with the Auditor and pay the Auditor's transfer charges.
  • Include a separate payment for the Recorder, and the Auditor forwards the deed to the Recorder once the transfer is complete.

Most owners never write a deed from scratch. If a title company or attorney is handling your sale, it drafts the deed from the prior recorded one and walks it through each step. Writing it yourself works only if you are comfortable copying a legal description exactly and following the county document standards, since a document that fails them costs an extra $20.

Paying off a mortgage does not call for a new deed. The lender files a release of mortgage as its own document.

Recording fees

Fees follow Ohio Revised Code 317.32, and the Recorder offers a fee calculator for checking your math.

Franklin County Recorder fees
ChargeFee
First two pages$34
Each additional page$8
Document that fails standardization requirements$20
Each indexed marginal reference$4
Debit or credit card payment3% convenience fee
No self-addressed stamped envelope supplied$1 document return fee

Make checks and money orders payable to the Franklin County Recorder, since checks payable to second or third parties are refused. Cards are limited to Discover, Mastercard and Visa. The $34 and $8 figures each combine a base fee with a housing trust fund fee of the same amount.

Auditor's transfer charges

The Auditor's transfer and conveyance office handles more than 30,000 property transfers a year. The conveyance fee is $3 per $1,000 of the sale price, made up of $1 per $1,000 set by the State of Ohio and $2 per $1,000 set by the Board of Commissioners. There is also a $3 minimum and a $0.50 transfer tax on any transfer that is not exempt. An exempt transfer owes only the $0.50.

If the seller is receiving the homestead exemption at the time of transfer, the county's $2 piece is waived and the fee drops to $1 per $1,000. You can verify homestead status on the Auditor's property search under the Homestead Credit entry on the parcel summary. Round the sale amount up to the next $100 when you use the calculator.

  • Pay by cash, business check or cashier's check made out to the Franklin County Auditor.
  • Personal checks are not accepted, and the office can give change only on cash.
  • Do not add payments for other county offices to the same check.
  • Transfers must carry the exact amount to be processed.

Questions go to the Transfer and Conveyance Department at 614-525-3253.

E-recording a deed

An e-recorded deed must come through Simplifile, and mostly from professionals. The Recorder runs no e-recording platform of its own. Private companies, including CSC Global, ePN, Indecomm Global Services and Simplifile, send documents in for recording and may add their own charges.

A deed that transfers real property can be e-recorded through the Auditor, Engineer and Recorder, but only via Simplifile, and it has to come from a title company, bank or similar entity. Individuals may e-record other documents through Simplifile, but an individual's e-recording cannot transfer property. If e-recording is out of reach, mail the deed or bring it to the 18th floor.

The Recorder also accepts documents completed with electronic and online notarization that meet Ohio legislature and Secretary of State requirements.

Getting the original back

Enclose a self-addressed, stamped envelope and the original deed comes back by mail. Without one, the Recorder charges postage or the $1 return fee.

Regular filers can open an escrow account at the Recorder with a starting deposit of $100 or more, so they do not bring a check for each filing. Certain public servants whose home addresses are exempt from public record may ask to have the address redacted from documents posted on the Recorder's website. They use the Request to Redact Address form and email it to the Recorder.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Franklin County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What to bring to the courthouse

Gather these items so one trip covers the Auditor and the Recorder:

  • The signed, notarized deed with a legal description copied from the prior recorded deed
  • The Auditor's payment: cash, business check or cashier's check for the transfer and conveyance charges
  • A second payment made out to the Franklin County Recorder, so the Auditor can forward the deed
  • A self-addressed, stamped envelope for the original
  • Proof of homestead status if the seller receives the exemption, since it lowers the conveyance fee

The Recorder's fee calculator and the Auditor's transfer calculator both help you total these amounts before you leave home. Add the two payments together on paper, then double check that each check names the right office, because a check made out to the wrong payee is refused and costs you the trip.

In a cash sale the title company or attorney usually assembles this packet for you. Your part is to sign in front of the notary and tell them whether you receive the homestead exemption. Ask whether they plan to use Simplifile, since e-recording of a property transfer is limited to a title company, bank or similar entity and an individual cannot do it alone.

Selling in Franklin County

Columbus is the county seat and the state capital, and Franklin County had 1,323,807 residents in 2020, the most of any Ohio county. Suburbs such as Bexley, Dublin, Gahanna, Grandview Heights, Grove City, Hilliard, New Albany, Upper Arlington, Westerville and Worthington all record deeds at this same courthouse. A house in Dublin and a house in Whitehall follow the same path through the Auditor and then the Recorder, so a complete packet saves a second trip.

Frequently asked questions

How much does the Franklin County Recorder charge for a deed?

The Recorder lists $34 for the first two pages and $8 for each additional page. A $20 fee applies if the document misses the standardization requirements, and cards carry a 3% convenience fee.

Do I file with the Auditor or the Recorder first in Franklin County?

The Auditor first. After the transfer is complete, the deed goes to the Recorder, and the Auditor forwards it if you included a separate payment for the Recorder.

Does a deed need a notary in Franklin County?

Yes. All transfers must be signed in front of a notary, and electronic or online notarization is accepted when it meets Ohio requirements.

What is the Franklin County conveyance fee?

It is $3 per $1,000 of the sale price, with a $3 minimum and a $0.50 transfer tax. The fee drops to $1 per $1,000 if the seller receives the homestead exemption.

Can an individual e-record a deed in Franklin County?

An individual can use Simplifile for some documents, but an individual's e-recording cannot transfer property. Deeds that transfer property come through a title company, bank or similar entity.

What the Fulton County Recorder does

The Recorder indexes and files each land document in the county. Buyers use the index to trace past owners, and lenders use it to see what debts attach to a parcel.

West of Toledo, Fulton County is part of that metro area. County business happens in Wauseon, including filings for homes in Archbold, Delta, Swanton, Fayette, Lyons and Metamora.

Office location and hours

The Recorder is at 152 S. Fulton St., Suite 175, Wauseon, OH 43567. The counter serves the public on weekdays from half past eight until half past four, and the number is (419) 337-9232.

  • Recorder: Suite 175, where a deed ends up.
  • Auditor: Suite 165, same building, where it starts. Real estate questions go to (419) 337-9200.
  • Land records search: linked from the county's Records Search page, handy for finding earlier deeds and mortgages.

The Recorder page also carries a Real Property Conveyance Standards PDF plus printable plats and land surveys. Read them before you draft a legal description.

Steps before the deed reaches the Recorder

The county's conveyance standards put every legal description through the same review. The aim is to catch visible errors and describe the parcel properly for tax purposes. Unusual cases are sent to a panel of the County Engineer, the Auditor and the Planning Director.

  1. Draft the deed, copying the legal description from the most recent recorded deed.
  2. Have it acknowledged by a notary. R.C. 5301.01 also allows a judge, court clerk, county auditor, county engineer or mayor.
  3. Take it to Suite 165 for the description review, the conveyance fee and the transfer.
  4. Then walk it to Suite 175 and pay the recording fee.

Ohio's transfer tax statute makes the grantor settle with the Auditor first, so do not reverse the order. Ask the Recorder which endorsement it expects to see.

Auditor's transfer and conveyance fees

The rate is $4.00 for every thousand dollars of total consideration, with the amount rounded up to the next $100, and a $0.50 per parcel transfer fee.

That figure has two state layers. A statement-of-value fee of ten cents per $100 comes from R.C. 319.54(G)(3), and a county may add up to thirty cents per $100 under R.C. 322.02. The grantor pays when the deed is delivered.

Certain transfers owe no fee under R.C. 319.54(G)(3):

  • a gift to a spouse, or from parent to child;
  • a deal with no money or other valuable consideration that is also not a gift;
  • a no-money conveyance among heirs or devisees of a single decedent;
  • a trustee returning property to the grantor of a revocable trust.

If your sale looks like one of these, check with the Auditor's real estate office before assuming a fee is owed.

Recording costs

Recording fees are set by the state, and half of each fee funds the Ohio Housing Trust Fund. A printed side counts as a page. A county can tack on a preservation surcharge of no more than $5.00 per document, so call the Fulton Recorder for the final amount before you mail a check.

Common charges on a Fulton County deed
ChargeAmountPaid to

Deed formatting rules

A standard layout applies to any deed you give the Recorder under R.C. 317.114. Miss it and the deed is still accepted, at the cost of another $10 base fee and $10 housing trust fee.

  • Ten point type or larger.
  • Paper at least letter size, up to 14 inches long.
  • Black or blue ink, with no highlighting.
  • An inch of blank margin on each side and at the bottom of every page.
  • A three inch blank band at the top of page one for the Engineer, Auditor and Recorder endorsements, then one and a half inches at the top of later pages.

Court and tax-authority papers, plats, state and federal documents, and anything signed before July 1, 2009 are outside the rule.

Fulton County housing market

The April 2020 count was 42,713 people, and the July 2025 estimate of 41,853 is down 2.0 percent. Of all homes, 80.2 percent are owner-occupied, with a median value of $191,000 for those. The county gave out 57 building permits in 2025, and median household income is $72,864.

Across 405 square miles of land, at roughly 105 residents per square mile, parcels range from farm acreage to village lots in Archbold and Wauseon to homes in any of its twelve townships.

Other items in the land records

Expect a title search to look past the latest deed. At a sheriff's sale, liens are paid in order out of the proceeds and then cancelled against the property, but a federal lien survives and stays on file with the Recorder. Buyers at such sales must check each lien themselves.

  • Mortgages, releases and assignments are kept in the very office that holds the deed.
  • Filing a federal tax lien costs $5.00, and releasing one costs $3.00.
  • There is no charge to record military discharge papers.
  • Plats and condominium drawings are charged by area, ten cents per square inch, with a $40.00 minimum.

Search the parcel in the Recorder's land records and in the Auditor's property search before setting a closing date.

Tax rules a seller should check

Bills arrive twice a year, due in February and July. The lien date is January 1, and billing trails by a year. A bill paid in 2025 covered tax year 2024 and reflected the home's worth as 2025 began.

  • Owner-occupied reduction: residences only, never applied by itself. Enroll at (419) 337-9200.
  • Value complaints: file with the Board of Revision any time from January 1 to March 31.
  • Payments and mailing address changes for tax bills: the Treasurer handles both, not the Auditor.

Ask the Fulton County Treasurer for a payoff figure on the parcel, and have the title company spell out who covers which bill.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Selling for cash in Fulton County

With cash there is no lender, but the route through the courthouse is unchanged: signed, notarized deed to Suite 165, then to Suite 175. Stick to the layout rules above to avoid extra fees. Because payment is part of the filing, phone ahead for the exact total, as the county decides the preservation surcharge. Also have a photo ID, your latest tax bill and any payoff letter ready, so the title agent can finish the same day.

Frequently asked questions

Is there a transfer tax collected by the Fulton County Recorder?

Not by the Recorder, which collects only the recording fee. The $4.00 per $1,000 conveyance fee and the $0.50 per parcel transfer fee go to the Auditor, paid by the grantor before filing.

Can a Fulton County deed skip the Auditor and go straight to recording?

No. Visit the Auditor first. The grantor pays there under R.C. 322.02 before the Recorder sees the deed, and each legal description is reviewed under the county standards.

What hours does the Wauseon Recorder keep?

It is open on weekdays, half past eight until half past four, at Suite 175, 152 S. Fulton St. Call (419) 337-9232. The Auditor is down the hall in Suite 165.

What happens if my deed has a small font or thin margins?

It will be filed, with $10 more in base fee and $10 more in housing trust fee under R.C. 317.114. Court papers, plats, state and federal documents and instruments signed before July 1, 2009 are exempt.

Where do I send a complaint that my Fulton County home is overvalued?

Send it to the Board of Revision by way of the Auditor's real estate office, (419) 337-9200. Complaints are accepted January 1 to March 31, and staff can mail a form or direct you to the printable copy.

Who records deeds in Gallia County

The Gallia County Recorder in Gallipolis records deeds, mortgages, leases, land contracts, liens and plats for the county. Ohio's first legislature had judges appoint a recorder in each county, the post became elective in 1829, and the term was fixed at four years in 1936.

Gallia County dates to March 25, 1803, and runs along the Ohio River where Ohio meets West Virginia. Gallipolis is the seat, with Cheshire, Crown City, Rio Grande, Centerville and Vinton as the other villages, and every one of them files into the same land records. A sale in any of those villages follows the same path through the Auditor and then the Recorder.

Office address and hours

The Recorder is at 18 Locust Street, Gallipolis, Ohio 45631. Weekday hours run eight to four. Call 740-446-4612 and ask for extension 1247, 1248 or 1329.

  • County Auditor: same address, Room 1264, with the real estate desk on extension 1201.
  • Recorder's property search: an online index of recorded documents.
  • Auditor's parcel search, GIS parcel viewer, sales reports and delinquency reports: available from the Auditor's website.

Looking at the land records costs nothing. Public access is free, so a buyer, a title agent or you can review the index before closing.

Auditor first, then Recorder

A deed must be transferred in the Auditor's office before it is recorded, so the Auditor is your first stop.

The Auditor's website posts a conveyance fee calculator and a tax estimator under Tools, with the statement of value form for the conveyance fee among its forms. The statewide piece of the conveyance fee is a dollar, or ten cents per hundred dollars of value if that is larger (R.C. 319.54(G)(3)). A county board may stack a tax of up to thirty cents per hundred on top (R.C. 322.02). Use the Auditor's calculator for Gallia County's total, and ask the real estate desk about exemptions such as a transfer with no money or other consideration.

The county has more than 29,000 parcels and more than 2,500 manufactured and mobile homes. A Community Reinvestment Area began on December 2, 2024, so ask the Auditor what that program covers for your parcel.

What the Recorder requires on a deed

The Recorder publishes a checklist, and a deed or mortgage that misses an item comes back. The list includes:

  • a full legal description naming the township or city, lot or subdivision and acreage;
  • grantor names spelled exactly as they are signed and notarized;
  • the permanent parcel number wherever the real estate is described;
  • a notary signature, seal and expiration date;
  • a "prepared by" line, which Ohio requires;
  • names typed beneath the original signatures;
  • a stamped, addressed return envelope big enough to hold the papers.

Deputies cannot fix a lot number or other typo. Whoever made the document must make the change. Documents boxed for pickup must be claimed within a week or they are mailed out at the box holder's cost.

Recording fees

State rules put a deed at $34 for pages one and two and $8 for every later page, with an optional county preservation surcharge of up to $5. Gallia posts $39.00 for the opening two pages and $8.00 for each later page. The state splits each of its fees evenly with the Ohio Housing Trust Fund.

Selected Gallia County Recorder charges
Document or serviceFee

Format rules that can add $20

Ohio's standardization statute, R.C. 317.114, took effect on July 1, 2009. It calls for type of ten points or larger, black or blue ink, no highlighting and paper between letter size and 14 inches long. Leave an inch of white space on the sides and the bottom, three inches at the head of the first page and an inch and a half at the head of later ones.

The Recorder will still accept a deed that does not conform, but adds $20.00 to the bill. The statute exempts court and tax authority documents, plats, DD-214 discharges, state and federal papers and anything executed before the effective date. Marginal clutter such as page numbers, initials and bar codes is not charged.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Gallia County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Other records that show up in a sale

Title work on a Gallia County house often turns up more than the deed. These other filings sit in the same indexes:

  • Mechanic's liens and notices of commencement.
  • Federal tax liens and releases, personal property tax liens and workers' compensation liens.
  • Land contracts, powers of attorney and trust documents.
  • A Notice to Medicaid Estate Recovery of Pending Transfer of Property, a form the Recorder links on its fees page.

Run the parcel through the Recorder's search and the Auditor's search before you sign a contract. A lien found after a contract is signed holds up the closing.

Gallia County housing

Gallia had 29,220 people in 2020, and the July 2025 estimate is 29,072. Owners hold 74.7 percent of homes, the median value is $155,600, and the median rent is $813 against a median household income of $56,830. Of 13,430 housing units, 13.1 percent were vacant in 2020, and only seven building permits were issued in 2025.

A seller here is often handling an older house in a county where new construction is thin, which makes the title and lien check worth doing early. Gallipolis is the county seat and largest village. A buyer from across the state line in Cabell or Mason County, West Virginia, still records the deed in Gallipolis.

With a cash buyer you skip the lender's timeline, but the same two stops apply: the Auditor's transfer, then the Recorder. Before you go, confirm the legal description against your last deed, check that the notary block shows a seal and expiration date, and enclose a stamped return envelope big enough for the papers. Any of those gaps sends the deed back and costs you days. If you are unsure about a detail, call the Recorder on 740-446-4612 before you make the trip, because the deputies can tell you what a checklist item means even though they cannot fix the document.

Frequently asked questions

What is the first-two-pages recording fee in Gallia County?

The Recorder lists $39.00 for the first two pages and $8.00 for each page after them. The state base is $34, which a county may raise with a preservation surcharge of up to $5.

Which Gallipolis office comes first, the Auditor or the Recorder?

The Auditor. The transfer has to happen there before recording. Both offices are at 18 Locust Street, and the Auditor's real estate desk is on extension 1201.

Can the Recorder correct an error in my legal description?

No. Deputies cannot change lot numbers or other details even when the error looks like a typo. The person who prepared the document has to fix it and sign again.

Is there a charge to record a military discharge in Gallia County?

No. The Recorder records discharge papers and the Honorable Discharge Certificate at no cost, and one certified copy of a service discharge is free.

How do I look up an old Gallia County deed?

Use the Recorder's online records index, or the Auditor's parcel search by owner, parcel or address. The counter at 18 Locust Street runs on weekday hours, eight to four, and browsing the records costs nothing.

How a deed is recorded in Geauga County

A Geauga County deed passes through three offices in Chardon, and the county publishes a one-page reference sheet, effective June 30, 2026, that lays out the order. First the Engineer approves the legal description. Next the Auditor transfers the parcel and takes the conveyance fee. Last, the Recorder files the deed and sends it back.

Geauga sits in Ohio's northeast corner inside the Cleveland metropolitan area, with Chardon as its seat.

The three Chardon offices

The reference sheet lists three stops, their addresses and what each one needs from you.

  • County Engineer, 12665 Merritt Rd, Chardon, phone (440) 279-1800: reviews the legal description and stamps it with an original (wet) stamp. No fee. Allow 2 to 3 business days. Bring a legible copy of the prior deed with its volume and page reference.
  • County Auditor, 231 Main St, Suite 1-A, phone (440) 279-1600: transfers the property and updates the tax records. Needs the original signed and notarized deed.
  • County Recorder, 231 Main St, Suite 1-C, phone (440) 279-2020: records the deed and mails the original back.

The Auditor is two doors down the hall from the Recorder. To send a deed by mail, enclose a brief letter saying what you want done, your phone number, a stamped return envelope and two separate checks, payable to the Recorder and to the Auditor.

Auditor's transfer charges

The Auditor charges $4.00 per $1,000 of transfer value and $0.50 per parcel, and checks for both are made payable to the Geauga County Auditor. Fee questions go to the Auditor.

Some transfers are exempt, among them spousal and parent-to-child gifts, deals with no consideration and certain trust moves.

Send a completed DTE 100 or DTE 100EX conveyance form with the deed. A Transfer on Death Affidavit is the exception: it has no Auditor fee.

Recorder's fees

State law fixes the Recorder's charge at $34.00 for the first two pages and $8.00 for each page that follows. A check that is short or too large gets the document returned unrecorded, so count pages before writing it.

Geauga County recording and transfer charges

Conveyance fee$4.00 per $1,000Auditor
