Electronic recording and turnaround

Electronic recording of conveyances is available and lets you skip the paper steps. Legal descriptions presented that way do not need the wet Engineer stamp. Call (440) 279-2020 to confirm what the office will take before you rely on it.

Paper filings move fast. The Recorder turns documents around the same day, and an electronic recording is returned when it is recorded. Leave a self-addressed stamped envelope with an in-person deed, or come back the next day to pick it up.

Document rules

Each deed needs the following before it reaches the counter.

  • Legible signatures, and printed names under any that are hard to read.
  • A line naming whoever prepared the deed.
  • Notary acknowledgments for each grantor.
  • Original wet stamps from the Engineer and the Auditor.
  • The 8-digit permanent parcel numbers.
  • A completed conveyance form.

The extra $20 for a non-standard document comes from R.C. 317.114, which wants at least ten point type, black or blue ink and three blank inches above the text on page one. Staff cannot notarize or give legal advice, and state law keeps them from running title searches. The Recorder no longer accepts Torrens registered land filings, and it does not sell blank forms.

Other things the Recorder keeps

Geauga County has no tract (geographical) indexing, and only the indexes of recorded documents are online, so a full copy of an old deed means a copy request. Copies made by the public cost ten cents a page, while a copy made with staff help is two dollars a page.

  • Releases and assignments do not need a legal description, but they do carry the $4.00 marginal notation fee.
  • Soldier discharge records (DD214) are recorded, and a recorded discharge is what the office uses to issue a military ID card.
  • For a blank form, try a title company, an attorney or an office supply store.
  • The office will not search the title for you, and it will not notarize or give legal advice.

A shortage or overage on the check sends the document back unrecorded, so call (440) 279-2020 with the page count if you are unsure. The mailing address and the delivery address are the same, 231 Main Street, Suite 1-C, so a courier and the postal service reach one door.

Selling in Geauga County

The 2020 population was 95,397, and the July 2025 estimate is 95,676. Owner-occupancy is 87.2 percent, the median owned home is valued at $331,100, and median household income is $107,860. Builders pulled 180 permits in 2025.

Chardon, Burton, Middlefield, South Russell and Hunting Valley are the municipalities. In November 2024 voters dissolved the Village of Aquilla, and a transition board oversees the change.

Because three offices touch every deed, a cash sale still takes a few days of stops. Start with the Engineer's stamp, since it can take 2 to 3 business days, and line up the notary, your photo ID and both checks in the meantime.

Before you leave home, check the deed against the list above: signatures legible, preparer named, notary block complete, parcel numbers present and the conveyance form attached. A deed that comes back for a missing item costs you another trip through all three offices. If you are mailing it, count the pages first so the Recorder's check is exact, and keep copies of everything you send. Ask your title company whether it prefers to handle the filings for you, since many do it as part of closing. Either way, you sign the deed in front of a notary, so bring a photo ID.

Frequently asked questions

What are the total charges to record a deed in Geauga County?

At the Recorder, plan on $34.00 for two pages, $8.00 for each extra one and $20.00 more for a non-standard deed. The Auditor bills $4.00 per $1,000 of value and $0.50 per parcel on its own.

Do I need the County Engineer for a Geauga County deed?

Yes, for paper filings. The Engineer reviews and approves the legal description with an original stamp at no fee, usually within 2 to 3 business days. Legal descriptions sent through electronic recording are the exception.

Where is the Geauga County Recorder located?

At 231 Main Street, Suite 1-C, Chardon, Ohio 44024. Call (440) 279-2020. The County Auditor is in Suite 1-A of the same building.

Will the Recorder search the title to my house?

No. State law prohibits the office from doing title searches. Try the online index of recorded documents, or hire a title company or an attorney.

How long does recording take in Chardon?

The Recorder turns documents around the same day. Mailed deeds come back to you after recording in the self-addressed stamped envelope you include, and an electronic recording is returned when it is recorded.

Recorder's office hours and location

The Greene County Recorder is on the third floor of 69 Greene St. in Xenia. The recorder's page gives two sets of weekday hours: the counter is staffed until 4:00 p.m., but recording stops at 3:00 p.m. A deed that arrives after that sits until the next business day, so on closing day plan to get documents there early.

The office keeps the permanent land records for the whole county. A seller will run into several of these filings during a sale:

  • Deeds, mortgages and releases of mortgage
  • Easements, leases and land contracts
  • Affidavits, trusts and powers of attorney
  • Mechanic's liens, federal tax liens and child support liens
  • Plats, condominium documents and annexations

The office also files and certifies military discharges. Those records are closed to the public, and the person discharged or their heirs can get a copy free of charge.

Steps before a Greene County deed is recorded

Start at the auditor's office, not the recorder. The transfer desk there wants a completed Statement of Value (DTE 100) or the exempt version (DTE 100 EX), fees payable to the auditor, the grantor's name spelled exactly as it appears on the grantor's own deed, and map department initials. The grantor signs, and a notary acknowledges the signature.

R.C. 5301.01 lists who may take that acknowledgment, from notaries and mayors to court clerks, auditors and engineers. Recording protects the buyer too. Under R.C. 5301.25, a deed that is never recorded is treated as fraudulent against a later purchaser who bought in good faith without notice of it.

If the land is in the CAUV farm program, in the filing year or the year before, attach that program's conveyance statement. If a survey was done, the deed has to carry the surveyor's name.

What recording a deed costs in Greene County

R.C. 317.32 sets the fee schedule, and each charge pairs a base amount with an equal housing trust fund amount. Senate Bill 94 allows as much as $5.00 more per document, but a January 2, 2026 notice from the Greene County Recorder says standard fees stay the same.

Recording fees under R.C. 317.32

Copies cost less if you make them yourself: $.10 a page for self-service official copies, against $2.00 a page when staff make them.

Transfer charges collected before recording

The auditor collects these before the deed goes to the recorder. The county's transfer page shows a combined $2.00 per thousand dollars of purchase price, made up of a $1.00 conveyance fee and a $1.00 transfer fee, plus $0.50 per parcel. An online calculator is posted on the same page.

The grantor owes the tax. R.C. 322.02 caps a county's own transfer tax at 30 cents per hundred dollars of value. Some transfers carry no fee under R.C. 319.54, including these:

  • Moves among heirs or devisees of one decedent where no money is paid
  • Gifts between spouses or from parent to child
  • Deeds into a revocable trust, and back out to the grantor
  • Deeds given only to secure or release a debt

The reason for the exemption is written on the statement, so go over it with the closing agent before anyone signs.

Liens that can turn up against a Greene County seller

The recorder files several kinds of liens, and a buyer's title company searches for each one under the seller's name and the parcel. The county's list covers mechanic's liens, Medicaid fraud liens, federal tax liens, child support liens, unemployment compensation liens, personal tax liens and workers' compensation liens. A Notice of Commencement is filed here as well.

Fees differ by lien type under the Ohio Recorders' Association fee table:

  • Federal tax lien (IRS): $5.00, with $3.00 to release it.
  • Unemployment compensation lien and workers' compensation lien: no fee.
  • Personal property tax lien and Medicaid fraud lien: no fee.
  • Mechanic's lien and its release: the standard per-page fee.

If you know about a lien, ask the lienholder for a recorded release well before closing day. Once the release is filed it shows up in the same index as the original lien, and the title examiner can clear the exception.

Deed forms used in Greene County sales

The state fee table names the usual choices, all recorded at the same per-page rates: warranty, limited warranty, quit claim and survivorship deeds. Estate and trust sales bring executor's, administrator's, guardian's or trustee's deeds, depending on who holds authority. A transfer on death designation affidavit is also recorded here.

Survivorship deeds fall under R.C. 5302.20. Language showing clear intent creates the tenancy, and a conveyance signed by every tenant ends it. Co-owners who inherited together should read the recorded deed to see whether they hold in survivorship or in common, since that decides who has to sign the sale deed.

Where Greene County land is recorded

Land is recorded in the county where it sits, so parcels in every city, village and township here go through the Xenia office. Beavercreek, Bellbrook, Fairborn and Xenia are the cities, and Kettering reaches into Greene County even though most of it is in Montgomery County.

The auditor's rolls hold more than 73,000 parcels. Each has its own chain of recorded documents, and a buyer's title search reads that chain back through earlier deeds. A gap in it can slow a sale, so a seller who has an old unrecorded deed or a missing release in the file should fix it before listing.

Searching records and finding a mortgage release

Online, the Recorder's Document Search covers filings from 1984 onward. Images on the website carry a watermark, and a watermarked page cannot be submitted for recording, so get clean copies at the counter. A transfer tracking table shows where a newly submitted transfer stands, and a fraud alert service can notify an owner when something is filed against a registered property.

A lender gets 90 days after payoff to file the release or satisfaction of mortgage. An owner who paid off a loan long ago should look up that release before listing, since a missing one can stall a closing. If it never was filed, contact the lender and ask for one to be recorded.

Greene County housing numbers

Greene County had 68,166 households in the 2020 to 2024 survey, averaging 2.38 people, and roughly 74,000 housing units in 2025. Monthly owner costs have a median of $1,702 with a mortgage and $700 without one. Builders pulled 567 permits in 2025.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

What to bring to the Greene County office

For a standard sale the closing agent usually handles the paperwork, but it helps to know the order. First the auditor reviews the Statement of Value and collects the transfer charges. Then the signed, notarized deed goes to the recorder, who records and indexes it. After recording, the buyer gets the original back.

A seller handling things directly should bring the signed deed, the completed DTE form, any survey or farm program statement, and payment for the auditor's fees. Bring a separate payment for the recorder's fees. Arrive before 3:00 p.m. so the deed is recorded the same day.

Frequently asked questions

When does Greene County stop recording documents each day?

At 3:00 p.m. on weekdays, with recording starting at 7:30 a.m. The office itself stays open until 4:00 p.m., so bring anything urgent early in the day.

Did Greene County raise recording fees after the state change?

Not for standard documents. A January 2, 2026 recorder notice says fees stay put, although Senate Bill 94 permits up to $5.00 more.

Which office collects the Greene County transfer charge?

The auditor collects it from the grantor before recording. The county shows $2.00 per thousand dollars of price and a $0.50 per-parcel charge.

How do I get a copy of my Greene County deed?

Go to 69 Greene St., third floor, or use the online document search. Self-service official copies cost $.10 a page, and staff-made ones cost $2.00 a page.

How soon must a lender record a mortgage release in Greene County?

Within ninety days of payoff. The recorder holds the release, and copies come from the counter or the document search.

Contacting the Guernsey County Recorder

The county recorder page gives weekday hours of 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. Call 740-432-9275, or fax 740-439-6267. Cambridge is the county seat, and the auditor works from the Administration Building at 627 Wheeling Avenue.

Ohio recorders hold the ownership record for land and each lien against it. A seller whose own deed was never recorded should expect the buyer's title company to pause the sale until that gap is closed, so check your deed's recording stamp before you list.

Does Guernsey County take electronic deeds?

Yes. Four submitting vendors can send eRecordings to the recorder, a route used mostly by lenders, banks, attorneys and title companies. Only document types the office accepts by regular mail qualify, and each vendor sets its own price.

A second route, described on the auditor's page, is e-filing through Kofile Technologies. Files can be sent every hour of every day, but staff process them only between 8 a.m. and 3 p.m. on weekdays, so a late upload waits a business day. Plats and military discharges (DD-214) cannot go this way. When a deed or conveyance form is rejected, processing restarts once the corrected version arrives.

What happens at the auditor before recording

Real estate staff at the auditor move the deed onto the tax records and then pass it to the recorder. The office is in suite 301 at 627 Wheeling Avenue, and the phone is (740) 432-9243, option 1 for real estate. Forms for sellers and closing agents include:

  • DTE 100, the real estate conveyance form, and DTE 100 EX for exempt transfers
  • DTE 101, the statement of conveyance of homestead property
  • DTE 102, the statement of conveyance of CAUV property
  • A routing sheet and a timeline for deed transfers
  • Transfer and Conveyance Standards effective October 1, 2022

A conveyance fee calculator sits under tools on the auditor's site. State fees come from R.C. 319.54 ($1.00 per thousand) and R.C. 322.02 (a county transfer tax of up to 30 cents per hundred dollars), so use the calculator or call the auditor for the Guernsey County total.

What the conveyance statement asks

R.C. 319.202 governs the form. The buyer or the buyer's representative files it before the auditor endorses the deed. It declares the property's value, meaning the whole price with any mortgage or vendor's lien included, and willfully falsifying that figure is prohibited.

The same statute adds questions on tax reductions and farm status:

  • Either an affirmation that the seller was asked about a homestead or owner-occupancy reduction on the current or prior year's taxes, or a sworn statement giving the reduction and its estimated amount.
  • Either an affirmation about current agricultural use valuation (CAUV) status, or a sworn statement noting a possible recoupment charge.
  • The reason for any exemption, written on the form when no fee is due.

After endorsement the auditor retains the original, sends a copy to the tax commissioner and hands one to the buyer. Residential rental property gets an added notice telling the buyer to register with the auditor.

Recording fees at the Guernsey County Recorder

Charges follow R.C. 317.32. Combined, the Ohio Recorders' Association table reads $34.00 for the opening two pages, $8.00 per page after that and $4.00 per marginal notation, with up to $5.00 per document for preservation. Half of every fee funds basic recording and the other half the state's Housing Trust Fund.

The table also lists a $10.00 plus $10.00 standardization fee for a document that misses the formatting rules. Call the recorder at 740-432-9275 to ask whether Guernsey County adds the surcharge, because each county decides that for itself.

Who can notarize a deed signed in Guernsey County?

After the grantor signs, someone from the list in R.C. 5301.01 has to witness the acknowledgment. That list takes in notaries, mayors, the auditor, the engineer, and judges or court clerks. Banks, title companies and law offices usually keep a notary on staff.

R.C. 5301.25 sends each deed to the county where the land sits and treats an unrecorded one as fraudulent against a later buyer acting in good faith. A deed made after a survey must carry the surveyor's name.

Homestead reduction and your sale

The auditor's information page explains the homestead rules behind the statement questions above. A homeowner qualifies by owning and occupying the home as a principal residence on January 1 of the year of application, and by meeting one of three tests: age 65 by December 31 of the filing year, total and permanent disability, or being the surviving spouse of a past recipient who was at least 59. Owners with more than one home count as living where they are registered to vote and where their federal income tax form places them.

Ohio returned to income testing in 2013, but anyone who received the credit for tax year 2013 keeps it without an income limit. Owners with a qualifying federal disability rating from military service receive a reduction equal to the tax on $50,000 of true value, compared with $25,000 for the standard credit. The spouse of a public service officer killed in the line of duty receives the same $50,000 level with no income limit.

The auditor's delinquent tax notice cites R.C. 5721.03 and warns that listed parcels will be certified for foreclosure or a tax certificate sale unless every delinquent tax, assessment, interest and penalty is paid within a year. If your parcel is on that list, pay it at or before closing.

Owners and housing in Guernsey County

The auditor counts 40,170 parcels, and Census estimates give 38,379 residents in 2025, about level with 2020. Owners hold 72.1 percent of homes, with a $157,700 median in the 2020 to 2024 survey, while renters pay a $864 median gross rent. There are 16,318 households averaging 2.31 people, and 19,116 housing units as of 2025. Monthly owner costs have a median of $1,237 with a mortgage and $505 without one. Forty-one building permits were issued in 2025.

The auditor's forms list includes a Mineral Deeds section, so ask the buyer's title company to search for any recorded mineral deed or lease on the parcel.

Where Guernsey County deeds are recorded

Buffalo, Kimbolton and Salesville are census-designated places outside Cambridge, and deeds for land there are recorded in the same Cambridge office. The same is true for every township in the county.

In practice a sale here runs in order. The closing agent prepares the deed and the DTE form, the grantor signs before a notary, the auditor endorses and moves the deed on the tax records, and the recorder files it. The buyer's title company usually handles the trip, but a seller can ask for the recording date to confirm the deed is on file.

Frequently asked questions

When is the Guernsey County Recorder open?

Weekdays from 8 a.m. until 4 p.m. Call 740-432-9275, and note that electronic filings get processed only until 3 p.m.

Can a deed be eRecorded in Guernsey County?

Yes, through one of four submitting vendors or through Kofile e-filing. Plats and military discharges are excluded, and a title company usually handles the upload.

Does the deed go to the auditor or the recorder first?

The auditor, who transfers it on the tax records with a conveyance form and then forwards it to the recorder. The auditor posts a timeline for deed transfers.

The Ohio Recorders' Association table shows $34.00 for two pages plus $8.00 for each added page, and up to $5.00 as a preservation surcharge. Ask the recorder about any county surcharge.

R.C. 5301.25 treats it as fraudulent against a later buyer who acted in good faith without notice. Record it as soon as the auditor has transferred it.

Where to take a deed in Hamilton County

Go to Room 205 at 138 East Court Street in Cincinnati. The office admits the public from 7:30 AM until 4:00 PM on weekdays, though the desk that accepts new filings shuts at 3:30 PM.

Mail goes to the same room. Include a stamped envelope bearing your own address, and expect the office to return the recorded deed in about two or three business days. Blank forms are not sold there, so a deed has to come from a lawyer, a closing agent or your own drafting.

Staff are not permitted to search records for customers. Anyone who needs title work should hire an examiner. Employees will gladly teach you the online index, and both the index and the document images cost nothing to view.

Hamilton County homes and owners

Hamilton County fills the southwest corner of Ohio, with Cincinnati as its seat, and it ranked third in population among Ohio counties after the 2020 count. The 2025 estimate is 838,418 residents, up from 830,639 in 2020.

  • Housing stock: 383,689 units, with 59.3% of households owning.
  • Homeowners report a median home value of $241,900 for 2020 to 2024.
  • Renters pay a median gross rent of $1,075, and the county logged 1,162 building permits for 2025.

The county was created in 1790, and that early start explains why the Recorder's site can display scanned deed books from 1794 onward. An old parcel here can have a long chain of recorded documents behind it.

Which office sees the deed first

The Auditor comes first and the Recorder second. By mail, the Recorder takes a conveyance only with the Engineer's and Auditor's stamps already on it, and staff will not carry the deed through those stops on your behalf.

  1. Have the deed drafted, signed and acknowledged.
  2. Fill out the conveyance form: DTE Form 100 when value is declared, DTE Form 100 EX when an exemption applies.
  3. Bring the deed, forms and fee to Room 304, the Auditor's Transfer Desk, on the same street.
  4. Take the stamped deed to Room 205, adding a return envelope if you want it mailed back.

The Transfer Desk keeps the same weekday hours, but paperwork arriving after 3:20 PM is held until the next business day. Because that cutoff comes before the Recorder's 3:30 PM close, leave time for the Auditor stop in the morning.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Hamilton County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Recording fees at the Hamilton County Recorder

Two pages of a deed, mortgage, lease or power of attorney cost $34.00 together, with $8.00 for every further page. The Ohio General Assembly, and not the county, sets these amounts.

ServiceFee
First two pages$34.00 (minimum fee $34.00)
Each added page$8.00

Self-serve copy$0.10 a page

Underpaid filings come back unrecorded, while overpaid filings are recorded and the difference refunded. Cards carry an added charge of $2.00 for debit, or the larger of $2.00 and 2.39% for credit.

What the Auditor collects at transfer

The Auditor charges three things on a taxable transfer here: a state conveyance fee of 1.00 per thousand of price, a county permissive tax of 2.00 per thousand, and .50 per parcel as the state transfer fee. Ask the Transfer Desk for the total on your price.

Certain transfers skip the price-based charges. Form DTE 100 EX names reasons such as gifts within a marriage or from parent to child, passage to an heir or devisee, and deeds that merely fix an earlier recorded one. Two exemption boxes always call for an affidavit of facts: security for a debt, and a no-money transfer that is not a gift.

Other forms may join the packet. A seller who had the homestead reduction last year or this year files DTE Form 101, and land with an agricultural use valuation calls for DTE Form 102.

Registered (Torrens) land

Registered land is no longer a separate track in Hamilton County. The Board of Commissioners passed Resolution 25 on August 6, 2014 to abolish it, and since November 10, 2015 any registered land document is recorded in the traditional system at the standard $34.00 and $8.00 rates.

No new certificate of title is issued under that change. A preparer should cite the existing certificate of title as the prior instrument until the parcel has changed hands.

Tell your title agent early if your parcel was ever registered. State law bars adverse possession claims against registered land, so such a parcel's history deserves a closer look.

Older records you can view online

The Recorder's home page opens a historic search that goes well past modern deeds. It lists grantor and grantee deed indexes for 1914 to 1988, deed books from 1794 to 1903, mortgage and mortgage release books from 1794 into the early 1900s, and mechanic lien, lease and power of attorney documents from the same early period.

  • Cemetery lot documents (1794 to 1934).
  • Church and organization documents (1794 to 1919).
  • Military discharge records (1794 to 1965).
  • Plat maps, a 1913 Cincinnati street index and a 1824 map of the Symmes survey.

These help a seller trace how a very old parcel was first conveyed, and they help a title examiner find an old easement or lien that never got released.

Page format for a deed

A single statute, ORC 317.114, sets the page standard statewide, and the Recorder's FAQ links to its standardization guidelines. Off-standard deeds are still taken, with $10 plus another $10 added.

  • Type at least size ten, in dark ink without highlighter.
  • Sheets from letter size up to legal length.
  • One inch of white space at the sides and the foot.
  • Three inches left clear at the head of page one, plus one and a half inches on later pages, for county endorsements.

Releases and assignments must carry a full legal description under ORC 5301.46, and a Hamilton County deed that describes the land differently from the last recorded deed may need a boundary survey approved by the County Engineer before the Auditor will transfer it.

Does Hamilton County offer a deed fraud alert?

Yes. The Recorder's Real Estate Fraud Alert is a free notification service. If a document is recorded under an identity you are watching, you receive an email.

The office's online search, called Acclaim, lets anyone browse the index and document images without paying. For owners who live out of town or hold inherited property, signing up costs nothing and gives early warning of an unexpected filing against the parcel.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Will the Hamilton County Recorder write my deed for me?

No. Blank forms are not sold there and staff cannot do searches or title work. Have a lawyer or closing agent draft the deed.

Can a deed be mailed to the Hamilton County Recorder?

Yes, once the Engineer's and Auditor's stamps are on it. Add a prepaid return envelope with your own address so the recorded deed can find its way home.

When does the Hamilton County recording desk shut?

At 3:30 PM, half an hour before the office itself closes. Items handed to the Auditor's Transfer Desk after 3:20 PM wait for the next business day.

Is one payment enough for both Hamilton County offices?

No. Each office bills separately: conveyance and transfer charges go to the Auditor, and the recording fee goes to the Recorder.

Must a new owner in Hamilton County record the deed?

In practice yes. ORC 5301.25 treats an unrecorded deed as fraudulent toward a later good-faith buyer who knew nothing of it, leaving the new owner's title exposed until the Recorder indexes the deed.

Where Hancock County deeds are filed in Findlay

The filing counter is at 300 S. Main Street, Room 23, Findlay, Ohio 45840, and the number to call is 419-424-7091. Doors are open weekdays from 8:30 am to 4:30 pm. The day's recordings end at 4:00 pm, so a document delivered later waits for the following business day.

Walk-in, mail and electronic filing are all accepted. A mailed package should hold the document, payment, a return envelope with your address, conveyance forms if ownership is changing hands, and recording instructions where the filing calls for them.

Hancock County homes and owners

Findlay is both the county seat and the largest city in this northwest Ohio county. The 2020 count was 74,920 residents, and the July 2025 estimate of 75,034 shows almost no movement. Roughly 70.8% of households own the home they live in.

  • Typical home value among owners: $204,700 for 2020 to 2024.
  • Median household income of $73,141.
  • 34,342 housing units, and 361 permits pulled during 2025.

A steady market with few new homes means a seller's deed history, not the neighborhood, is usually what decides how fast a closing goes.

Recording fees and the 2025 increase

A $5 increase took effect January 1, 2025, bringing the first two pages to $39 while added pages stay at $8. The Recorder's fee page credits Senate Bill 94 and cites ORC 317.32.

Hancock County Recorder fees
ServiceFee
First two pages of a deed, mortgage or lease$39
Each additional page$8
Marginal entry$4
Copies, assisted, per page$2
Copies, unassisted, per page$0.15
Non-conforming document (ORC 317.114)$20
Federal tax lien, and its release$5 and $3

Payment is by cash or check only, never card. Make the check out to the Hancock County Recorder and write a second check for the Auditor.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Hancock County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What goes to the Auditor with a deed

The Auditor's conveyance fee is $3.00 per thousand and the transfer fee is $0.50 per parcel. A deed that changes ownership stops at the Auditor before the Recorder, and the two offices coordinate so the transfer and recording line up.

ORC 319.202 has the buyer or the buyer's representative file the value statement. It counts the full consideration paid or to be paid, mortgage and vendor's lien included, as the value, and it forbids willfully falsifying that figure. An exempt transfer needs only a statement of the reason.

If the land had a homestead reduction or an agricultural valuation, ask the Auditor which extra forms apply, since the statute has the buyer question the seller on both.

Risk of an unrecorded deed

A deed left unrecorded loses ground to a later buyer. ORC 5301.25 sends deeds to the recorder of the county where the land lies, and until that happens they are fraudulent against a subsequent good-faith purchaser with no knowledge of them.

The same statute deals with surveys. When land being conveyed was surveyed, the Auditor requires the surveyor's name in the deed, in a line reading "A survey of this property was made by" and then the name.

  • File within days of closing.
  • Staple nothing: keep the Auditor's endorsement and the returned copy in one folder.
  • Compare the new legal description line by line with the prior deed.

Why indexing matters to a seller

Land records must stay current, legible and easy to reach, and indexing is what lets a searcher find each one. With it an examiner can assemble a chain of title, the line of ownership, and see debts or encumbrances against the land. Users include the public, attorneys, historians, genealogists and title examiners.

Some Ohio counties hold Torrens registered land, whose boundaries are certified and whose title a state insurance fund guarantees. For a seller here, a tidy deed history keeps a title search short, while a gap can delay closing.

Getting a copy of a deed or plat

There are three routes to a copy of a deed or mortgage: come to the office, phone with your name and address so staff can locate it, or search the website for anything recorded since January 1, 1985. Staff-assisted copies cost $2 a page, and copies you make yourself cost $0.15 a page.

  • Plats 24 by 36 inches: $50 a page.
  • Plats 11 by 17 inches: $40 a page.
  • Township zoning resolutions: $50, and zoning amendments: $20.

Township names in deed descriptions

Farmland outside Findlay is often described by township, so deeds for those parcels will cite these units. Check that your new deed repeats the description from the deed you received, word for word, before anyone signs.

Searching Hancock County land records yourself

The online search holds documents recorded and imaged from January 1, 1985 to the present, and historical indexes can be viewed online as well. Enter names last name first, such as Doe John, and enter companies as they normally appear.

You cannot search by parcel number at the Recorder's office. You need the owner's name and the legal description. If you lack either one, start at the Hancock County Auditor's website to find the owner and parcel details, then return to the Recorder.

Anything recorded before 1985 has to be searched in the office. The Recorder will also provide copies by phone, in person or through the website.

Can you e-record a deed in Hancock County?

Yes. Electronic filing is accepted for every document type, including deeds that must pass the Auditor's conveyance step. The office works with four outside submission services.

E-recording suits title firms, lenders and law offices best. A homeowner can simply ask whoever handles the closing whether the deed will be sent electronically.

After the deed is recorded

Once the Recorder indexes the deed, the new owner appears in the public chain of title and the buyer is protected against a later claim. Ask the closing agent for the recording date and keep the returned copy with the Auditor's endorsement. If anything looks wrong on it, such as a misspelled name or a changed legal description, call the Recorder at 419-424-7091 right away, because a correction is simpler the sooner it is caught. A seller who also owes on a mortgage should confirm the lender records a release, so the old loan does not linger in the index and trip up the next title search.

Steps for a typical sale

Have the deed prepared by an attorney or title office, since the Recorder does not hand out blank forms. Sign it before a notary. Take it with the conveyance form to the Auditor, pay the conveyance and transfer fees, then carry the endorsed deed to Room 23 before 4:00 pm with a separate check for the recording fee. If you mail it, enclose a return envelope. When the recorded deed comes back, keep it with your closing papers.

Frequently asked questions

Will the Hancock County Recorder add or remove a name on my deed?

Not without a new deed. Adding or removing someone, or changing a name, takes a newly prepared deed, and the office only records documents. An attorney or title office can prepare it.

Who holds my original deed after I pay off my mortgage in Hancock County?

Neither the Recorder nor your bank holds the original deed during the loan. You should get it back shortly after closing, so contact the attorney or title office that handled the sale. If it is lost, the Recorder can make a copy.

Does the Hancock County Recorder provide blank deed forms?

No. Blank deeds, mortgages, liens and other real property forms are not handed out there. Ask an attorney or title office to prepare one.

How much is the Hancock County conveyance fee?

The Auditor's conveyance fee is $3.00 per thousand, and the transfer fee is $0.50 per parcel. Confirm the total with the Auditor before you pay.

What time must I get a deed to the Hancock County Recorder?

By 4:00 pm. The office stays open until 4:30 pm, but recording for the day ends at 4:00 pm and later filings are recorded on the next business day.

Hardin County Recorder location and hours

The Hardin County Recorder is at One Courthouse Square, Suite 220, Kenton, Ohio 43326. Dial 419-674-2252 or 419-674-2250, or fax 419-675-2802. The counter opens at half past eight and closes at four on weekdays.

The Auditor is in the same courthouse, Suite 250, at 419-674-2239, and keeps hours of 8:00 to 4:00 on weekdays. Since a conveyance has to touch both offices, a short walk down the hall is often how a deed gets done.

The Recorder's page links to an online search run through Kofile, and it points visitors to the Ohio Recorders' Association site for more fee information. The office keeps the record of land ownership and of every lien against it, which is why a clean recorded deed matters to the next buyer.

Hardin County housing at a glance

Hardin County is small and mostly rural. The population has slipped from 32,058 in 2010 to 30,696 at the 2020 count and about 30,072 by July 2025. Owners occupy 74.7% of homes (2020 to 2024), and the typical owner-reported home value is $151,200. Median gross rent is $793, and the county has 12,944 housing units.

With a falling population and many single-person households, a house can sit listed for a while. A sale to someone paying cash and closing at a local title office still ends with the same Auditor stamp and the same Recorder filing, so the deed steps below apply to either route.

Why the Auditor's stamp comes first

A mailed conveyance is taken only when the Auditor's stamp is already on it. The office will not walk a conveyance through the map department and the Auditor's office for you.

That sets the order: map department and Auditor first, Recorder last. A seller who mails a deed straight to the Recorder should expect it to come back unrecorded. A seller who lives far away can hand that errand to the attorney or title agent running the closing.

On the Auditor's forms page you will find the DTE 100 value statement, the DTE 100EX exemption statement and the DTE 101 homestead conveyance statement, with a reminder to confirm the newest version with the Ohio Department of Taxation.

What recording costs in Hardin County

The recording fee comes from state statute. ORC 317.32 builds the opening pair of pages from a $17 base fee and a $17 housing trust fund fee, with $4 and $4 for each page that follows. A county may also charge a document preservation surcharge of up to $5.

State fee schedule for recording
ServiceFee
Recording, opening two pages$34.00 (surcharge up to $5.00 may apply)
Recording, each additional page$8.00
Marginal notation$4.00
Certified copy$2.00 per page and $1.00 per seal
Document not meeting format standard$20.00
Release of federal lien$3.00

Call the Recorder at either number to learn exactly what the county adds per document, and keep the receipt with your closing papers. Pay the Recorder for recording, and expect separate Auditor charges.

Signing and acknowledging the deed

The seller signs and then acknowledges the deed in front of an authorized official. Under ORC 5301.01 that can be a judge or clerk of a court of record, a county auditor, a county engineer, a notary public or a mayor, who certifies the acknowledgment.

Many sellers visit a notary at a title company or bank. The deed then goes to the Auditor with a completed DTE 100, or a DTE 100EX for an exempt transfer. Ask the Hardin County Auditor for the conveyance rate and per-parcel transfer fee before closing.

ORC 317.114 sets the page format here as in every Ohio county: legible print, black or blue ink, no highlighting, and empty space at the head of the page for county stamps.

Manufactured home sales

Manufactured or mobile homes that are taxed like real property use their own set of forms. The Auditor posts a registration certificate (DTE 41), a conveyance fee statement of value and receipt (DTE 100M), and an exemption statement (DTE 100MEX) for that category.

A refund or waiver application for destroyed or damaged manufactured homes (DTE 49) is posted too. When the home sits on land you own, ask the Auditor whether your sale takes the real property forms, the manufactured home forms, or both.

The Real Estate section adds the 2 1/2% reduction application (DTE 105C), the valuation complaint (DTE 1) and a deduction application for damaged or destroyed property (DTE 26). Ask about the 2 1/2% reduction at closing if the buyer will make the house a primary home.

Tax dates that affect a sale

The Auditor describes a full reappraisal of real property every six years with an update every three. Find out where your parcel sits in that cycle, because a new value can change the tax bills a buyer inherits.

On the Auditor's calendar, February 11 is the last day to pay the first half of the real estate bill without penalty and July 8 is the last day for the second half. The Board of Revision complaint period opens January 3 and closes March 31. Homestead and 2 1/2% rollback applications are due in early June. Check your tax bill for exact dates, since weekends and holidays can move them.

  • Learn from the closing agent how taxes will be prorated.
  • Ask whether the parcel has a homestead reduction, because DTE 101 then travels with the deed.
  • Photograph the stamped deed before it goes to the Recorder.

What to bring to the courthouse

Bring the signed and acknowledged deed, the completed DTE form, and a check for the Auditor's fees. If the land has a homestead reduction, add the DTE 101. If it has an agricultural valuation, ask whether another statement is needed. Know the parcel number and the legal description from your own deed, since the map department compares the new description against the old one. A new description that differs from the prior deed can get a deed sent back.

Order of steps for a Hardin County sale

Have the deed prepared by an attorney or title agent and signed before a notary. Visit the map department and the Auditor in Suite 250 with the DTE form and the fees. Walk the stamped deed to Suite 220 and pay the recording fee. If you mail it, make sure the Auditor's stamp is already on it and include a return envelope.

Once recorded, the deed is indexed in the online search, which a later title examiner will read. If you paid off a mortgage on the property, check that the release was recorded too. A missing release is a common reason a closing stalls, and the lender is the one who has to fix it.

Frequently asked questions

Can a deed go by mail to the Hardin County Recorder?

Only if the Auditor's stamp is already on it. Without that stamp the Recorder's Office will not take the conveyance, and staff will not walk deeds through the map department or Auditor.

When is the Hardin County Recorder open?

It opens at half past eight each weekday morning and closes at 4:00 p.m., at One Courthouse Square, Suite 220 in Kenton.

Who can notarize a deed in Ohio?

Under ORC 5301.01 a notary public, a county auditor, a county engineer, a mayor, or a judge or clerk of a court of record can take the acknowledgment. Most sellers use a notary.

Is there a Hardin County online records search?

Yes. The Recorder's page links to an online service and search provided through Kofile.

Who tells me the Hardin County conveyance fee?

The Auditor, at 419-674-2239. That office collects the conveyance and transfer fees before the deed moves on to the Recorder.

Harrison County Recorder location and hours

The Harrison County Recorder's Office is at 100 West Market Street, Cadiz, Ohio 43907. The phone is 740-942-8869 and the fax is 740-942-4693. The office is open Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., excluding holidays.

Recording stops at 4:15 p.m. Anything received between 4:15 and 4:30 goes on the next day's business. A recorded document comes back by mail in about two to three working days, and a self-addressed stamped envelope is required for every mailing.

The office does not furnish forms, and only completed documents are recorded. Staff inspect each document and try to have errors corrected before filing.

Harrison County homes and owners

Harrison County is a rural county in eastern Ohio, with Cadiz as the seat and largest village. It is among the least populous counties in the state: 14,483 people at the 2020 census and an estimated 14,070 in July 2025. Townships and villages all record in Cadiz.

  • Median value of an owner-occupied home: $121,500 (2020 to 2024).
  • Owner-occupied rate: 76.3%, with 7,361 housing units.
  • Median household income: $54,414.
  • Building permits in 2025: 2.

With so little new construction, most sales here are resales of older homes and land, so a clean deed history matters a good deal to the buyer's title agent.

Deed preapproval in Harrison County

Since October 1, 2022, every transfer is preapproved before recording. The Harrison County Auditor and Engineer adopted minimum requirements for instruments of conveyance so that land is described accurately for tax purposes.

The steps run through three offices, and all three must finish before the deed is recorded:

  1. Submit an unsigned copy of the deed, not the original meant for recording, with a completed Document Conveyance Form. It can go by email to the Map Office, by mail, by delivery or in person.
  2. Wait at least four days while the Map Office, the Auditor and the Recorder review it and return it with any changes explained.
  3. After approval, bring the signed documents in person, by mail, by delivery or to the dropbox. The Map Office forwards them to the Auditor, and the Auditor sends them on to the Recorder.

The Auditor's goal for its own part is 24 hours, though workload can stretch it. If you hand in several documents, say in what order they should be processed.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Harrison County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What the Auditor charges on a transfer

The conveyance fee is $4.00 per thousand of the sale price, with no rounding, and the transfer fee is $0.50 per parcel. Both are due before the transfer is approved. The Auditor accepts check or cash only.

Under ORC 319.202 the grantor pays the conveyance fee and any county transfer tax, while the grantee files the value statement. Every transfer needs a named seller and buyer, an accurate legal description with the full parcel numbers, and a stamp of approval from the Map Office.

  • DTE Form 100 declares value on a taxable transfer.
  • DTE Form 100EX explains the reason on an exempt one.
  • DTE Form 101 is required if the parcel participates in the homestead reduction.
  • DTE Form 102 is required if the parcel participates in the agricultural valuation program.
  • A DTE Attachment Sheet helps when many parcel numbers will not fit on the form.

Splits and combinations of parcels need Auditor preapproval and a minimum of three days. Those requests are made by form and emailed, since they are no longer taken in person.

Recording fees at the Harrison County Recorder

The Recorder charges $34.00 for the first two pages and $8.00 for each page after that, under ORC 317.32. Half of all recording fees go to the state for the Ohio Housing Trust Fund. The statute also permits a document preservation surcharge of up to $5, so call the office for the total before you write a check.

Harrison County recording and copy fees
ServiceFee
Recording, first two pages$34.00
Recording, each additional page$8.00
Marginal reference by separate instrument$4.00
Certified photocopy$2.00 per page, plus $1.00 for the seal
Photocopy of a record$2.00 per page
Plat, minimum fee$40.00

Certified copies of military discharge papers are free to the person discharged.

Deed abbreviations in Harrison County records

The Auditor's transfer page lists common deed types with short codes that appear in county records. Knowing them helps you read a chain of title.

  • WD is a General Warranty Deed, and QC is a Quit Claim Deed.
  • ED is an Executor's Deed, AD an Administrator's Deed and FD a Fiduciary Deed.
  • TD is a Trustee's Deed, and SD is a Sheriff's Deed.
  • SV is a Survivorship Deed, and TO is a Transfer on Death Designation Affidavit.
  • CD is a Corrected Deed or re-recording, and MD is a Mineral Deed.
  • AF is an Affidavit, AT an Affidavit Relating to Title, and RW a Right of Way or Easement.

A seller who inherited the house will often hold an ED, AD or TO in the chain. A buyer's title agent will want that document and the preceding ones in order.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Harrison County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Zoning filings and the records commission

The Recorder serves on the county records commission, which decides how long county records are kept and when they may be disposed of. Each year the office notifies the county commissioners and township trustees of their duty to file zoning resolutions, maps and amendments. Those zoning filings can matter to a seller with land in one of the 15 townships.

Mineral rights on Harrison County deeds

They can show up. Harrison County sits over the Utica shale, and its history includes oil finds near Jewett in 1895 and the Scio area in 1898. Because of that, a deed may reserve or convey minerals separately from the surface.

The Auditor's list of common deed types includes a Mineral Deed, along with the General Warranty Deed, Quit Claim Deed, Survivorship Deed, Transfer on Death Designation Affidavit and others. The state recorders' fee table also lists a claim to preserve mineral interests as a recordable item.

  • Ask the title company whether minerals were reserved in an earlier deed.
  • Ask whether any oil and gas lease is of record on the parcel.
  • Make sure the new deed states exactly what is conveyed.

Searching Harrison County records online

The Recorder offers an online records search through Kofile's CountyFusion and a newer cloud search at harrison.oh.publicsearch.us. A Property Alert service is also listed on the Recorder's page.

If you ask for copies by mail, the Recorder charges $2.00 per page, and payment is due before the copies are sent. To find a record, give the owner's name, the volume and page, or the subdivision, lot, township, range and section.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Putting it together for a Harrison County seller

Start with the Map Office, because nothing moves until the unsigned deed is approved. Plan on at least four days for that review. Once approved, sign before a notary, pay the Auditor's fees by check or cash, and let the Map Office pass the documents along. The Recorder then files the deed and mails it back within about two to three working days. Build that timeline into your closing date.

Frequently asked questions

How long does Harrison County preapproval take?

A minimum of four days. The Map Office, Auditor and Recorder all review the unsigned copy before returning it with any needed changes.

What does Harrison County charge per thousand dollars of price?

The Auditor charges $4.00 per thousand of the sale price, without rounding, plus $0.50 per parcel, payable by check or cash.

What time does the Harrison County Recorder stop recording?

4:15 p.m. Documents received after that until 4:30 p.m. are recorded the next business day.

Does the Harrison County Recorder supply deed forms?

No. The Recorder's office does not furnish forms. The Auditor does not prepare deeds either and recommends a legal representative for a transfer.

Can I get a copy of discharge papers in Harrison County?

Yes. Certified copies of military discharge papers are free to the person discharged, and certified copies of DD214s go to funeral homes.

Where Henry County deeds are recorded

Henry County deeds are filed in Napoleon, in Suite 202 up the stairs in the courthouse at 660 N. Perry Street. The Recorder's number is 419-592-1766, and the counter shuts at 4:30 on weekdays. Nobody is there on weekends or holidays.

One recorder covers all of Henry County, roughly 416 square miles. A farm along the Putnam County line and a house inside Napoleon are handled at the same window. The county's recorder page calls the office custodian of land records. It accepts deeds, mortgages, mechanic's liens, powers of attorney, IRS liens, subdivision plats, military discharges, partnership papers, and the zoning resolutions of the county and its townships.

Why old chains of title matter here

Henry County was organized in 1834, so its recorded deeds reach back about two hundred years of farm and town sales. Inherited houses and family farms can carry decades of easements, mortgages and affidavits. A title company digs those out of the recorder's index, so a seller should expect them to come up. Napoleon is the county seat and its biggest city.

Forms and the Auditor's role

The Henry County Auditor works in the same courthouse and can be reached at 419-592-1956. These Ohio sale forms are posted on the auditor's site:

  • DTE 100, the value statement and receipt that goes with a conveyance.
  • DTE 100EX, where you write down why a transfer owes no such fee.
  • DTE 101 for a homestead parcel, DTE 102 for a parcel in the farm valuation program.
  • The Henry County Land Transfer Policy. Ask the auditor's staff for a copy early.

Before the Recorder, the deed goes to the auditor. Under section 319.202 the buyer files a value statement, the auditor endorses the deed, and a rental house triggers an extra landlord filing under Chapter 5323. After that it moves on to the Recorder.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Henry County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What the Auditor charges on a sale

The auditor's charge comes from section 319.54(G)(3): $1 at minimum, or a dime for each hundred dollars of value if that is more, with part of a hundred counted whole. The seller pays. Get the dollar figure for your price from the counter before closing day.

Any Ohio county may add a transfer tax of up to thirty cents per $100 under section 322.02. The grantor pays it before the Recorder sees the deed. Ask the auditor whether Henry County levies it, and check that your settlement sheet reflects the answer.

Some transfers owe no statement fee. Examples are a gift deed, a conveyance worth $100 or less, a deed that only pledges the land as security, and a split among one estate's heirs. The reason is written on DTE 100EX.

Recording charges for a deed

Fees follow section 317.32. Every charge has a base fee and a matching housing trust fund fee. For the first two pages that is $17 plus $17, and for each later page $4 plus $4. Counties can also add a preservation surcharge, up to $5. The office can quote the total for your deed.

Pages are counted at 8.5 by 14 inches, and the caption page is page one. If a deed runs a few lines onto a third sheet, the cost rises, so keep the format tight.

The state's layout rule in section 317.114 applies too, and some Ohio counties charge $20 for a deed that breaks it. Ask what Henry County adds before you sign one with odd margins or tiny type.

Henry County housing numbers

Owners live in about 82.5% of the occupied homes here, and a typical owner-occupied house is valued at $168,600. Just 19 building permits were issued in 2025, so a resale seldom competes with new construction, and a nearby farm sale can set the tone for pricing.

Henry County housing and income
MeasureHenry County

Housing units (July 2025)12,144
Share living in their own home82.5%
Typical owner-occupied value$168,600
Typical monthly rent$849
Typical household income$80,099

About a third of residents lived in urban areas at the 2020 census and two thirds in rural ones, which is why farm parcels and big lots show up in the recorder's queue as often as town lots.

Sheriff sales and the Recorder

Online sheriff sales through RealAuction cover orders received after August 1, 2022. Tax sales take place downstairs in the courthouse. Bidders must wire or ACH a deposit, never cash. The deposit depends on the appraised value:

  • $2,000 for an appraisal up to $10,000.
  • $5,000 for an appraisal from $10,000 to $200,000.
  • $10,000 for an appraisal above $200,000.

Following the auction, the buyer waits 30 to 45 days for the court to confirm the sale and for the sheriff's deed. The former owner keeps title until the judge signs, and the new owner gets title only when the sheriff's deed lands in the Henry County Recorder's index. Within 14 days, the judgment creditor and the first lienholder may redeem by paying the clerk of courts the full price.

Property tax help in Henry County

The Treasurer's mailing address is P.O. Box 546, Napoleon, and the phone is 419-592-1851. Monthly payment plans for unpaid back taxes and current taxes halt added interest and penalties. A Tax Installment Prepay plan breaks the annual bill into coupons, and a late coupon draws no penalty as long as each half is paid in full by its closing date.

Henry County has 40 taxing districts, each with its own rate, and taxable value is 35% of market. Reappraisal comes every six years, with an update in the third year. An owner who disagrees with a valuation can file with the Board of Revision between January 1 and March 31. The 2 1/2% owner-occupancy rollback needs one application, due before the first Monday in June.

On the homestead page, the TY2025 figures are a $40,000 income limit and a $28,000 exemption, with more for disabled military service members. Owners who are struggling can contact NOCAC, the Northwestern Ohio Community Action Commission, or Maumee Valley Planning's housing program.

If you owe on the house at closing

Any mortgage balance and unpaid tax are normally paid from your proceeds by the title company, and the lender then records a release. Get a payoff figure from the Treasurer ahead of closing. Also ask the auditor if the parcel has a homestead reduction, because DTE 101 then travels with the deed. Carry the parcel number and the legal description from your own deed so staff can match the new deed to the tax record without a callback.

Allow time for each stop. The deed goes to the auditor first, then to the Recorder in Suite 202, and mailing it adds days. A seller who is out of town can ask the closing agent to carry the paperwork across the courthouse.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Who records Henry County deeds, and where?

The Henry County Recorder, in Suite 202 on the second floor of the courthouse at 660 N. Perry Street in Napoleon. The phone is 419-592-1766.

Do I visit the auditor before the recorder?

Yes. The auditor receives the buyer's statement of value and endorses the deed, then the recorder files it. Both offices sit in the Napoleon courthouse.

How is the Ohio conveyance fee figured?

Whichever is larger: $1, or ten cents for each $100 of value, rounding any part of $100 up. The seller pays it unless an exemption applies.

Is there a county transfer tax in Henry County?

Ask the auditor. Ohio allows a county to levy up to thirty cents per $100 after two hearings.

Can a sheriff-sale buyer record immediately?

No. The judge must confirm the sale and the sheriff must receive the deed, which takes 30 to 45 days after the auction. Title passes when the sheriff's deed is recorded.

Highland County Recorder location and hours

The Highland County Recorder works from Suite 108 at 119 Governor Foraker Place in Hillsboro, with mail going to P.O. Box 804, Hillsboro, OH 45133. The county's recorder page gives 937-393-9954 and an 8 to 4 weekday schedule.

One rule catches late arrivals. Anything handed in after 3:30 PM waits overnight and is run the next business day, so a seller racing a closing should be at the counter early in the afternoon at the latest.

The auditor, who has to see your deed first, is at the same street address and answers at 937-393-1915. A seller in Greenfield, Lynchburg or a rural township has to drive to Hillsboro to record.

What the Highland County Recorder charges per deed

The recorder's page prints a flat price by page count, effective January 1, 2025. Two pages or fewer cost $39, and every added page raises the price by $8.

Recording price by page count
Length of documentPrice
One or two pages$39
Three pages$47
Five pages$63
Seven pages$79
Ten pages$103

Only cash or a check works for recording, and cards are not taken at this time. A marginal notation adds $4 per reference. A UCC form is $12, plus $4 for each name, and only when the filing involves real estate and carries a full legal description.

Formatting mistakes that cost extra

Highland County enforces the Ohio layout rule in section 317.114. A document notarized after July 1, 2009 that ignores it draws a $20 surcharge. Four habits avoid it:

  • Use sheets from 8.5 by 11 up to 8.5 by 14 inches.
  • Print in type of ten points or more, black or blue ink only, with nothing highlighted.
  • Keep a three-inch strip clear on the first page for official stamps.
  • Send a stamped, self-addressed envelope if you want the original mailed back.

The recorder's page also links a county conveyance standards sheet on the auditor's website. Read it before the deed is drafted. A rejection by the tax map office or the auditor costs a second trip even when no money penalty follows.

How a deed moves between Highland County offices

The county publishes a recording procedure with a set order. First you bring the packet to the Recorder for a quick look at whether it is recordable and the fees are right. Next you visit the Auditor to confirm forms and the conveyance fee. Then you return to the Recorder with payment and contact details.

Behind the counter the packet goes to the Tax Map office, which stamps it or rejects it for fixes. The Auditor checks it again, and the Recorder records it and calls you, or mails it in your envelope. Ask your title company whether it will carry the packet in person.

The auditor's forms page lists the Ohio paperwork: DTE 100 and DTE 100EX for the fee statement and its exemption, DTE 101 for homestead property and DTE 102 for the farm valuation program. The auditor's tools menu also has a conveyance fee calculator that adds a parcel transfer fee. Confirm any figure it produces with the staff.

State rules that apply to a Highland County sale

The auditor endorses the deed after the buyer files a value statement under section 319.202. The seller pays the statement fee in section 319.54(G)(3), which is the larger of $1 or ten cents per $100 of value.

A county can add a transfer tax capped at thirty cents per $100 by section 322.02. Ask the Highland County Auditor whether this county has done so. Exemptions cover gifts within a family, deeds for no payment, tax-sale deeds and deeds that only secure a debt.

Farmland needs one more answer on the statement. Land that leaves the valuation program owes a recoupment charge equal to three years of tax savings, so a farm seller should ask the auditor for the figure before signing a contract.

What a seller can look up on the auditor's website

Before you list, spend ten minutes on the auditor's site. These pieces matter most to a seller:

  • A parcel search by number, owner or address, with a GIS viewer for boundaries.
  • A sales report and sales list of recent transfers.
  • A delinquency report for past-due balances.
  • A conveyance fee calculator and a tax estimator.

Those tools answer the questions a buyer's agent will ask. Which nearby parcels changed hands, and for how much? Does the house you are selling show a past-due balance? What would the tax estimator say on the contract price? A seller who has run those lookups can set a price and a closing date without waiting on a title company's search.

Steps for a typical Highland County sale

Your closing agent usually prepares the deed, but you can follow the order yourself. Have the deed drafted to meet the layout rules and signed before a notary. Take the packet to the Recorder in Suite 108 for a first look, then to the Auditor in the same building to confirm the forms and the conveyance fee. Return to the Recorder with payment by cash or check. Plan to arrive before 3:30 PM so the deed is recorded that day.

Once the deed is recorded, ask for the recording information and keep the returned original with your closing papers. If you paid off a mortgage, search the parcel afterward to see that the release was recorded. A release that never reached the index is the kind of gap a later buyer's title company will flag.

Watching for deed fraud

The recorder's page links two guides under the Fraud Sleuth name, one plain and one step by step with pictures. Ask the office how the service works and how to enroll your parcel. That matters most for a vacant, inherited or rented house that nobody checks every day.

Records can be searched through the online records link on the same page, so a seller can pull up the last recorded deed, mortgage or lien before listing. Finding a paid-off mortgage that was never released is better done early than at the closing table.

Anyone who inherited a Highland County house should search the parcel before promising a closing date. The last deed on file may be under a relative's name from long ago.

Highland County housing context

The Census estimate is 43,823 residents in 2025 and 19,196 housing units. Owners live in 74.3% of occupied homes, with a typical home value of $168,900 and typical rent of $780. Buford, Highland Holiday and Rocky Fork Point are census-designated places inside the county, all recorded at the same Hillsboro counter.

Frequently asked questions

What does a two-page deed cost to record in Highland County?

$39 under the rates effective January 1, 2025. A three-page deed costs $47, and each added page adds $8 up to $103 at ten pages.

Can I pay the Highland County Recorder by card?

No. Recordings are cash or check only, so bring one of those and a stamped, self-addressed envelope if you want the deed mailed back.

How late can I bring a deed in for same-day recording?

Before 3:30 PM. The office stays open to 4:00 PM, but anything received after 3:30 PM waits for the next business day.

Why is the auditor involved in recording a deed?

Ohio has the auditor review the buyer's value statement and endorse the deed first. In Highland County the packet runs from the recorder to the auditor, the tax map office and back to the recorder.

What if my deed ignores the state layout rules?

The recorder adds $20 for a nonconforming document notarized after July 1, 2009, and the tax map office or auditor may reject it. Black or blue ink and the right margins avoid both.

Where to record a deed in Hocking County

Hocking County deeds go to the ground-level office inside the courthouse at 1 East Main Street, Logan. Mail goes to P.O. Box 949, Logan, OH 43138. Call 740-385-2031 for the office or 740-385-0377 for fax.

Two clocks apply. Visitors are welcome until 4 in the afternoon, but recording stops at half past three, the same cutoff as copy requests, and the research room shuts at 3:45. In bad weather the office opens at 10 a.m. under a Level 2 snow advisory and stays closed under Level 3, so phone before driving in from the Hocking Hills side.

The index covers records from 1818, and electronic indexing began on January 1, 1992. Buchtel, Laurelville and Murray City use the same counter as everyone else in the county. The office also links an online payment portal and a land records search from its page.

Recording fees

The county posts its own fee sheet. Recording costs a flat $39 for the first two pages and $8 for each page after, and that price includes a $5 restoration fee. Payment can be made at the counter.

Hocking County Recorder fees
ServiceCharge
Recording, first two pages$39
Recording, each page after$8
Marginal reference$4 each
Document that breaks the layout rules$20
Print made in the office$1 a page
Print made by staff, or an emailed copy$2 a page

The office does not run title searches, give legal advice or prepare documents. Have the deed drafted ahead of time by your closing agent or lawyer, then bring it in with the payment.

Layout rules for a deed

House Bill 525 created the layout standards, now section 317.114 of the Revised Code, effective July 1, 2009. A deed that falls short costs $20 more. Hocking's counter checks each deed against this list:

  • Print no smaller than 10 point, in black or blue ink. Highlighter is never allowed.
  • Leave a one inch border down both sides and along the foot of every sheet.
  • Keep the top three inches of page one blank for the recorder, auditor and engineer stamps. Later pages need only an inch and a half.

Court and taxing authority papers, plats, DD-214 discharges, state or federal documents and anything signed before the law took effect are exempt. A deed you draft yourself is not. If you are selling without an agent, check the margins before you print the signature page.

What the recorder files

The county's list is long, and a seller's file may touch several items on it. Deeds can be warranty, quit claim, survivorship or sheriff's deeds. Mortgage papers include releases, assumptions, assignments, subordinations and waivers of priority. The office also files certificates of transfer, affidavits, easements, leases, land contracts, plats, condominium records, powers of attorney and trusts.

A title search will turn up liens, so read this part of the county's list closely:

  • Mechanic's liens and notices of commencement.
  • Federal tax liens and personal tax liens.
  • Workers' compensation and unemployment compensation liens.
  • Child support liens and Medicaid fraud liens.

If you know of one, tell your buyer or title company early. Annexations, street name changes and vacated streets and alleys are also recorded here, which can affect a rural lot's frontage.

The auditor and the conveyance fee

The auditor sees the deed first and collects the Ohio conveyance fee. Call 740-385-2127 for the figure on your sale price. The auditor's tools menu includes a calculator that adds a parcel transfer fee to its answer. Ask at the same time whether the county levies a real property transfer tax, since that is optional for each county.

A January 2026 message on the auditor's site says short-term rentals are now valued apart from residential property, at their market value as short-term rentals. If you are selling a cabin near the state park, ask how the parcel is classified before you quote taxes to a buyer.

The same message says the budget commission, commissioners and township trustees trimmed inside millage so collections stayed near the 2024 level after the 2025 valuation update. Without that, the auditor estimates inside millage would have drawn about $1.25 million more, a 22% increase.

Reducing or contesting a tax bill

The owner occupancy credit, once called the 2 1/2% reduction, is for owners who live in the house as their main residence. File with the auditor between January 1 and the first Monday in June. It does not cover rentals, corporate or partnership owners, units in commercial buildings, taxed manufactured homes and acreage beyond one acre.

If you disagree with the value, the Board of Revision hears appeals filed with the auditor from January 1 through March 31. The board is made up of the treasurer, the auditor and the president of the commissioners. The best evidence is a recent sale price shown by closing papers, or sales of comparable homes, plus photographs of the property's condition.

A late-payment penalty can be removed on request for these reasons:

  • You never got a correct bill and made an effort to get one.
  • Your payment was mailed on time with a proper postmark but never processed.
  • Serious injury, death or a hospital stay within 60 days before the due date, with payment inside 60 days after it.
  • A mistake made by the auditor or treasurer.
  • Reasonable cause without willful neglect, for owners timely in each of the last three years.

Taxes and the land bank

The treasurer is in Suite 201 of the courthouse, phone 740-385-3517. If you sell near a collection date, ask the treasurer to confirm that both halves of the year's bill have posted before closing.

Five state tax bills were signed December 19, 2025. House Bill 186 raises the owner occupancy credit from 2.5% toward 15.38% by tax year 2029 and phases out the 10% non-business credit, and House Bill 335 slows growth in inside millage to the rate of inflation. Most of that shows up on bills from 2027 on.

The county also runs a land bank. It acquires vacant, abandoned and tax-foreclosed properties, waives delinquent taxes on property it takes, and deed-restricts residential parcels to prevent nightly rentals. Owners of worthless or low-value parcels can offer them to the bank instead of leaving them to a tax foreclosure. Houses the bank sells go to buyers who show a need for single-family housing and agree to owner-occupy.

Housing numbers that help set a price

Hocking County had 27,512 people in July 2025 and 13,024 housing units. Owners live in 78.8% of occupied homes, the typical home value is $186,400, typical rent is $808 and household income is about $62,960. Lodging and restaurant sales were high for the region, which points to a visitor economy. A seller near the park should not assume every buyer wants a year-round home.

A typical sequence for a sale

Most Hocking County sales follow the same path. Your closing agent or lawyer drafts the deed to the layout rules above. You sign it, and the auditor collects the conveyance fee. The deed then goes to the recorder before 3:30 p.m., with the recording charge. Any mortgage release your lender files after payoff is recorded at the same counter, so ask your title company to confirm both were filed.

A flat $39 covers the first two pages, and each extra page adds $8, including a $5 restoration fee. A deed that breaks the layout rules adds $20.

When does the Hocking County Recorder stop taking documents?

At 3:30 p.m. on weekdays. The office stays open to visitors until 4:00, and the research room closes at 3:45.

Yes. Emailed copies cost $2 per page, and requests should arrive by 3:30 p.m. A copy printed at the office costs $1 per page.

Farm tracts that pass between families often carry old metes and bounds wording, and that is what the Tax Map staff read line by line. Budget one workday for each submission.
