Where to record a Madison County deed

The Madison County Recorder is at the courthouse in London: 1 N Main St, Room 40, London, OH 43140. Call 740-852-1854. The counter opens at 8 AM and closes at 4 PM on weekdays, though recording ends at 3:30 PM, so a deed handed over at 3:45 waits until the next business day.

Electronic recording runs through four platforms: CSC eRecording (866-652-0111), Simplifile, ePN and Hopdox. Ask your title company or attorney which one they use. The deed can then be recorded without a trip to the courthouse.

Recording fees

A two-page deed is $39.00 and each extra page is $8.00. Senate Bill 94 added a $5.00 surcharge to most documents to fund the preservation and digitizing of records and the office's running costs, under section 317.32.

That statute builds the amount from half a base fee, half a housing trust fund fee, plus an optional county surcharge. Copies, certified copies, references to older documents and zoning filings carry their own listed amounts. Phone 740-852-1854 to price any unusual document before you mail payment.

How far back the online land records reach

Different record types start at different dates. Checking the right category saves a trip to the courthouse.

Online coverage by record type, Madison County Recorder
Record typeOnline coverage
DeedsScanned, indexed and online from March 1, 1920 to present
Mortgages, indexingIndexed from July 17, 1964
Mortgages, imagesScanned and indexed from September 25, 1968
Miscellaneous, lease, lien, federal tax lien, mechanics lien, unemployment compensation lien, mortgage releaseHistorical Archive online, dating to at least 1980, some older

All the original books remain in the office. If a search turns up a gap, call the counter and ask staff to follow up in the books.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Madison County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What the Auditor does with a deed first

Ohio makes the Auditor endorse the deed before the Recorder files it. Under section 319.202, the buyer's representative submits a statement of value, or a statement of the exemption reason, and the Auditor notes the conveyance fee on the deed itself.

The Madison County Auditor is at 1 N Main St, PO Box 47, London, OH 43140-0047, phone 740-852-9717, weekdays 8 AM to 4 PM. The property transfer forms page lists the packet pieces a closer may need:

  • DTE 100, the conveyance fee statement of value and receipt.
  • DTE 100EX, the statement of the reason for an exemption.
  • DTE 101, a statement of conveyance of homestead property.
  • DTE 102, a statement of conveyance of current agricultural use valuation property.
  • DTE 100M and DTE 41 for manufactured or mobile homes.
  • Affidavits of trustee and successor trustee under sections 317.22 and 5302.171.

The Auditor's site also carries a conveyance fee calculator under its Tools menu. Run your sale through it, or phone the office, rather than guessing at the county's rate.

Sale price, gifts and the value statement

For an arm's length sale, the measure under section 319.202 is everything paid or promised, including any mortgage balance the buyer takes over. For a gift, the measure shifts to what the house would sell for on the open market. Misstating either figure on purpose is unlawful.

The buyer's statement also answers two questions. Was the seller asked whether tax reductions for owner occupancy or homestead apply? Was the land under the agricultural use valuation? A yes to either needs a sworn instrument attached. If the house is a rental, the endorsement points the buyer to a landlord filing under section 5323.02.

Free tools on the Auditor's website

The Auditor's home page lets you search any parcel by owner, address or parcel number to see its appraisal and payment history. A menu of tools sits beside the search box, and several help a seller price and plan:

  • A sales report and a sales list of recent transfers.
  • A delinquency report.
  • A conveyance fee calculator and a tax estimator.
  • A levy estimator, plus a GIS parcel viewer reached from the map link.

Conveyance fee rules

Two statutes work together. Section 319.54(G)(3) sets the state charge at a dollar or a dime per hundred, whichever is bigger. Section 322.02 lets commissioners layer on a local tax up to thirty cents per hundred, owed by the grantor.

Exemptions cover several family and estate situations:

  • Gifts within a marriage, or handed down to a son or daughter.
  • Transfers among the heirs of one decedent when nobody pays money.
  • Moves into or out of a revocable trust.
  • A corrective deed that fixes an earlier recorded deed.

The exemption reason belongs on the form. Without it the Auditor will not stamp the deed as exempt, and the Recorder will not accept a deed that skipped the Auditor.

Madison County housing and the 2026 reappraisal

Madison County lies in central Ohio west of Franklin County, with London as the seat and largest city. Population was 46,985 in mid-2025, up 7.1 percent since 2020, with 17,383 housing units. A typical owned home is valued at $250,100, owners occupy 77.5 percent of homes, and rent runs a median $943. The Auditor has finished a countywide reappraisal for tax year 2026, with tentative values shown for each parcel on its website, so look up your own parcel before setting a price.

Land across a county line

Neighbors include Union and Champaign counties to the north and northwest, Franklin County to the east, Pickaway to the southeast, Fayette to the south, and Greene and Clark to the west. An owner with land across a county line needs a separate recorder and auditor filing in each county.

Putting the sale together

The title company or attorney prepares the deed and the Auditor's form. Take both to the Auditor first for the endorsement, then to the Recorder in Room 40 before 3:30 PM, or send the packet through an e-recording platform. A cash sale with no lender payoff means no mortgage release to record, so the paperwork is usually just the deed and its transfer form.

Before you go, confirm the deed has the legal description and prior deed reference, that every signature is notarized, and that the page count matches the fee you are bringing. If a document is unusual, such as a trust affidavit or a corrective deed, call 740-852-1854 first so the office can tell you the charge. When the sale involves a rental, remember the landlord filing the Auditor's endorsement points to, and when it involves farmland, ask whether the parcel sits under the agricultural use valuation.

Frequently asked questions

When does Madison County stop recording each day?

3:30 PM. The office is open until 4 PM on weekdays but stops recording at 3:30, so deliver deeds earlier in the afternoon or use an e-recording service.

What is Madison County's price for recording a deed?

A two-page deed is $39.00 and each extra page is $8.00. Check with the office for extra charges that apply to references, copies or special filings.

Can I e-record a deed in Madison County?

Yes. The Recorder names CSC eRecording, Simplifile, ePN and Hopdox as the electronic routes. Ask your title company or attorney which one they use.

Does the Madison County Auditor have a form for a trust or estate transfer?

The forms page lists DTE 100EX for exemption reasons and affidavits for a trustee or successor trustee under Revised Code sections 317.22 and 5302.171. An attorney should pick the right ones for your situation.

How old are Madison County's scanned deeds?

Deeds are scanned, indexed and online from March 1, 1920 forward. Mortgages are scanned and indexed from September 25, 1968, and the original books stay in the office.

Reaching the Mahoning County Recorder

Walk in at 120 Market Street, Youngstown, OH 44503, on the building's first floor. Counter service runs weekdays from eight in the morning until half past four, while the basement self-serve room closes at four. Dial 330-740-2345 for the office or send a fax to 330-740-2347.

Employees will pull a copy when you can name the recording details, yet they do not run searches for the public. Anyone who must look something up can sit at one of thirteen public terminals or use the online index. Legal advice is not offered by phone or at the desk.

Online searching runs on a system called Laredo Anywhere, with a basic search link and a professional one. An owner tracing an old deed, or checking that a mortgage release was ever filed, can begin there and then ask for a copy using the recording reference the search returns.

At the counter you pay with a check or cash, because credit cards are not taken. Documents sent by mail are returned when the check exceeds the exact recording charge, so verify the amount first.

Recording fees

Every charge is set by state law. Senate Bill 94 added $5.00 to most recording charges. The figures below assume the paper meets the state layout rule.

Mahoning County Recorder charges
ServiceCharge
Deed, mortgage, lease and similar records$39.00 covers pages one and two, then $8.00 per further page or side
Marginal notation (release, assignment, re-recording)Standard fee and another $4.00 per notation
PlatTen cents a square inch, with a $40.00 floor
Certified copy$2.00 a page and $1.00 to certify
Uncertified copy$2.00 a page
Military discharge (DD214)No charge
Paper that breaks the layout ruleAdditional $20

A short two-page warranty deed falls under the first line. A long legal description or attached exhibit adds pages, and each one adds cost. Smaller lines in the same schedule include $5.00 to file a federal tax lien, $3.00 to release one, $4.00 to release a personal property tax lien, and $50.00 for a zoning resolution. A seller whose title search turns up an old lien should ask the recorder whether a release is on file, because a missing release can hold up a closing.

What the Auditor must approve first

Start at the auditor's counter. An incomplete deed comes back with all its attachments for correction. The auditor looks for:

  • Whether the grantor is married, single or signing with a spouse
  • Where the buyer wants tax bills mailed
  • The legal description, tied back to the previous deed
  • Seller and spouse signatures, plus a notary clause and stamp
  • Who drafted the deed, with contact information
  • A finished state form: DTE 100 for a sale, or DTE 100 EX for a transfer with no payment

Leave a contact name and phone number with the drop-off. The auditor wants a separate check for each transaction, payable to the Mahoning County Treasurer, and will not take a blank one. On a sale the charge is $1.00 per $1,000 of price as the conveyance fee, plus $3.00 per $1,000 as a permissive fee, plus 50 cents for each parcel. An exempt transfer owes just the parcel charge. For questions call 330-740-2010 and press 0.

Land measured in acres, a slice of a platted lot or an outlot needs one extra visit first. The GIS and Tax Map desk, in the lobby at 21 West Boardman Street, signs off before the auditor moves the parcel. The recorder sees the deed only once the auditor has stamped it.

Layout rules that add $20 to a deed

A state standardization law has applied since mid-2009, and the recorder enforces it on ordinary deeds. A page that ignores it is still taken, but with a $20 surcharge. The rules:

  • Print no smaller than a 10 point font
  • Sheets from letter size up to legal length
  • Dark ink only, in black or blue, and no highlighter
  • A margin of one inch down both sides and along the bottom
  • Three blank inches above the text on page one, reserved for office stamps
  • Inch-and-a-half headroom on every page after the first

Court and tax authority papers, plats, DD214 forms, state or federal documents, and anything signed before the law began are exempt. The recorder's home page also carries a notary fraud alert. A title company that prepares the package normally takes care of all of this.

Filing a deed online

Deeds, mortgages and related papers can be filed electronically. The recorder names three vendors:

  • ePN, 888-325-3365
  • Simplifile, 800-460-5657
  • CSC eRecording Solutions, 866-652-0111

Title companies and lenders tend to use these services, which skips the drive downtown and the no-card rule at the counter. A family member handling a quitclaim is more likely to bring paper. Both routes still require the auditor's stamp before recording.

Mahoning County housing snapshot

Youngstown is the seat, and every city and village in the county, from Struthers, Campbell and Canfield to Sebring, Poland and Lowellville, records in this one Youngstown office. Owned homes carry a midpoint value of $154,700, and owners live in 70.3 percent of the housing. Population fell from 238,823 in 2010 to 228,614 in 2020. Twenty school districts cover the county, including Austintown, Boardman, Canfield, Poland, Springfield and Struthers.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Mahoning County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What to settle before filing

Each item below is a call to a different office:

  • Ask the treasurer, at 330-740-2460, for the unpaid balance on the parcel
  • Get a recorded release from any lender whose loan was paid off
  • Look for liens at the recorder, since mortgages, judgments and mechanic's liens never show on a tax bill
  • Ask the probate court who has authority to sign after an owner's death
  • Compare the legal description in your old deed with the auditor's parcel record

A cash sale follows the same path: the auditor first, then the recorder, with the same layout rules and the same page-count fees. It simply leaves out the lender's release, so the closing agent has fewer items to chase before the deed can be filed. Owners who inherited the house should also confirm who has authority to sign before anyone prepares the deed.

On the day of the filing

Bring the signed deed with the auditor's stamp, a check made out for the exact recording charge, and a daytime phone number. If you are mailing, include a return envelope, and count the pages first so the check matches the schedule above. Employees cannot tell you what a document means, so have your attorney or title agent answer any question about the wording. Allow time for the auditor's stamp first, since the recorder will not see the deed until that step is done.

Frequently asked questions

What number reaches the Mahoning County Recorder?

330-740-2345. Faxes go to 330-740-2347, and the counter is staffed on weekdays.

Does the recorder accept credit cards?

No. The fee schedule lists check or cash only. People who file electronically pay through their vendor.

Is there an added surcharge on Mahoning County recording fees?

Yes. Senate Bill 94 added $5.00 to most fees, and the schedule now shows $39.00 for a deed's first two pages and $8.00 for every page after.

Does the auditor see the deed before the recorder?

Yes. The auditor reviews the deed and collects the transfer charges, and then the deed goes to the recorder. A deed lacking a required item is sent back.

Is a military discharge copy free?

Yes. The schedule lists military records, including the DD214, at no charge and cites Ohio Revised Code section 317.24(A).

Selling in Marion County?
We buy Marion County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

Which offices touch a Marion County deed

Three county offices handle every Marion County deed, always in the same sequence: engineer, auditor, recorder. The recorder comes last and is the one that places the deed in the permanent public record. You can reach the recorder at 740-223-4100, the auditor at 740-223-4020 and the engineer at 740-223-4110.

Beyond deeds, the recorder files mortgages, easements and related land papers. An online records system lets anyone look up property documents. Paper copies and certified copies require a visit in person or a written request with payment enclosed. The online system warns users to read the actual document, because database entries can be changed without notice.

What each office does with the deed

The order differs from counties that send the deed to the auditor first.

  • Engineer. Staff compare the deed's legal description with the engineer's records and stamp it approved. That stamp expires after 60 days, so a deed left sitting must be stamped again.
  • Auditor. The seller completes and signs a conveyance form. Payment has to arrive before processing begins, and the auditor then stamps the deed as transferred.
  • Recorder. The office confirms the deed was signed and acknowledged correctly and carries both earlier stamps. After recording, the original is kept for imaging and data entry and then mailed back or picked up.

Several other papers follow the same route: a certificate of transfer, an affidavit of survivor, a life estate, a transfer on death designation and a land contract. Putting the engineer first means a faulty description is caught before any money is paid to the auditor.

Fees at the engineer, auditor and recorder

The auditor's conveyance charge is a local rate, and the recorder's charge follows state law. Senate Bill 94 added $5.00 to recording fees for most documents.

Marion County deed steps and rates by office
OfficeStep or rate
EngineerApproval stamp on the legal description, valid 60 days
Auditor, conveyance$4.00 per $1,000 of the sale price
Auditor, line fee50 cents per parcel in the transfer
Auditor, very small sale$4.00 minimum conveyance fee plus line fees under a $1,000 price
Recorder$34.00 covers two pages, $8.00 each later page, plus the $5.00 surcharge

The auditor's online fee calculator asks for the total price, rounded up to the next dollar, and the parcel count. A box marks transfers that qualify as exempt on state form DTE 100 EX. Let the auditor confirm the final total before you write a check.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Marion County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Sending a deed through the mail

You can, provided the stamps come first. No deed is accepted by mail unless it already bears current engineer and auditor stamps. The county describes three mailings:

  • The deed alone goes to the engineer, with a stamped, self-addressed return envelope
  • The approved deed then goes to the auditor with a signed conveyance form, a check and another return envelope
  • The twice-stamped deed finishes at the recorder with the recording fee

Expect the recorder to take about five days. That window covers proofing, imaging, and a side-by-side comparison of the image against the original before the deed goes back in the envelope you provided. Electronic filing skips the mail altogether. Four companies handle it: CSC at 855-200-1150, ePN at 888-325-3365, Simplifile at 800-460-5657 and Indecomm at 651-765-6400.

Closed days and your closing date

The recorder's closure list goes beyond the usual holidays. It has included Good Friday, Juneteenth, parts of the days around the Fourth of July, most of Thanksgiving week, Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. In September the office has closed for the Popcorn Festival because of parking.

A deed cannot be recorded on a closed day. A buyer's lender sometimes wants proof of recording before releasing funds, so ask the title company which date it plans to file, and plan around the office calendar when the target falls near a holiday.

Marion County housing snapshot

Marion County sits in the middle of Ohio, and the city of Marion holds the seat and the largest population. The 2025 estimate is 65,115 people, close to the 65,359 counted in 2020. Owners live in 67.5 percent of occupied homes. A typical owned home is worth $156,800, typical monthly gross rent is $864, and typical household income is $59,371. Of 27,348 housing units in 2020, 8.8 percent stood empty. Only 60 building permits were issued in 2025, so existing houses make up most of the sales.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Marion County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Fraud alerts and other notices

The recorder's home page carries two warnings, a property fraud alert and a notary fraud alert, each linking to details. The Documents and Forms page holds three items: a public records policy, security procedures for electronic recording, and a notice to Medicaid Estate Recovery of a pending transfer of property by transfer on death deed.

That last notice concerns transfer on death deeds. Ask the office whether it applies before you plan a transfer of that kind. Staff cannot give legal advice and some questions may need an in-person visit, so bring the deed and any prior recording references.

Property taxes and a Marion County sale

Call the County Treasurer at 740-223-4030, the office that takes every property tax payment. The rate on a bill is the sum of voted levies and bond issues, and Ohio limits unvoted taxation to 10 mills, which works out to $10 per $1,000 of assessed value. Whatever exceeds that was approved by county voters.

The auditor's property search site accepts payments: look up the parcel by number, owner or address, open the tax tab on the property record, and add the amount due to your online cart, where you can adjust it before checkout. Debit and credit cards incur a 2.5 percent fee with a $1.50 floor, e-checks cost a flat $1.50 up to $10,000, and the page shows the amount before you submit.

For a seller, the practical step is to request a balance from the treasurer ahead of closing, so the title company can pay anything owed out of the proceeds and the buyer receives a clean record.

Steps for a typical sale

Have the deed drafted, then carry it to the engineer for the legal description stamp. Take the stamped deed to the auditor with the conveyance form and payment, and finish at the recorder with the recording fee. The engineer's stamp lasts 60 days, so do not stamp the deed until the closing date is firm. If the sale has no lender, there is no mortgage release to chase, and the three stops are all that stand between signing and the public record.

When you want proof for the buyer's lender, ask the title company to confirm the recording date once the original comes back. If you file by mail, keep the return envelopes handy and put a daytime phone number on each package. Call the recorder at 740-223-4100 if a package has not come back after about five days, and ask what stage it has reached.

Frequently asked questions

What number reaches the Marion County Recorder?

740-223-4100. The engineer's line is 740-223-4110 and the auditor's is 740-223-4020.

How many days does the engineer's stamp last?

Sixty. A deed that waits longer needs a fresh stamp before the auditor and recorder will take it.

What does the Marion County auditor charge on a sale?

The county charges $4.00 per $1,000 of sale price plus 50 cents per parcel. A non-exempt sale under $1,000 pays a $4.00 minimum plus the line fee.

What the Medina County Recorder does

Land records for Medina County live permanently with the Recorder: deeds, mortgages, easements and any other paper that moves or burdens a piece of land. The office is at 144 N. Broadway Street, Room 117, in the city of Medina, and the main number is 330-725-9782. A document search page on the recorder's website lets you look up recorded deeds and mortgages from home.

Staff take in each paper, index it and keep it in archival form. They never rule on who owns a house. Your title company reads the index to confirm the chain of owners and to spot any open mortgage that has to be released at closing.

Recording fees for a deed

A deed costs $34 for its first two pages. Each extra page adds $8, and each marginal notation adds $4. Of every recording fee, half funds the recorder and half funds the Ohio Housing Trust Fund, as section 317.32 of the Ohio Revised Code requires.

Medina County Recorder fees
Document or serviceFee
First two pages (deeds, mortgages, easements, land contracts, leases)$34

A county may tack on a preservation surcharge of up to five dollars. Before you mail a check, phone the office and ask for the exact total at your page count.

Who collects the transfer charge on a sale?

The county auditor collects it, and that happens before the deed reaches the recorder. On real property the conveyance fee runs $3.00 for every $1,000 of price, with the price rounded up to the next $100. The auditor's website has a calculator if you want a number before closing.

Ordinary sales use DTE Form 100. A transfer that qualifies for an exemption uses DTE Form 100EX. The auditor's exemption list covers:

  • gifts inside a family, such as spouse to spouse or parent to child;
  • property passing to an heir, a devisee or a surviving spouse;
  • a corrective or confirming deed for one already on record;
  • a court-ordered transfer that is not a sale;
  • a deed into a revocable trust.

Manufactured homes are charged $1.00 per $1,000 instead. Before the signing, ask the auditor which form your deed needs.

Which county offices a house sale touches

A house sale usually passes three counters in Medina, and the sequence matters. Reverse it and you lose a few days.

  • Auditor: takes the statement of value and the conveyance fee.
  • Recorder: records the endorsed deed, any mortgage release and any affidavit.
  • Treasurer: holds the real estate tax payoff. Your title company will want that payoff figure.

Professional filers can e-record and skip the trip. The office works with Simplifile, ePN and CSC eRecording Solutions, and File and Go covers notices of commencement. Each filer makes one ACH payment per day no matter how many documents go in, so nobody writes a check for the wrong amount.

Selling for cash changes nothing at these counters. There is no new mortgage to record, yet the auditor must still stamp the deed first.

Papers from a sale that go through the recorder

The recorder handles these documents at the standard rate. Most Medina County sellers will meet only a few of them.

  • Warranty, quit claim and survivorship deeds.
  • Sheriff's deeds, which close out a foreclosure sale.
  • Mortgages, mortgage releases, assignments and subordinations.
  • Affidavits, powers of attorney and various trust documents.
  • Land contracts, leases and easements.

An inherited house often needs an affidavit or certificate alongside the deed. A house with a lender needs a release recorded after payoff, which carries the $4 release fee. Each paper is priced separately by page count, so a closing with a deed, a release and an affidavit produces three charges.

Make your deed easy to record

A formatting law, ORC 317.114, has applied since July 1, 2009. A deed that falls short can be charged an extra $20. Get it right the first time and you skip both the charge and the call back.

Use a preparer who knows Ohio's format and legal description rules, and confirm the page total before you pay. Call 330-725-9782 with questions. The auditor's site also has a sales report of nearby parcels, handy for sanity-checking the price on your statement of value.

From signing to a recorded deed

On the records side, a typical sale runs in this order. If you know the sequence, you can see where a hold-up sits.

  • Your title company requests payoff figures from the treasurer and your lender.
  • You sign. The preparer completes the statement of value, DTE Form 100 for a normal sale or Form 100EX for an exempt one.
  • The auditor stamps the deed and takes the conveyance charge.
  • Next the stamped deed travels to the recorder, alongside a release if a lender is paid off.
  • Once indexed, the deed appears in the online search.

With a cash buyer, the lender steps drop out and the sale can move faster, since nobody waits on loan underwriting. The recording steps stay the same. Keep a copy of the recorded deed and the release for your own files after closing.

Housing in Medina County

The county's population was 185,025 in July 2025. Eight in ten homes (80.3 percent) are lived in by their owners, across 73,086 households, so most recorded deeds here are ordinary owner-to-owner sales. Rental and inherited houses make up the rest.

  • The middle owner-occupied house is valued at $287,000.
  • Homeowners with a mortgage report $1,726 a month in costs; those without report $650.
  • Renters pay a median $1,143 in gross rent.
  • Household income reaches $94,968 at the median.
  • The county counted 77,727 housing units and issued 430 building permits during 2025.

Guarding against deed fraud

The recorder offers a free Property Fraud Alert. Enroll on the recorder's website and an automated system emails or calls you whenever a transaction naming your property is recorded. That gives you a chance to catch a forged deed early. The office at 330-725-9782 can help with the sign-up.

A veteran can record a DD214 at no cost, and the office issues a free Veteran's Identification Card once the discharge is on file. Recording the paper creates a certified source if the original is ever lost.

Where is the Medina County Recorder's office?

It is at 144 N. Broadway Street, Room 117, Medina, Ohio 44256. The office phone is 330-725-9782. Call before you go to confirm hours and the total fee for your document.

What are the recording fees in Medina County?

The fee is $34 up to two pages and $8 per page beyond. A document that fails the state formatting rules draws an extra $20. Ask the office whether the optional preservation surcharge applies to your filing.

Does the recorder charge the real estate transfer tax?

No. The county auditor collects the conveyance fee, set at $3.00 per $1,000 of the sale price. Exempt transfers use DTE Form 100EX and pay no conveyance fee.

Can lenders and title agents e-record Medina County deeds?

Yes, through Simplifile, ePN or CSC eRecording Solutions, all under contract with the office. Homeowners generally do not e-record on their own, so ask your closing agent.

Yes. The recorder runs a free Property Fraud Alert program that sends an email or phone notice when a transaction involving your property is recorded.

Filing a deed in Meigs County

Deeds for Meigs County land are filed at the recorder's office, 100 E. Second Street, Pomeroy, Ohio 45769. The office keeps weekday hours of eight in the morning to four in the afternoon. Anything that conveys, mortgages or otherwise burdens a parcel gets a permanent entry in its records.

Sellers should care about that entry because a title company reads it before closing. An old mortgage, a lien or a gap in the chain of owners has to be cleared first, or the buyer cannot take clean title.

When you go in person, bring the signed deed, the auditor's receipt for the conveyance fee and a check or cash for the recording total. Call first for the exact amount, since it depends on page count and on any references to earlier documents.

Meigs County recording charges

Recording charges are fixed by Ohio law, and the Ohio Recorders' Association publishes the schedule. Each fee splits evenly between the recorder and the state's Housing Trust Fund. Counties may also add a preservation surcharge capped at five dollars, so ask the Meigs office whether it applies before you write a check.

Copy charges differ from county to county. Call the Meigs office for its price on plain and certified copies.

The conveyance fee on a sale

The conveyance fee, often called the transfer tax, goes to the auditor and not the recorder. The auditor charges $4.00 for each thousand dollars of price, on houses and manufactured homes alike.

The auditor's paperwork includes DTE Form 100 (statement of value and receipt) and DTE Form 100EX (exemption). Form 101 covers the conveyance of homestead property. Conveyance standards dated July 1, 2025 are posted on the auditor's site, and a surveyor or attorney should read them before drafting a legal description.

A used manufactured home sold after January 1, 2000 must be transferred through the auditor, who adds a 50-cent transfer fee. Once the conveyance is paid, the clerk of courts can move the title with no sales tax.

How values are set and contested

The auditor values real property at the price it would bring in an arm's-length sale. Staff review permits, land splits and boundary surveys, and they inspect new construction.

Disputes go to the Board of Revision. The auditor serves as its permanent secretary, with the county treasurer and the president of the commissioners. Get the complaint form (DTE Form 1) from the auditor's office, and file it by March 31 each year.

Owners who live in their house can also seek the 2.5 percent tax reduction. The auditor applies three tests:

  • the applicant owns the home;
  • it is the applicant's main residence;
  • the application is filed between January 1 and the first Monday in June.

Rentals, corporate or partnership owners and acreage past the first acre do not qualify.

Meigs County housing and local market

Meigs County had 21,587 people in July 2025, a drop of 2.8 percent since the 2020 count. About three of every four households (75.4 percent) own their home, out of 9,102 households. The 2020 census found 10,649 housing units and a 13.6 percent vacancy rate, so roughly one home in seven stood empty then.

Low values and little new construction mean a seller's price often rests on a few nearby sales. Expect buyers to ask about the condition of older homes.

Land over old mine workings

Coal mining, strip and underground, left its mark on Meigs County from the late nineteenth century onward. Anyone selling land over old workings should read the auditor's posted guide, Developing on Abandoned Mine Land, before listing.

Manufactured homes

The Meigs County Auditor keeps a separate page on manufactured homes. Homes bought after January 1, 2000 are taxed like real property under the appraisal method, with values reset every three years at 35 percent of estimated market value. Older homes may stay on the depreciation method or make a one-time switch to the appraisal method after all taxes are paid.

  • Owners must register a home with the auditor within 30 days of locating it in the county, and a failure to register can bring a $100 fine.
  • A relocation notice, required to move a home on a public road, costs $5 at the auditor's office and requires that taxes be paid.
  • A home on a permanent foundation on land the owner also owns may qualify to be taxed as real estate after the title is inactivated and surrendered.

If you plan to sell a manufactured home that has moved or changed tax methods, call the auditor first so the transfer paperwork matches the home's status.

Parcel maps and boundary questions

The county tax map office now runs its own website at meigscountytaxmap.com. Land splits and boundary surveys go through the tax map department before the auditor reviews them for new values, so a seller dividing a parcel should start there. Ask that office for its current requirements before you order a survey.

Papers recorded when a house changes hands

Most sales involve a deed and, if the seller owed money, a mortgage release. Each one is recorded on its own and priced by page. A release or assignment also carries the per-reference charge shown in the table above.

  • Warranty or fiduciary deed from seller to buyer.
  • Mortgage release recorded after payoff.
  • Affidavit or court certificate when an estate is the seller.

If the lender has started a foreclosure, the auditor's page points owners to the county sheriff's website at meigssheriff.org for the list of upcoming sheriff's sales.

Before closing, ask your title company for a list of everything it plans to record and a total for the page count. Then you can check the figure against the table above and avoid a surprise at the signing. A cash buyer needs no new mortgage recorded, so the packet is usually shorter.

The county auditor charges $4.00 per thousand dollars of the sale price for both real estate and manufactured homes. A 50-cent transfer fee also applies to manufactured homes. Ask the auditor which form your deed needs.

When must a Meigs County valuation complaint be filed?

By March 31 of the year you are contesting. File it with the county auditor, who is secretary of the Board of Revision. Forms are available from the auditor's office.

Office location, hours and payment

The recorder works from Room 203 of the Celina courthouse, 101 N. Main Street, Celina, Ohio 45822. Call (419) 586-4232 to reach staff. Doors open at half past eight each weekday. Mondays run later, to five, while Tuesday through Friday end at four. The office closes on federal holidays.

Anything that deals with land can be recorded there and read by the public. Recording is paid in cash or by check payable to the Mercer County Recorder. Cards are not accepted for recording. Copy requests are the exception, because the office has an online payment link for card or eCheck.

Deed recording charges

Ohio Senate Bill 94 took effect October 24, 2024. It lets a recorder add a preservation surcharge of up to $5.00 per document, and Mercer County began charging it January 1, 2025. The base is $39.00 through page two and $8.00 for each page after that.

Mercer County recording fee by page count
PagesFee
1 or 2$39.00
3$47.00
4$55.00
5$63.00
6$71.00
7$79.00
8$87.00
9$95.00
10$103.00

References add $4.00 each, and the formatting rules below still apply. Papers that carry their own fee under the Revised Code, among them federal tax liens, plats, township zoning and UCC filings, skip the new $5.00 charge.

Formatting mistakes that cost extra

Ohio's standardization law, ORC 317.114, covers documents prepared after June 30, 2009. A paper that misses the mark draws a $20.00 charge. The recorder's standard looks like this:

  • Print in a font of at least ten points.
  • Use paper no smaller than letter size and no longer than 14 inches.
  • Use black or blue ink with no highlighter.
  • Keep a one-inch border at the sides and bottom.
  • Leave three inches clear at the head of the first page, where the recorder, auditor and engineer stamp, and an inch and a half at the top of later pages.

The rules exempt court and taxing authority papers, plats, DD214 forms, state or federal documents and anything signed before the law took effect. The office also wants an original rather than a photocopy, a legal description, the preparer's name, a notary and English text. A deed that conveys land has to clear the Tax Map office and the auditor before it gets to the recorder.

A quick check before you leave home saves a second trip. Confirm the original is signed and notarized, the legal description matches the Tax Map approval, and the check is written to the right office for the right amount. A cash sale needs no lender paperwork, so the deed packet is usually the whole filing.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Mercer County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Can a deed go in by mail or e-recording?

Both routes are open. Since November 1, 2024 the auditor, tax map and recorder offices have accepted mail-in conveyances together, under firm conditions. The Tax Map office must approve the legal description first, and the packet needs the email showing it did.

  • Complete the auditor's forms.
  • Send separate checks to the auditor, the recorder and the treasurer. A combined check gets the packet rejected.
  • Add any recording instructions and a return envelope with postage.

Expect a one-day turnaround by mail and an immediate one at the counter. Electronic filing has been taking documents since 2010, and from November 5, 2025 conveyances can be sent through all three vendors (Simplifile, CSC and ePN). Title companies and lenders usually handle that for you.

Copies of recorded deeds and sheriff's sales

Prints made by the office cost $2.00 a page. Deeds recorded since 1946 can be viewed and printed free from the recorder's records search website. For a mailed copy, send the owner name or property address and the exact fee, plus a stamped envelope addressed to yourself, to the Room 203 address, or email the office. Staff cannot do title searches.

The recorder is the last office to see paperwork from a sheriff's sale. After a foreclosure ends, the Mercer County Sheriff's Office sends the sheriff's deed to the recorder. The sheriff keeps a searchable list of properties going up for sale, and you can read the foreclosure case itself on the Clerk of Courts website once you have the case number.

Selling with taxes owed: what to ask the treasurer

The treasurer's office is Room 201 in the courthouse, reachable at (419) 586-2259. Ohio bills real estate tax one year behind. Who owes what at a sale therefore comes down to the closing agreement, and tax that falls due after the purchase date belongs to the buyer.

Bills are mailed in January and June, usually with payment due on the 20th of February and July. Pay within ten days of the deadline and the penalty is 5 percent. Pay later and it is 10 percent. A remission application goes before the Board of Revision (treasurer, auditor and a commissioner). Monthly ACH or coupon plans are available too.

A delinquency notice goes out in late September. Parcels still unpaid in early November with no installment plan are advertised. Request a payoff figure well ahead of closing, so any penalty is paid from your proceeds and not left for the buyer to find.

Values and credits

The auditor's 2026 triennial update reviews arm's-length sale prices from 2023, 2024 and 2025. It does not repeat the full exterior inspection of each parcel done for the 2023 reappraisal. New values will appear on the 2027 tax bills.

The Inflation Cap Credit from House Bill 186 reached second-half 2025 bills payable in 2026. Every parcel gets its own figure, and a few get none. Any overpayment rolls into the first-half 2026 bill. The auditor's site includes a conveyance fee calculator, which is the place to get the county's rate for a sale.

Mercer County market snapshot

Mercer County lies along Ohio's border with Indiana. Celina holds the courthouse and is the county's only city, and Grand Lake St. Marys is the largest inland lake in Ohio. The county had 42,737 people in July 2025, a small gain over 2020, and the housing numbers describe a steady owner market.

  • Close to four in five households (79.6 percent) own their homes, out of 16,408 households.
  • The middle owner-occupied house is valued at $210,600.
  • Those paying a mortgage spend $1,340 a month on owner costs, and those without spend $553.
  • Renters pay $804 in median gross rent.
  • Household income is $76,782 at the median.
  • Builders pulled 83 permits in 2025 for a stock of 18,384 housing units.

Frequently asked questions

When can you reach the Mercer County Recorder?

It opens at 8:30 a.m. on weekdays, closes at five on Mondays and at four Tuesday through Friday, and shuts on federal holidays. The office is in Room 203 of the courthouse at 101 N. Main Street in Celina.

What does it cost to record a short Mercer County deed?

A deed of one or two pages costs $39.00. Each further page adds $8.00, and a $4.00 reference fee or a $20.00 non-standard charge may apply.

Can I pay recording fees with a card in Mercer County?

No. Recording is paid by check or cash, with checks payable to the Mercer County Recorder. Copy requests can be paid by card or eCheck online.

What does a veteran pay to record a DD214 in Mercer County?

Nothing. The office records a DD214 and issues copies free. Copies go only to authorized people with identification, such as the veteran or an estate executor.

Since when can conveyance deeds be e-recorded in Mercer County?

Conveyance documents have gone through each of the office's three e-recording vendors since November 5, 2025. Other e-recordings began in 2010.

If you mail the original, enclose a stamped return envelope addressed to yourself.

Approvals needed before the Recorder

A deed must clear the County Engineer and the Auditor first. Under the conveyance standards adopted August 12, 2025, every instrument is approved for transfer by the Engineer's Office, with a signed DTE 100 value statement or a DTE 100EX exemption form turned in alongside it.

Three rules in those standards matter to sellers:

  • No transfer is approved when the grantor never appears as an earlier grantee, unless the deed or an affidavit under section 5301.252 explains the gap in the chain of title.
  • A deed that carves a piece off an existing parcel, or changes the legal description, needs a boundary survey plat that the Engineer reviews.
  • Anyone claiming an exemption must prove it to the Auditor. If doubt remains, the fee is charged or the parcel does not transfer.

The Auditor's fee comes from section 319.54: $1, or ten cents per $100 of value if that is larger. Separately, section 322.02 lets county commissioners levy a transfer tax that tops out at 30 cents on each $100. Sellers pay both. Call the Miami County Auditor to learn which applies before you build a closing statement.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Miami County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Other documents the Recorder files

Deeds are one entry on a long list. The Recorder also accepts affidavits, easements, land contracts, leases, mechanic's liens, notices of commencement, powers of attorney, sheriff's deeds, survivorship deeds, trust documents and warranty deeds. A few carry their own prices:

  • Federal tax lien: $5.00 to file and $3.00 to release.
  • Release of a personal property tax lien: $4.00.
  • Financing statement: $12, plus $4 for each name indexed.
  • Living will or durable power of attorney for health care: $28 minimum, $40 maximum.
  • Plats: ten cents a square inch, minimum $40.00.
  • Faxed pages: $2 local or toll-free, $4 long distance.

Sellers most often meet the mortgage release. If a lender never recorded one after an old payoff, the lien still shows on the record, so ask the title agent to check before the buyer's lender does.

What the value statement asks the seller

The buyer's statement under section 319.202 records whether the seller expects a reduced tax bill, such as the homestead or owner-occupancy credit, and whether the land was enrolled in the agricultural use valuation. A yes on either needs a sworn paper that both sides have accounted for the amount.

Farm ground deserves a question. If a seller's acreage was enrolled, leaving the program can trigger a recoupment charge, and the buyer and seller are expected to account for it before the Auditor endorses the deed.

For a rental, the Auditor's stamp also reminds the buyer to file landlord information with the Auditor under section 5323.02.

Looking up and copying land records

The county's records search page offers a free basic search by last and first name, or business name, in the AVA database. Images carry a watermark, and a watermarked copy is not accepted for recording.

  • Basic search: free to view and print, with a watermark.
  • Clean copies: email or call the Recorder's Office. Since January 2026 copies cost $2.00 per page, paid in advance.
  • Credit cards: a service fee of $2.00 or 2.65% applies, whichever is greater. Cash and check are also taken.
  • Title searchers: Laredo Anywhere, run by Fidlar Technology, reaches deeds back to the county's start in 1807.

Deeds from 1807 through 1979 are scanned as whole books. Records for 1980 through 2008 are only partly indexed, and for anything before 1980 you should contact the office. A certified copy is $2.00 a page, and each seal adds $1.00.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Miami County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Can a title company e-record a deed?

E-recording suits businesses that file regularly, not one-time submissions. The e-recording page lists five vendors: ePN, Simplifile, Hopdox, Indecomm and CSC. Each sets its own pricing, so a title agent signs up with a vendor directly.

A private seller closing without a title company can send the deed by mail or hand it over at the window. Ask the Recorder's Office at (937) 440-6040 whether your document type can go electronically before you plan around it.

Miami County at a glance

Troy is the county seat, and the county's cities are Troy, Piqua and Tipp City, plus slices of Huber Heights and Union. The 2025 headcount is 112,634, a 3.5% gain on the 2020 base, spread over 47,930 housing units. Roughly three in four homes are lived in by their owners (73.4%). Median home value stands at $229,100 and median household income at $76,817. The county issued 340 building permits in 2025.

A sale of any kind, from a tidy listing to a tenant-occupied fixer, follows one path here: Engineer, Auditor, Recorder. For a cash sale the lender's paperwork disappears, but those three stops stay. Start the Engineer's review early if the legal description needs any change, because a survey plat adds time.

Frequently asked questions

What is the address of the Miami County Recorder?

The office sits at 201 West Main Street in Troy, OH 45373. Call (937) 440-6040; it is open weekdays from 8 am until 4 pm.

What is the Miami County deed recording fee?

Two pages cost $39.00, which includes a $5.00 preservation fee, and every extra page adds $8.00. A $4.00 marginal notation fee applies to mortgage releases, assignments and modifications, and a $20.00 fee applies when a document misses the Ohio standardization rules.

Who covers the conveyance fee when a Miami County house sells?

The seller settles it with the Auditor before recording. State law sets the minimum at $1, rising to ten cents per $100 on larger values, and a local transfer tax may be added if the commissioners adopted one. The Auditor can tell you what applies to your parcel.

Does Miami County need a survey to split a parcel?

Yes. A boundary survey plat is required when a deed cuts up an existing parcel or changes its legal description, and the County Engineer reviews it before the Auditor accepts the deed.

Can I print my deed for free in Miami County?

Yes. Anyone can pull up and print a watermarked image through the basic records search without paying. A copy without the watermark must be requested from the Recorder's Office and costs $2.00 per page.

Recorder's Office location and hours

The Recorder's Office is on the 5th floor of the County Administration Building, 451 West Third Street, Dayton, OH 45422. The full deed and index collection, 1805 to the present, is kept there on books and microfilm.

Older material sits at the County Records Center and Archives, 117 South Main Street, 6th floor, reached by the Main Street elevator. Call 937-225-6366 for the archives. Paperwork is recorded, scanned and indexed the day it arrives, whether it comes by mail, over the counter or from the Auditor's Deed Transfer Department. Documents go back in the mail the next business day, and the office works from 8 am to 4 pm on weekdays.

What recording a deed costs

The base charge for the first two pages is $34.00, made up of $17 for the recorder and $17 for the housing trust fund under section 317.32 of the Ohio Revised Code. Each added page is $8.00. A county may add a preservation surcharge of up to $5, which brings the first two pages to $39.00 where it applies. Call the office to confirm the total the day you file.

Montgomery County recording charges
ChargeAmount
First two pages$34.00, or $39.00 with the preservation surcharge
Each added page$8.00
Mortgage release or assignment, marginal notation$4.00
No clear 3-inch top margin on page one$20.00 standardization fee

Pay at the counter in cash, or by check or money order made out to Montgomery County Recorder.

What a deed must contain

The clerk at the window checks for these elements. A deed needs:

  • The names of the buyers and sellers.
  • A legal description, which you can get from the Copy Center.
  • The sellers' signatures.
  • A preparation statement, if the deed was notarized in Ohio.
  • A Transfer or No Transfer stamp from the Auditor's Deed Transfer Department, plus the Engineer's approval where the property calls for it.

Notarization follows the law of the state where the signer stood. The notary block has to show a statement, a signature and an expiration date. A mortgage adds the loan amount and the lender and borrower names.

Changing a name on a deed means a new deed, a stop at the Auditor for a stamp and then the Recorder. Paying off a loan creates no new deed. Instead the lender records a Release or Satisfaction of Mortgage.

Transfers that visit the Auditor first

Anything that conveys land passes through the Auditor's Deed Transfer Department before recording. Under section 319.202 the buyer files a value statement, and the grantor pays the fee set in section 319.54, plus any transfer tax the county commissioners have levied.

For e-recording, mortgages, assignments and releases with no transfer can go in electronically through Simplifile. Deeds and anything needing a No Transfer stamp, such as a transfer on death designation, an easement or an affidavit that references a deed, must be mailed or walked through the Auditor's department first.

The Auditor and Engineer also publish conveyance standards, adopted August 2, 2021, governing legal descriptions and splits. Copies are on the Auditor's third and fifth floors and the Engineer's eighth floor at 451 West Third Street.

Finding and printing a recorded deed

Print any document you find on the Recorder's online search at no charge. If you cannot print, the Copy Center charges $2.00 per page, and certification adds $1.00. Staff do not run title searches, but the 5th floor Public Research Area has public computers for doing your own.

  • Deeds, releases and liens are searchable by name on the county's online system.
  • A veteran who recorded a DD214 can request a copy at no charge, and the Recorder issues a free Veteran ID card to those who record one.

Searching by street address happens on the Auditor's site instead of the Recorder's.

Tracing the history of an older house

Start with the chain of ownership in the Recorder's deed records, using either the alphabetical grantee-grantor index or the tract index, which is organized by legal description. Both index types run from 1805 to the present, with deed books and microfilm for 1935 on and microfilm for 1805 through 1934. Build the chain of owners from there, then check the Auditor's tax lists for hints about when the house was built.

  • At the Records Center and Archives, the alphabetical indexes cover 1805 to the present, and tract index microfilm covers 1805 to 1934.
  • The Auditor's tax lists run 1803 to 1954 as indexes and 1955 to 1985 as original books.
  • A jump of more than 50% in one year's taxable value usually points to construction or improvements.

Taxable values have been recorded at 35% of market value since 1973, and at 40 to 45% before that. The research is the individual's job, though the archives answer questions at 937-225-6366. New records are indexed the day they arrive, which keeps the chain current for a title search.

What to bring when you file in person

Walking a deed through two offices goes smoothly when the packet is complete. Gather the signed and notarized deed, the buyer's value statement, the legal description and a way to pay both the auditor's conveyance fee and the recorder's charge. If the property needs the Engineer's approval, get that first.

Ask your title agent whether they will deliver the deed or whether you are expected to. When they handle it, the recorded deed comes back by mail the next business day after recording. When a mortgage is being paid off, the lender records its own release, so look the release up in the online search a few weeks after closing.

Montgomery County housing for sellers

Dayton is the county seat, and the county has roughly 230,000 parcels. The county had 539,598 residents in 2025 and 254,375 housing units. Owners occupy 62.5% of homes, the median owner-occupied value is $180,900, and median gross rent is $1,026. Median household income is $66,139.

More than a third of homes are rented, so many sellers here are landlords. The Auditor's deed endorsement for residential rental property reminds the buyer to file landlord information under section 5323.02, so a rental sale carries one more form than an owner-occupied home.

Whether the buyer pays cash or finances, the path is the same: Auditor stamp first, then the Recorder. A cash sale simply leaves out the mortgage that a lender would otherwise record.

Frequently asked questions

What is the address of the Montgomery County Recorder?

The Recorder's Office is on the 5th floor of the County Administration Building at 451 West Third Street, Dayton, OH 45422. Records Center and Archives material is at 117 South Main Street, 6th floor.

How much does Montgomery County charge to record a deed?

The state schedule is $34.00 for two pages and $8.00 per added page, and a $5 preservation surcharge can bring two pages to $39.00. Call the office to confirm the figure the day you file.

Do I need the Auditor before the Recorder in Montgomery County?

Yes, for any deed. The Auditor's Deed Transfer Department stamps it Transfer or No Transfer and collects the conveyance fee, then the deed goes to the Recorder. Only non-transfer papers such as mortgages and releases can be e-recorded directly.

Is there a fee for a poorly formatted document in Montgomery County?

Yes. A $20 standardization fee applies when page one lacks a clear 3-inch top margin, and all Ohio standardization laws apply.

Can I get a free copy of my Montgomery County deed?

Yes, if you print it yourself from the Recorder's online search. The Copy Center charges $2.00 per page if you cannot print, with certification costing $1.00 more.

Where to take a deed for recording

The Morgan County Recorder's Office is in the Riecker Building at 155 East Main Street, Room 160, McConnelsville, OH 43756. Call 740-962-4051, or email recorder@morgancountyohio.gov. More is on the county recorder page.

The Auditor works from the same building and answers at 740-962-4475. Even so, a Morgan County deed does not go straight to the Recorder. Questions about prior deeds and recording fees go to the Recorder's counter on the first floor, so call that number before you drive in.

The order of offices for a deed

A deed starts at the County Engineer, moves to the Auditor and ends at the Recorder. The same route applies to transfer on death designations, land contracts, easements and covenants, and Auditor staff will take your papers to the other offices in the proper order. The details are in the Auditor's real estate FAQ.

The Engineer's number is 740-962-3171. The county's conveyance standards want these items in or attached to any document that transfers land:

  • The parcel number.
  • A full legal description.
  • The property address.
  • A reference to the prior instrument.
  • The tax-mailing address.

Signatures must be legible, and a printed name below an unclear signature is accepted. After the Auditor finishes, the county's property website refreshes within one to two business days.

What the Auditor collects on a sale

The Auditor's transfer page lists the charges that come before recording. The office takes cash, or a check made out to the Morgan County Auditor.

Morgan County Auditor transfer charges
ChargeAmount
Conveyance fee$3.00 per $1,000 (sale price x .003)
Transfer fee$0.50 per parcel
Split fee, for every split$100.00

State law sets the floor for the Auditor's fee in section 319.54, at $1 or ten cents on each $100. Section 322.02 lets commissioners add a local transfer tax with a ceiling of 30 cents per $100. If your closing statement needs a separate line for each, ask the Auditor how the $3.00 figure divides. For acreage splits, call the Engineer, since the survey and the split fee start there.

Recording fees at the Recorder

Call 740-962-4051 and ask for the current fee sheet. The ceiling comes from section 317.32. Two pages carry $17 for the recorder and $17 for the housing trust fund, and each page beyond them adds $4 and $4. On top, the county may tack on a preservation surcharge, capped at $5 an instrument.

The same section prices a certified copy at $1 plus $1 per page, a counter photocopy likewise, and a marginal reference made by separate instrument at $2 plus $2. Page counts use legal-size sheets and include the caption page, which is why a third page raises the bill.

Is a transfer taxable if no money changes hands?

It can be. A sale is taxable, and so is a gift with no money involved unless an exemption fits. Only the relationships listed on the DTE 100EX form are exempt, and the filer reads each lettered choice to see whether one fits.

The statute lists many of those exemptions in section 319.54(G)(3), including transfers among heirs of one decedent when no money is paid and transfers to the grantor of a trust the grantor can revoke. If someone on the deed has died, families are pointed to Morgan County Probate Court at 740-962-2861 when there is a will, and to a title agent or real estate lawyer when a survivorship deed or transfer on death designation was recorded.

Section 319.202 (full text) also has the buyer certify what the seller said about reduced taxes and farm-use valuation. An owner who sells a home that carried the homestead reduction also files form DTE 101, the Statement of Conveyance of Homestead Property. The farm program (CAUV) carries a $25 one-time filing fee and requires crops, animals or timber on at least 10 acres.

Parcels and tax bills after a sale

Parcel changes take effect at once, but the bills lag. After combining parcels, the owner keeps getting separate paper bills until the next tax year, and the owner of an original parcel receives the tax bill for the whole original parcel until the next year after a split. Raise that with a title company or real estate attorney before the sale closes.

Taxes are due in February and July, and the Treasurer at 740-962-3561 bills and collects them. Value complaints go to the Auditor between New Year's Day and the end of March. The standard Homestead Exemption exempts $25,000 of a home's market value for qualifying seniors and for owners who are permanently and totally disabled, with a $50,000 enhanced version for a qualifying disabled veteran.

Why a property's value can change

Value changes come from a short list of causes:

  • A full reappraisal, which Ohio law requires of every parcel once every six years.
  • A countywide update in the third year of that cycle, based on market trends.
  • New construction, as shown by local permits.
  • Corrections to square footage, bedroom or bathroom counts.
  • A Board of Revision decision, or damage to or destruction of the property.

The Board of Revision has three members: the Auditor, the Treasurer and the president of the county commissioners, or their designees. It adjusts values, not tax dollars. Ohio law generally allows one filing in a three-year period, and withdrawing a complaint still counts as that filing. Corporations should have an attorney file for them.

If you think your value is too high before you list, compare the parcel record with the house itself. Square footage, bedroom and bathroom counts are the easiest errors to fix, and a correction needs no hearing.

Plan the order of the offices when you set a closing date. Because Auditor staff carry papers between counters, leave a few business days between signing and the date you need the deed recorded, and ask the Recorder's counter what it needs on the first floor.

Morgan County housing

The 2025 estimate is 13,626 residents, down 1.3% from the 2020 base, with 7,437 housing units. Nearly four homes in five (78.9%) are owner-occupied. Median home value is $150,900 and median household income is $59,351. Only 23 building permits were issued in 2025.

With about 33 people per square mile, many sales involve acreage. The Engineer's survey and split steps are worth planning for if you are selling part of a larger tract. A cash buyer shortens the closing but not the Engineer, Auditor and Recorder sequence.

Frequently asked questions

Where is the Morgan County Recorder located?

It is in the Riecker Building, 155 East Main Street, Room 160, McConnelsville, OH 43756. The phone is 740-962-4051.

Who do I see first when I sell land in Morgan County?

Start with the County Engineer at 740-962-3171, then the Auditor, then the Recorder. The Auditor's staff will deliver your documents to the other offices in order.

What is the conveyance fee in Morgan County?

The Auditor charges $3.00 per $1,000 of sale price, plus a $0.50 per parcel transfer fee and a $100.00 split fee for every split. Payment is by cash or a check to the Morgan County Auditor.

Is a gift of a house taxable in Morgan County?

It can be. Only the relationships listed on the DTE 100EX exemption form qualify as exempt, so read each choice on that form or ask the Auditor at 740-962-4475.

How much will Morgan County charge to record my deed?

Call the Recorder at 740-962-4051 and ask for the current fee sheet. The state schedule behind it is $34 for two pages, $8 for each more, and a county may add up to $5 per instrument for preservation.

Where a Morrow County deed is recorded

The recorder's office, inside the courthouse at 48 E. High St., Mt. Gilead, OH 43338, takes deeds and mortgages for recording. Phone 419-947-3060. Weekday counter hours run from 8 to 4. More is on the recorder's page.

Sellers in Cardington, Marengo, Edison and the townships make the same trip to Mt. Gilead. To skip the drive, have an electronic recording company file for you (see below).

Documents the recorder accepts

The documents-filed list is broad. Sellers of a house, including an inherited one, usually need one of these entries:

  • Deeds, including warranty, quit claim, survivorship and sheriff's deeds.
  • Mortgages, along with releases, assignments, assumptions and subordinations.
  • Land contracts, leases, easements and powers of attorney.
  • Trusts, affidavits and certificates of transfer.
  • Liens of several kinds, such as mechanic's liens, notices of commencement and federal or personal tax liens.

Plats, condominium filings, annexations and zoning resolutions are on the list as well, so the same office holds the map side of the county's land records.

E-recording and online record searches

E-recording has been open for every document type since September 8, 2025. Four vendors can help: CSC, Simplifile, ePN and Indecomm. Most title companies and closing attorneys keep an account with at least one, which means a seller seldom signs up alone.

Record searching moved to a different system in the same period. The records search page sends visitors to RecordHub, where you must create a login before you can look anything up. The account costs nothing, and the login requirement protects the records from cyberattacks.

What the auditor does before the recorder

Under section 319.20, the county auditor moves the parcel into the new owner's name and endorses the deed. Before that, the incoming owner or an agent for that owner files a statement of value as described in section 319.202, electronically or in three paper copies.

The statement carries two questions that matter to a Morrow seller. Has the property received a tax reduction for owner-occupied homes? And was the land ever enrolled in the Current Agricultural Use Valuation program? If the answer to the second is yes, the statement must note that the land can face a recoupment charge when it stops qualifying.

The Morrow County Auditor's conveyance fee page shows $4.00 per thousand for both real estate and manufactured homes. The grantor pays it, together with the 50 cent transfer fee that section 319.54(G)(2) sets for each parcel entered.

Ohio recording fees

Prices for the basic filing are not the recorder's to set. Section 317.32 prescribes a base fee and an equal housing trust fund fee, and the office may add an optional preservation surcharge capped at five dollars, which the county keeps for general use. Pay when you hand the paper in. Electronic filers may pay later by electronic funds transfer or a similar method.

Recording charges in Ohio Revised Code 317.32
Document or serviceBase feeHousing trust fund fee
First two pages of an instrument$17$17

Exhibits push the page count up, and the price follows. Get a page count from the title agent ahead of closing so the check matches.

Transfers that owe no conveyance fee

Plenty of transfers skip the auditor's fee under state law. Family and estate sales run into these most:

  • Corrective or confirming deeds for something already on record.
  • Spouse-to-spouse gifts, and gifts from a mother or father to a son or daughter.
  • Heirs or devisees of one decedent passing property among themselves for no money.
  • A deed placing property in a revocable trust, and the deed taking it back out.
  • Any no-payment transfer that does not count as a gift.
  • Paperwork that only secures or releases a debt.

An exempt filing has to spell out why. Not sure a family deed qualifies? Ring the auditor before anything goes to the recorder.

Signing and witnessing a deed

The grantor signs the deed and acknowledges that signature before an authorized officer, as section 5301.01 directs. The list covers a court judge or clerk, a county auditor or engineer, a notary public and a mayor. Most sellers simply see a notary at the title company or a bank.

A mortgage paid off at closing leaves one more task for the lender. Section 5301.36 gives the mortgagee ninety days after satisfaction to record the release. Look in the recorder's index a few weeks later to be sure it is there.

Watching for fraudulent filings

Property Check is a free fraud alert service run by the recorder. Subscribers hear when any document is filed against a named property, so a forged deed or fake lien gets noticed fast. It is a good fit for a vacant house or an estate property, where no one is collecting the mail.

Alerts do not replace a periodic look at the record. A quick RecordHub search under your own name every so often costs only the time it takes to log in.

Morrow County housing

Central Ohio's Morrow County, part of the Columbus metro area, has an estimated 36,305 residents in 14,981 housing units for 2025. Homeowners live in 81.2 percent of the homes, at a median value of $222,300. With that much owner-held housing, ordinary owner-to-owner sales fill most of the recorder's deed work.

What belongs in the packet before closing

Start with a deed whose grantor name matches the last recorded deed letter for letter. The auditor's transfer step keys off the earlier instrument, so a spelling mismatch or a missing citation to it can stall the filing. Pack the full legal description, the grantee's mailing address and the signed statement of value.

Check, too, whether the parcel ever sat in the farm-use program. Applying costs a one-time $25, and the cutoff is the first Monday of March. Pulling land out triggers a recoupment charge equal to three years of savings, so a seller carving off a few farm acres should ask how the split changes it.

Last, find out who files the paperwork and how. Paper deeds work through the courthouse offices in sequence, while e-recorded ones move through the vendor's system, and the route tells you when the recorded copy will arrive.

Selling for cash trims the list. No lender means no new mortgage to record and no payoff release to chase, so the deed, the statement of value and the conveyance fee are usually the whole filing. Keep a copy of the recorded deed with your closing papers once it comes back.

Frequently asked questions

Which number reaches the Morrow County recorder?

Dial 419-947-3060. The counter sits in the courthouse at 48 E. High St. in Mt. Gilead and closes at four on weekdays.

Does Morrow County accept deeds filed online?

Yes, through electronic recording vendors: CSC, Simplifile, ePN and Indecomm. E-recording has covered all documents since September 8, 2025.

What is the Morrow County conveyance fee?

The county auditor charges $4.00 per thousand. The grantor pays it at the auditor's office, along with a 50 cent per parcel transfer fee set by state law.

Do I need an account to search Morrow County land records online?

Yes. The records search now runs through RecordHub, and users create a free login. The step protects the records from cyberattacks.

Is a deed between family members free of the conveyance fee?

Some are. State law exempts gifts between spouses and between a parent and child, and transfers among heirs of one decedent for no money. The filing must state the exemption, so check with the auditor first.

The same page says the office's holdings reach back to 1803, the year before the county itself was organized in 1804. Surveyors, genealogists, attorneys and title examiners all use them.

How far back do the online Muskingum County indexes go?

Not every record type was indexed from the same year, so a search that returns nothing may only mean you are looking before the index begins. The recorder's page prints a start year for each category, and a Historical Indexes tab covers earlier material.

For anything older than those years, use the Historical Indexes tab, and look at the training sheet in the office's Forms section for instructions.

What documents does the Muskingum County Recorder file?

  • Land contracts, leases, easements and powers of attorney.

What does the county do before a Muskingum County deed reaches the recorder?

The auditor's transfer page lays out the path. A document can be handed in at the counter, mailed, or sent through eRecording software. If the legal description uses metes and bounds, or covers something other than a full lot in a subdivision, it first goes to the County Engineer's Office on the third floor of the courthouse for approval. After that it goes to the Auditor's Office for the transfer, and only then to the recorder.

A full subdivision lot can skip the engineer and go straight to the auditor. The auditor's FAQ adds that every deed and related document must be notarized by a notary registered with the Ohio Secretary of State.

What are the Muskingum County conveyance and transfer fees?

The Muskingum County Auditor prints a conveyance fee of $4.00 per thousand of the sale price, rounded to the nearest ten cents, plus a transfer fee of $0.50 per parcel. State law sets a floor and a ceiling for this charge. Section 319.54(G)(3) requires $1 or ten cents per hundred dollars, whichever is greater, and section 322.02 lets commissioners add an optional tax of up to thirty cents per hundred.

The grantor, meaning the seller, pays these amounts to the auditor when the deed is delivered, according to section 319.202. The statement of value that goes with the deed is where the seller reports any owner-occupancy tax reduction or agricultural valuation tied to the parcel.

What does Ohio charge the recorder to record a deed?

The recorder's basic filing charge comes from section 317.32: a base fee of $17 for the first two pages and a housing trust fund fee of the same amount, followed by $4 plus $4 for each page after that. A document preservation surcharge of up to five dollars may be added.

Certified copies run $1 plus $1 a page, and a seal on a certification adds 50 cents plus 50 cents. The statute allows e-filers to pay after presentation by electronic funds transfer or a comparable method. Which transfers in Muskingum County are exempt from the conveyance fee?

  • Transfers by court order that are not the result of a sale ordered by the court.
  • Moves among heirs of the same decedent when nothing is paid.
  • Transfers into and out of a revocable trust.
  • Interests valued at $100 or less.

The statement of value must state the reason for any exemption claimed.

How can a Muskingum County owner guard against a forged deed?

Two free alert tools exist. The recorder offers Property Check, a fraud alert system that warns you about filings made on your behalf. The auditor's FAQ explains that you can also call (740) 455-7109, option 1, to have your phone number attached to your parcels so you hear when one appears on a deed to be transferred.

Anyone who suspects the ownership record has been changed should phone the auditor at that same number. The auditor says it will investigate the property record and coordinate with the proper authorities if needed.

Muskingum County is in east-central Ohio and is nearly split in two by the Muskingum River. Zanesville is the county seat and largest city. Higher education is local: Muskingum University, Zane State College and an Ohio University branch campus in Zanesville.

On the Census QuickFacts table, Muskingum County lists 38,597 housing units for 2025 and a 68.2 percent owner-occupied rate. The median owner-occupied value for 2020 to 2024 is $182,200, and median household income is $60,780. About one occupied home in three is rented, so many sellers here are landlords with tenants in place.

What happens to a Muskingum County deed after it is recorded?

Once the recorder indexes the deed, it appears in the online records, which the office says are refreshed each weekday. Documents are posted to the website within a reasonable time after filing, so a deed recorded this morning may not show up in a search until later in the week.

Two follow-up steps are worth doing. First, look up the parcel in the auditor's property search to confirm that the owner name and tax mailing address changed. The treasurer's FAQ says a billing address change needs a written, signed form, so a buyer who wants bills at a new address should send one. Second, when a mortgage was paid off at closing, search the mortgage index for the lender's release, since the lender has ninety days to record it under section 5301.36.

The recorder's page also carries a fair housing notice. Any deed provision that restricts the sale, rental or use of a dwelling because of race or color is invalid under federal law and cannot be enforced, which matters when you read very old deeds from the county's long record.

Weekdays from half past eight to half past four, except legal holidays. The phone line is (740) 455-7107.

The auditor's page prints $4.00 per thousand of the sale price, rounded to the nearest ten cents, plus $0.50 per parcel. The seller pays it at the auditor's office.

Yes, but the deed index starts in 1977. Older records are in the Historical Indexes tab on the recorder's site, which has its own training sheet.

Does the county offer a fraud alert for my property?

On the recorder's website the records search stays available all day and night, and the office says it is free of direct charges. Drafting is outside its job: if a deed still has to be written, ask the attorney or title agent on your sale.

The county is lightly settled. Census estimates for July 2025 show 18,727 people on roughly 416 square miles of land, about 45 per square mile.

Usually the closing agent takes care of it, and the seller never touches the deed again. Anyone doing it personally has two stops: the auditor transfers the parcel on the tax list, and then the recorder files the instrument.

Three electronic recording vendors are listed on the recorder's site: CSC, ePN and Simplifile. The listing states that eRecording submissions are taken on weekdays between 8:00 am and 3:00 pm.
