Health care power of attorney or living will$34.00
Staff-made copy, per page$2.00

Pay by cash, check, money order or card. Cards carry a 2.75 percent convenience fee. Checks go to the Stark County Recorder, and altered checks are refused. A page-count chart on the fee page tabulates totals up to 90 pages.

The Auditor's stamp comes first

The Auditor's real estate transfer department must endorse the deed before the Recorder will take it. A deed cannot be recorded until it carries the Auditor's stamp showing the conveyance form was filed correctly under Revised Code 319.202. The transfer line is 330-451-7333, with a second number at 330-451-7322.

  • Form DTE 100 states the value on a taxable sale, and DTE 100 (EX) states why a transfer is exempt.
  • Property already receiving the homestead or owner-occupied reduction adds its own statement of conveyance.
  • The conveyance charge is $.004 of the price rounded up to the next hundred dollars, plus fifty cents per tax parcel.
  • Payment at that counter is by check or cash only.

The Auditor recommends that an attorney prepare the deed, though owners may draft their own. Either way, the deed needs the items in the next section.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Stark County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What belongs on a Stark County deed?

A deed has to carry:

  • The grantor's marital status, which supports the release of dower rights.
  • The grantee's name and the tax parcel numbers.
  • A current legal description that follows the county's conveyance standards.
  • A reference to the prior deed instrument.
  • The signature of the grantor and of the grantor's spouse if married, whether or not the spouse is on the title.
  • A completed notary clause with the notary's signature.

Accepted deed types include administrator's, commissioner's, executor's, fiduciary, limited and special warranty, quit claim, sheriff's, survivorship, trustee and general warranty deeds. A sheriff's deed needs a description approval form, and a probate transfer arrives as a certificate of transfer or a judgment entry. A transfer on death designation affidavit, unlike most affidavits, does not require a certified death certificate.

Splits, combinations and the tax map office

Combinations and splits require a visit to the tax map office before the transfer. The Auditor offers a New Legal Description Application, a Tax Combine and Un-Combine Request and a Condominium Requirements checklist, and a sheriff's deed needs its own description approval form.

A seller of part of a lot or a corner of a farm should call the Auditor's maps line at 330-451-7341 before a closing is scheduled, because a deed cannot be recorded until the Auditor has stamped it. The office no longer asks for a stamped copy of the previous deed, but the new document must cite it.

Liens and special filings

Besides deeds and mortgages, the fee schedule prices a list of filings that can touch a house sale. Title searchers look for these, and a seller with an unpaid lien should expect a payoff request at closing.

  • Federal tax liens and Department of Justice liens, each with a separate release filing.
  • Abstracts of judgment, priced at five dollars.
  • State employment and workers' compensation liens, where the filing itself carries no fee.
  • UCC filings, priced per document and per name indexed.
  • Plats, priced by the square inch on the printed sizes of 11 by 17 up to 24 by 36.

Cross references at $4.00 each link a new document to an earlier recorded one.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Stark County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Can I record or look up deeds online?

Documents may be recorded electronically through the E-Recording link on the Recorder's website, and anyone can search the records free. Ohio law pushed this along: ORC 317.13 requires every recorder to offer e-recording of conveyances and to put indexes and images online for instruments recorded since 1980.

Copies cost nothing online. In the office, a self-serve copy is ten cents a page, and a staff-assisted copy is $2.00 a page. To get a certified copy by mail, send the Recorder a written request, the fee and a stamped self-addressed envelope.

Getting a deed from signing to the record

A typical sale follows four stages. The seller signs before a notary, and the title company or attorney checks the legal description against the prior deed. The deed goes to the Auditor's transfer desk with the DTE form and the conveyance fee, by check or cash. The stamped deed then goes to the Recorder with the recording fee. Finally, the Recorder files it and it becomes searchable on the website.

If you are handling the paperwork without a title company, call both offices first. Confirm the current total, bring the prior deed number and notary details, and for a split or combination, visit the tax map office before anything else. A mismatch in the description or a missing spouse signature is the usual reason a deed is sent back. Sellers who have a lien on the property should ask the title company to find it early, since a payoff or release has to be recorded before the new owner's title is clean.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Stark County Recorder's address?

Suite 170 at 110 Central Plaza South, Canton, OH 44702, on the first floor of the County Office Building. Hours run 8:30 to 4:30 on weekdays.

Is the Stark County recording fee really $34?

That is the printed amount for a deed's first two pages, with $8 for each added page. State law allows a surcharge of up to $5 per document, so ask the office to confirm the total before mailing.

Do I need the Auditor's stamp before recording in Stark County?

Yes. Recording waits for the Auditor's stamp, which shows the conveyance form was completed correctly. The Auditor accepts only a check or cash for the conveyance fee.

Can the Stark County Recorder take credit cards?

Yes, with a 2.75 percent convenience fee added. Cash, checks and money orders are also accepted, and checks should name the Stark County Recorder.

How do I get a certified copy of a recorded deed in Stark County?

Ask in person or mail a written request, the fee and a stamped self-addressed envelope. Staff-made copies are $2.00 a page, plus $1.00 to certify each document.

What the Recorder Division does

It records and preserves documents that touch real estate in Summit County. The Recorder Division sits inside the Fiscal Office, so the same elected Fiscal Officer who bills property tax also oversees recording. In a sale, the legal description check, the conveyance statement and the recording all run through that one county office. Deeds, mortgages and liens make up the core, and the division also keeps partnership papers, zoning amendments, military discharges, living wills and medical powers of attorney.

Anyone may view the records, with military discharges the one exception. Online search covers documents from 1988 forward, and an Index Book Archive Viewer reaches records from 1840 to 1988. The division performs no title or property searches, which leaves that task to the buyer's title company. Staff post a turnaround of three to five working days.

The county's Ohio Building in Akron is under renovation and Fiscal Office divisions are in temporary quarters. Write recorder@summitoh.net or phone before you deliver paper to a counter.

From signature to the record

A deed passes through the Fiscal Office's transfer desk first and the recording desk second. The usual sequence:

  1. The grantor signs, and the signing is acknowledged before a notary or another listed official under R.C. 5301.01.
  2. Bring the deed and the conveyance fee statement, DTE Form 100, or the exemption statement, DTE Form 100 (EX), to the Property Transfer Department. It approves the legal description and the conveyance.
  3. Deliver by 3:30 in the afternoon if you want the transfer completed on the same business day.
  4. Take the approved deed to the Recorder Division, with recording fees on their own check.

The recording guide wants legible pages, typed names under every signature, the complete legal description on first recordings, citations to earlier recorded documents, a return address with a phone number, numbered exhibits and a stamped return envelope.

Several e-recording vendors work with the office: Simplifile, Corporation Service Company and eRecording Partners Network. Title companies commonly file that way.

What are the recording fees?

Summit County recording and transfer fees
ChargeAmount
Standard recording$34.00 up to two pages, then $8.00 for each page beyond
Non-compliant filing$20.00 each
Cross-reference entry$4.00 apiece
Conveyance fee$4.00 per $1,000 of price, with the price stepped up to the next $100
Lot fee50 cents for every lot named in the description, on exempt and non-exempt transfers alike
Certified copy$1.00 added per document

The base schedule is in R.C. 317.32. The statute splits the first two pages into a $17 base fee and a $17 housing trust fee, adds $4 and $4 for every later page, and allows a county to tack on a preservation surcharge of as much as $5. Confirm the exact total with the Recording Division before you write the check.

A mailed copy of a deed costs $4, with $1 more to certify it. Walk-in copies are $2 per page. Military discharges go on record free.

Who pays the conveyance fee?

The seller pays it. R.C. 319.202 has the grantee submit a value statement while the grantor covers the fee. For a sale, value means the full consideration paid or to be paid, mortgage balances and vendor's liens included. Gifts are measured by estimated open-market price, and knowingly misstating value is prohibited.

Ohio also lets counties adopt a real property transfer tax of up to 30 cents per $100 under R.C. 322.02. Summit lists the conveyance fee and the lot fee. Ask the Property Transfer Department whether any further charge reaches your deed.

A rental house carries one extra step: the auditor's endorsement tells the buyer to file rental information under R.C. 5323.02.

Liens and releases on a record

Mortgages and liens that bear on title are filed with this division, which means a title search can surface them. The fee schedule sets prices for several types:

  • IRS lien: $5.00. IRS release: $3.00.
  • Workers' compensation lien and its release: no fee.
  • Unemployment lien: no fee. Its release: $4.00.
  • Plats: $0.05 per square inch, with sizes running from $40.00 for 11 by 17 inches to $86.40 for 24 by 36 inches.
  • Township zoning regulations: $50.00. Township zoning amendments: $20.00.

Uniform Commercial Code filings carry their own fees. Call 330-643-8143 for those.

Ask your title company for the recording reference of anything it finds. The recording guide asks submitters to cite earlier documents by number, by book and page, or by recording date.

How a recorded deed connects to the tax bill

The deed decides whose name lands on the next bill, and the county handles both jobs in one office. Details that matter around closing:

  • Bills show the legal owner's name, and a bill covers the prior year because Ohio collects real estate tax one year in arrears.
  • A change to the mailing address on a tax bill must come in writing from the taxpayer to the Fiscal Officer. Recording a deed does not replace that request.
  • The owner-occupancy reduction ends when the property transfers, so a buyer who will live there applies on their own.
  • The conveyance statement asks the seller whether the home currently receives a homestead or owner-occupancy reduction.

Have the title company check the tax balance with the Treasurer division ahead of recording, so any open amount gets paid at closing. A tax certificate lien sale is avoided by paying in full or entering a payment plan with the Delinquent Tax Department.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Summit County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Fixing a name or getting a copy

A recorded deed cannot be edited. To change a name, a new deed must be prepared and recorded, and only the person asking for the change or an attorney may prepare it. The new deed then goes back through the Property Transfer Department for the legal description and transfer before recording.

If you cannot find your own deed, request a copy by mail. Birth and death certificates are not kept here. Summit County Public Health issues them.

A family selling an inherited house often finds an old name or a missing transfer in the chain of title. Raise it with the title company at the start, because correcting it means a new recorded deed and another pass through the transfer desk, which adds days to a closing. Build in extra time for that, and do not schedule a closing date until the fix is on record.

Before you hand anything over, run through a short checklist. Is the deed signed and acknowledged? Do the typed names match the signatures? Is the legal description complete? Are the DTE form, the transfer fees and the recording fee on separate checks as the offices ask? Does the return address carry a phone number? A deed that fails any of these can be marked non-compliant, and the extra $20.00 charge applies on top of the normal fee.

Frequently asked questions

How long does recording take in Summit County?

The Recorder Division posts three to five working days. The Property Transfer Department can finish the transfer step the same business day when forms arrive by 3:30 p.m.

Is e-recording offered for Summit County deeds?

Yes. The Fiscal Office works with Simplifile, Corporation Service Company and eRecording Partners Network, and title companies commonly file that way.

Will the Recorder run a title search for me?

No. The division performs no title or property searches. Your title company or attorney handles that.

Who can prepare a replacement deed to change a name?

Only the person requesting the change or an attorney. The new deed is recorded after the Property Transfer Department approves it.

Which Summit County records cannot be viewed online?

Military discharges. Recorded documents from 1988 forward show on the website, and older index books from 1840 to 1988 open in the archive viewer.

Where a deed gets recorded in Trumbull County

Deeds for land anywhere in Trumbull County are recorded at the Recorder's Office, 160 High Street NW, Warren, Ohio 44481. Doors are open weekdays, 8:30 a.m. through 4:30 p.m. New filings stop at 4:00 p.m. while the staff close out the day.

The office records, files and indexes papers that touch real estate, including deeds, mortgages, easements, leases, powers of attorney, plats and mechanic's liens. The index follows owner names rather than street addresses, so searching one person lists every parcel held. Images and data are online for every record except military discharges, reaching back to 1795, the year of the first recordings in the county.

A seller does not usually deal with the recorder directly. Usually the title company walks the deed through the tax map office and auditor, then files it here. Knowing the sequence helps when a closing date is tight.

What does the Recorder charge to record a deed?

Fees went up April 1, 2025: the recorder now takes $39 for the opening two pages of most documents and $8 for each later page. Senate Bill 94 supplied the extra $5, a preservation surcharge layered over the base fees in Ohio Revised Code 317.32. Sample totals:

Trumbull County Recorder fees
Document or serviceFee
1 or 2 pages$39
3 pages$47
5 pages$63
10 pages$103
Marginal reference on a separate instrument$4 each
Document that misses layout standards$20 extra

Other charges:

  • Certified copy: $2 a page, plus $1 for the seal.
  • Copies made with staff help: $2 a page.
  • Plat recording: $0.10 per square inch, minimum $40.
  • Military records: no fee.
  • Cards: a 2.60 percent convenience fee applies to debit and credit payments.

Cash, checks, money orders and e-checks are also accepted. By mail, an underpayment or overpayment sends the package back unrecorded, and the office will not mail cash back, so send a check or money order.

Formatting mistakes that add $20

Any document that falls short of the state formatting standard is recorded with a $20 surcharge, and the same charge applies automatically to e-filed documents that miss the mark. The recorder posts the checklist on its requirements page.

  • Ten-point type or bigger, on letter or legal paper.
  • Blue or black ink, no highlighter.
  • Three blank inches at the head of page one, which county staff use for their stamps.
  • An inch and a half of space across the top of later pages, and one inch along the edges.
  • Notary seals that print cleanly and do not overlap the embossed seal.
  • A readable printed name beneath any hard-to-read signature, and a line near the end naming who prepared the instrument.

The checklist skips plats, discharge papers, government-issued records, anything from a court or taxing authority, and papers signed before mid-2009.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Trumbull County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How a deed moves through the county offices

A deed cannot go straight to the recorder. It must carry the required forms and a legible copy of the last deed of record, and it goes first to the Tax Map Office, then to the Auditor, and last to the Recorder. The auditor's conveyance room is upstairs in the Administration Building, phone 330-675-2420. Questions about legal descriptions go to the tax map department at 330-675-2473.

  • The Tax Map Office reviews the legal description and parcel split, if any.
  • The Auditor collects the conveyance fee and stamps the deed. The price is $4.00 for every thousand dollars of value conveyed plus $0.50 per parcel, and an exempt conveyance pays just the parcel charge.
  • The Recorder files and indexes the deed after that.

Two checks are needed: one to the Auditor for conveyance fees, a second to the Recorder for recording. Mailed transfers are accepted at the 160 High Street NW address with a stamped return envelope. Counties may add a transfer tax capped at 30 cents per $100 of value under section 322.02. Ask the staff in the conveyance room whether Trumbull County charges one on your deed.

The recorder tries to send originals back within 24 business hours, and most filings go out the same day. Deeds that must pass through other offices first can take longer. The office also takes eRecording through four partner vendors and accepts most documents, transfer documents included.

What the Recorder will not do for a seller

Recorder staff may not run title searches under state law, so nobody there can certify that a parcel is clear. Employees also cannot draft or notarize a deed, choose a form or advise on one, and the office sells no blank forms. Attorneys and title companies handle those jobs.

A few points to know before listing a house:

  • A deed is binding even when unrecorded, but recording protects the new owner, because the public record would otherwise still show the former owner holding title and able to borrow against it.
  • A recorded deed cannot be edited. To add or remove a name, record a fresh deed. Errors in a recorded deed are a matter for an attorney.
  • A deed covers the land, so building a house later does not produce a new deed.
  • Re-recording is allowed only when the document itself states the reason, and costs the standard fee plus $4.

Torrens (registered land) filings were taken through June 1996 and are no longer accepted.

Mortgage releases and liens

A mortgage is released when the lender records a satisfaction. The lender must start it. Some lenders mail the release to the borrower, who can carry the original to the recorder along with the fee and a stamped return envelope. After a payoff, ask the lender how the release will be filed, then check with the recorder that it landed.

Only the party that filed a lien can remove it, and the recorder does not report liens to credit bureaus or notify them when one is released. Mechanic's liens can be checked in the recorder's search, but judgment and other liens may sit with the Clerk of Courts or at the state level, which is why a title examiner is worth hiring. Deed restrictions and oil and gas interests also need an examiner's review.

Trumbull County in brief

Warren is both seat and largest city of Trumbull County, which fills a square block of Ohio's far northeast corner. Cities include Cortland, Girard, Hubbard, Niles and Warren, with villages such as Lordstown and Newton Falls. The county has 198,972 residents, and owners hold 71.3 percent of occupied homes. The typical owned home is valued at $141,800 and median rent is $797 a month.

Before you list, gather your last recorded deed and any lien releases, which saves a second trip through the county offices. If the house needs work and you plan a quick cash sale, the same sequence applies: tax map office, Auditor, then Recorder.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Trumbull County fee for filing a deed?

A deed of one or two pages is $39 at the Warren office, and every page beyond that adds $8. A reference to an earlier recorded paper adds $4, and a deed that ignores the layout checklist picks up a $20 surcharge. The auditor's conveyance fee is a separate check.

Does Trumbull County record deeds by mail?

Yes, mailing works. The package needs a deed already cleared by the tax map office and the Auditor, a check for the precise sum, and a return envelope with postage. Wrong amounts come back unrecorded.

Can the Trumbull County Recorder do a title search for me?

No. State law prohibits the office from doing real estate title searches. Title companies and attorneys search the records and back the result with title insurance. You can search the county's online index yourself.

How long does Trumbull County take to return a recorded deed?

Most documents go out the same day. The recorder aims to return originals within 24 business hours, and deeds that must clear other offices first may take a little longer. Originals go back to whoever submitted them.

Is a deed valid if I never record it in Trumbull County?

A deed binds the parties even when unrecorded, but recording is advised. Until it is on record, the public index still shows the former owner, who could take out a mortgage or have a judgment attach to the property.

What the Tuscarawas County Recorder does

The Tuscarawas County Recorder keeps the land records for every parcel in the county, and New Philadelphia is the county seat. Each document that conveys or encumbers land gets a permanent record, is stored in archival form and stays open to the public. Fees the office collects go into the county general fund.

Every filing is indexed, and that index is what lets a title searcher string the documents into a chain of title. The chain shows past owners and any debt that still rides with the land. Your buyer's title agent will run that search before closing, so a clean record helps a sale move along.

The county also holds registered land, called Torrens land, and the recorder handles those certificates of title. Most house sales involve ordinary deeds. If your parcel carries an older registered certificate, tell the title company early so it can examine that record.

Recording fees

The recorder lists the per-page rate and the notation rate together at the top of its page. The statute behind those figures is Ohio Revised Code 317.32. Each fee splits into a base amount and a housing trust fund amount, and a preservation surcharge can be added on top.

Tuscarawas County Recorder fees
ChargeAmount
First two pages of a document$39
Each additional page$8
Each marginal notation$4
Non-conforming document$20 extra

Certified copies, plats and other services carry their own statutory rates. Ask the office what applies before you send payment.

Documents the recorder files

The recorder sorts its filings by type. A home seller will run into these most often:

  • Deeds of every kind, including warranty, survivorship, quit claim and sheriff's deeds.
  • Mortgage papers such as releases, assignments, assumptions, subordinations and waivers of priority.
  • Land contracts, easements and leases, plus certificates of transfer and affidavits.
  • Plats and condominium drawings.
  • Mechanic's liens and notices of commencement, along with federal, personal-property and workers' compensation liens.
  • Military discharges, powers of attorney and trust records.

The page ends with a fair housing notice. Under federal law, a deed provision that restricts the sale, rental or use of a dwelling on protected grounds is void and unenforceable.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Tuscarawas County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Getting a deed approved before it is recorded

In this county the auditor's side of the courthouse reviews a deed before the recorder sees it. Start at the auditor's office in the Courthouse Annex, 125 E. High Avenue, New Philadelphia. Posted hours are weekdays from 8:00 to 4:30. The auditor's Deed Conveyance and Transfers section lays out the procedure step by step, with a conveyance requirements form and a separate procedure for mineral deeds.

  • The GIS and Map Office checks the deed against the tax maps. It takes deeds for pre-approval by email, using the surface Conveyance Form, the Mineral Conveyance Form, or both.
  • The auditor's office completes the transfer and collects the conveyance and transfer fees.
  • The recorder's fees are paid when the deed is filed.

The auditor sets the conveyance fees and the per-parcel transfer charge, so call the deed transfer staff for current rates before you write the check. A county may also adopt a transfer tax under section 322.02, capped at 30 cents on each $100 of value. The buyer files the value statement required by section 319.202, and the conveyance fee falls on the seller.

Recording electronically

Yes, you can. Since January 20, 2026 the recorder has accepted all document types by eRecording. Conveyance documents add a step: the submitter uploads the pre-approval forms and supporting papers first, beginning with the document type, and only then sends the conveyance itself.

Five eRecording providers are approved: CSC, Hopdox, Indecomm Global Services, ERecording Partners Network and Simplifile. Closing agents normally hold those accounts, so most sellers leave the electronic filing to the title company or attorney.

Records can be searched through the county's cloud search, and the recorder posts instructions for registering an account and setting up a property alert. Ask the office how an alert works before you count on it to watch your parcel. There are two search tools, a cloud search site with quick and advanced modes and a separate county index site, so it can help to check what each one shows for your parcel.

Maps and surveys from the GIS and Map Office

The GIS and Map Office keeps the county tax parcel maps and sells printed copies. A first county road map is free and each extra one costs $1. A plat book of all 22 townships is $25. Tax maps are priced by size:

  • 8.5 by 11 inches: $0.50 without a photo, $1 with one.
  • 11 by 17 inches: $1 without a photo, $2 with one.
  • 18 by 24 inches: $2 without a photo, $4 with one.
  • 24 by 36 inches: $4 without a photo, $6 with one.
  • 36 by 48 inches: $6 without a photo, $8 with one.

Surveys are filed by location and old tax map page. Surveys from 2014 on are online through the parcel viewer. Older ones sit in drawers in the map office while scanning continues as time allows. If a buyer asks for a survey of your lot, look there before you pay for a new one.

The $20 non-conforming charge refers to the state formatting standard in section 317.114, which sets type size, margins and ink color. Have the closing attorney confirm the deed meets it before filing.

Selling a rural or older parcel

Tuscarawas County has a visible Amish and Mennonite community, and plenty of rural land. For a rural parcel, ask the title company to check easements and any recorded survey. Homes here have a median value of $185,400, and 68.9 percent of homes are owner-occupied, so most buyers you meet will be people who plan to live in the house.

Before you set a price, ask the auditor for the parcel's county value and ask the title company for the last recorded deed. Those two papers tell you what the county thinks the property is worth and who held title before you.

Steps from signed deed to recorded deed

Here is the order most sellers follow once a buyer is lined up.

  • Have the deed drafted and checked against the formatting standard so no $20 charge applies.
  • Email the deed and the right conveyance form to the GIS and Map Office for pre-approval.
  • Take the approved deed to the auditor's office, pay the conveyance and transfer fees, and get the transfer completed.
  • File with the recorder, usually by eRecording through the closing agent, and pay the recording fee.

If you sell for cash, you skip the lender's paperwork, but the deed still goes through the same approval and recording steps. Allow time for each stop and call ahead if the deed is unusual, for instance one that involves minerals.

Frequently asked questions

What does recording a Tuscarawas County deed cost?

Expect $39 for pages one and two and $8 for every page after that. A marginal notation adds $4, and a deed that fails the formatting standard adds $20. The auditor bills the conveyance charge separately.

Do I need pre-approval before recording a Tuscarawas County deed?

Yes. The GIS and Map Office and the auditor approve deeds before the recorder files them. The map office takes deeds by email, and mineral conveyances use their own form and procedure.

Can I record a deed electronically in Tuscarawas County?

Yes. The recorder accepts every document type through eRecording as of January 20, 2026. Conveyance documents must upload the pre-approval forms and supporting papers before the deed is submitted.

Where is the Tuscarawas County Auditor's deed desk?

The auditor's office is in the Courthouse Annex at 125 E. High Avenue in New Philadelphia, open weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Its website has a Deed Conveyance and Transfers page.

Does the Tuscarawas County Recorder handle registered land?

Yes. The office files certificates of title to registered (Torrens) land. If your parcel carries one, tell your title company early so it can examine the registered record.

Union County Recorder's Office in Marysville

You will find the Union County Recorder at 233 West Sixth Street in Marysville, Ohio 43040, inside the County Office Building. The counter is staffed Monday through Friday from 7:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Call 937-645-3032 to reach the front desk. This is the official land records office for county real estate.

Every filing is indexed, which lets a searcher follow the chain of title and spot any debt still tied to the land. Images and indexes are online from 1995 forward. Older indexes now run through 1994: grantor and grantee deeds back to 1875, mortgages back to 1944, and miscellaneous records back to 1960. When an older paper has not been digitized, staff will send a copy by email, fax or mail.

The auditor and treasurer work in the same building. A deed, a tax question and a filing can often be finished in a single visit.

Recording fees

Recording got $5 more expensive on January 1, 2025, when Senate Bill 94 let counties add a document preservation surcharge under Ohio Revised Code 317.32. One rate covers deeds, mortgages, affidavits, easements, leases, land contracts and powers of attorney: $39 for the opening pages, then $8 for each page after.

Union County Recorder fee schedule
ServiceFee
Deed, mortgage or similar document, first two pages$39
Each added page$8
Marginal reference on a separate instrument$4 each, on top of the recording fee
Copy, per page$2

The page chart prints $39 for one or two pages, $47 for three, $63 for five and $103 for ten. Plats and condominium drawings run $0.10 per square inch, on sheets sized 18 by 24 inches. Zoning resolutions are $50 and zoning amendments $20.

How a deed reaches the recorder

Mail a conveyance only after the Auditor has stamped it, because the Recorder will not file one without that stamp. Plan on two stops in this order: Auditor, then Recorder.

  • A representative of the buyer turns in the value statement that section 319.202 requires, on the state's DTE 100 form. An exempt transfer uses the exemption statement, DTE 100EX.
  • The conveyance fee, $4 per $1,000 of value, is paid at the Auditor's office.
  • After the stamp goes on, the Recorder files the deed.

The Auditor, Engineer and Recorder adopted a shared set of Real Estate Conveyance Standards on May 1, 2014, after public hearings in February and March of that year. Each of the three offices holds a deed to those standards, so ask your attorney or title company to compare the draft with them. Separately, section 322.02 lets a county adopt a transfer tax, so confirm with the Auditor what applies.

The office turns away any paper that displays a Social Security number unless an affidavit comes with it (section 317.082). Read through your draft for one before you submit it.

Layout rules for filed papers

Section 317.114 sets a formatting standard, and a paper that falls short gets labeled non-conforming and billed an extra $20. Here is what the Union County schedule spells out:

  • Type of at least 10 point.
  • A blank band of three inches across the top of page one.
  • Margins of 1 inch at both sides and the bottom of every page.
  • One and a half inches of clear space above the text from page two on.

Ask your closing agent to measure the draft before it goes out. The extra charge lands on every filing that misses one of these points.

Filing or watching records online

In part. Since July 15, 2024 the office has accepted eRecorded filings that are not conveyances. For a deed, call the office to ask how it should be submitted.

Residents can also sign up for a free fraud alert service. It is a notification service meant to help combat real estate fraud, and the Recorder page links to the sign-up details.

What to bring to the Recorder

Pack these items so the counter clerk at 233 West Sixth Street has no reason to send you back.

  • The original signed deed, already stamped by the Auditor if it conveys land.
  • A check or other payment for the recording fee, which depends on page count.
  • A draft that has been scanned for Social Security numbers.
  • The marginal references, if the paper releases or assigns an earlier recorded mortgage.

Clerks will describe how the records are arranged, but a full title search belongs to an attorney or title company. If your paper is unusual, phone 937-645-3032 first.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Union County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Liens and releases in the records

Read the schedule's lien entries if your title search turns up a surprise, since they show what each kind of lien costs to file and to clear. Federal tax liens and federal court judgment abstracts cost $5 to file, and a release of either costs $3. Several state liens are filed with no fee, including workers' compensation liens, Ohio EPA liens, franchise tax liens, personal property tax liens and unemployment compensation liens. A release, partial release or discharge of a franchise tax, personal property tax, tangible or intangible tax, or unemployment compensation lien costs $4.

Fixture-type UCC filings tied to land run $12, plus $4 per indexed name. Marginal references, the $4 charge that links a release or assignment to the original recorded mortgage, are billed on top of the normal recording fee. If you paid off a mortgage, check that the lender actually filed the release, because an unreleased mortgage keeps appearing in the title search.

From signed deed to recorded deed

Most Union County sales follow one route, and knowing it ahead of time can spare you a second trip.

  1. Your attorney or title company prepares the deed and compares it with the layout rules and the shared Conveyance Standards.
  2. Someone for the buyer fills out DTE 100, or DTE 100EX when no fee is owed.
  3. At the Auditor's desk you pay $4 per $1,000 of value and receive the stamp.
  4. Upstairs or down the hall, the Recorder accepts the stamped deed along with any mortgage release.

With a cash purchase there is often no new loan to record, yet the stamp and the filing charge are still required. Have the title company confirm that your old mortgage release made it into the index, since a missing release can stall a closing. Because both offices share one building, a missed signature or a page that needs fixing can be handled before you leave.

Market snapshot for sellers

Growth is the story in Union County. The estimated 2025 population is 73,446, up 17.0 percent from the 2020 base, and 968 building permits were issued in 2025. The typical owned home is valued at $344,900, and 79.2 percent of homes are owner-occupied.

If your home is in a platted subdivision, have the title company pull the plat and recorded restrictions together with the deed. Part of Dublin and part of Plain City lie inside the county, so confirm which jurisdiction your parcel falls in when you fill out forms.

Frequently asked questions

What is the fee to record a deed in Union County, Ohio?

Two pages of deed cost $39, and each page past two adds $8. Every marginal reference is another $4, and a deed that fails the formatting standard adds $20. The Auditor's conveyance fee is a separate payment.

Does the Union County Recorder accept deeds by mail?

Only when the Auditor's conveyance stamp is already on the deed. Take it to the Auditor first, then mail the stamped original with the right payment.

What are the Union County Recorder's office hours?

Walk-ins are welcome Monday to Friday between 7:30 a.m. and 4:00 p.m., at 233 West Sixth Street in Marysville. Call 937-645-3032 with questions.

Can I eRecord a deed in Union County?

The recorder has accepted eRecorded non-conveyance filings since July 15, 2024. For a deed, ask the office how to submit, since the Auditor's conveyance stamp has to be on it first.

What does the Union County Auditor charge to transfer a deed?

The conveyance fee is $4 for each thousand dollars of value. Ask the Auditor's office about any per-parcel charge and any local transfer tax.

Where a Vinton County deed gets recorded

Deeds are recorded at the courthouse in McArthur, 100 East Main Street, OH 45651. The recorder answers at 740-596-4314 from 8:30 am to 4:00 pm on weekdays.

Besides deeds and mortgages, the counter takes oil and gas leases, military discharge papers, and tax, unemployment and workers compensation liens. Staff help where they can, but they do not run searches, help with wording or sell blank forms. If you need a deed written, line up a title company or lawyer before the trip.

Selling a house in Vinton County

Vinton County is rural, with about 13,000 people, and McArthur is the seat. Over eighty percent of the land is wooded, and state parks, forests and part of the Wayne National Forest draw hikers, boaters and hunters. Many sales here involve acreage, so expect buyers to ask about tract boundaries, wells and septic systems.

If you are fixing up a house before a sale, the Development Department at 740-596-3529 can tell income-eligible residents about loans or grants for emergency repairs, septic systems or potable water. Rural splits are common, which is why the engineer's office sits at the start of the paperwork trail described below.

Looking up a recorded deed

The office holds deed books and indexes from 1850 through December 31, 1985. From January 1, 1986 on, the index is searchable on the county's Ava site, with names and index data but no images.

New filings can go in electronically. The office is fully online for transfer documents, and ePN (888-325-3365) and CSC (866-652-0111) are the e-recording routes. Property owners can also enroll in a free fraud alert at propertyfraudalert.com or 1-800-728-3858, which pings them when something is filed against their parcel.

Recording costs

Ohio's section 317.32 prices the opening two pages of an instrument at $34, split into two $17 halves, and each extra page at $8, split $4 and $4. Counties may layer on a preservation charge, capped by the statute at $5. A revised fee schedule and guidelines took effect January 1, 2025, so confirm the total with the office before sending a check.

  • Zoning resolutions: $25 plus $25.
  • Zoning amendments: $10 plus $10.
  • A certified copy: $1 plus $1 per page, and the seal costs 50 cents plus 50 cents.

Courthouse offices a sale touches

Every office a seller needs sits at the same address, so one morning can cover the whole list.

Vinton County courthouse offices in a home sale
OfficeRole in a salePhone
EngineerApproves deed and land contract descriptions, keeps tax maps740-790-7014

The county engineer approves every deed and land contract description. Splitting a rural tract is common here, so that stop comes first. The auditor's endorsement comes next, and the recorder will not accept the deed without it.

Auditor charges on a sale

The auditor posts a single conveyance rate of $4.00 per $1,000 of the sale price, for houses and manufactured homes alike. The grantor pays it when the deed is handed to the auditor. State law, in 319.54 and 322.02, allows a $1 per $1,000 fee plus an optional county tax of up to thirty cents per hundred dollars.

The same office keeps the valuation side of the file. State law expects values to land between 90 and 110 percent of market, measured against sales from the preceding three years, and owners were warned to expect a notable jump after the last triennial update. If you think a value is too high, bring a complaint to the Board of Revision, where the auditor serves as secretary beside the treasurer and the president of the commissioners. Complaints must reach the auditor on or before March 31 each year.

The homestead credit shields up to $26,200 of market value from local taxes for qualifying seniors and permanently disabled owners. New applicants need adjusted income under $40,000, so call the auditor for the current limit.

Transfers with no conveyance fee

The statute carves out many cases, and a filing in one of them lists the reason instead of a price. These are the likeliest in a family sale:

  • A gift between spouses or from a parent to a child.
  • A deed that fixes an error in an earlier recorded deed.
  • A trust deed the maker can revoke.
  • Property split among heirs for no payment.
  • A transfer to a nonprofit charity without payment.
  • An easement valued at $1,000 or less.

Property taxes around a closing

Second-half real estate and manufactured home tax comes due near the end of July. An unpaid second half draws a 5 percent penalty past the due date and 10 percent ten days after, under ORC 323.121. Payment can be made by check, money order, cash or credit card, with 2.75 percent added on cards. A labeled drop box stands in the alley behind the courthouse and the former sheriff's office, and cash does not belong in it.

The county is divided into 18 taxing districts, and rates for residential and agricultural property run per thousand dollars of valuation. For tax year 2025, Brown-Vinton is 34.280207, the Hamden corporation is 43.440994, Zaleski is 43.551322 and the McArthur corporation is 48.162418. Village parcels carry a higher total than township parcels.

If a bill has not arrived, call the treasurer at 740-790-7045, because a title company needs the true balance before closing.

Steps from deed to recording

Here is the usual path for a seller.

  • Have a title company or lawyer draft the deed.
  • Take the legal description to the engineer for approval, especially if you are splitting a tract.
  • Bring the approved deed to the auditor, file the statement of value and pay the conveyance fee.
  • Send the endorsed deed to the recorder, in person or through an e-recording route, with the recording fee.

A cash buyer skips the lender's appraisal and underwriting, but these four stops stay the same. Ask the treasurer for the true tax balance first so nothing surprises you at the table.

Bring a photo ID, the signed deed and a check for the fees. If the property is a manufactured home, the same conveyance rate applies, so the auditor treats it like a house. Call ahead if your deed involves heirs, a trust or an easement, since those can change which fees apply. Allow extra time for a rural tract, where the engineer may need to look at the description before anyone else signs off.

What is the phone number for the Vinton County recorder?

The number is 740-596-4314. Weekday counter hours are 8:30 am to 4:00 pm, in the courthouse at 100 East Main Street, McArthur.

Can a deed be e-recorded in Vinton County?

Yes. The recorder accepts transfer documents electronically through ePN and CSC. Paper still goes to the courthouse counter.

How much is the Vinton County conveyance fee?

It is $4.00 per thousand dollars of the sale price, for house and manufactured home sales alike. The seller pays at the auditor's office ahead of recording.

Will the Vinton County recorder help draft a deed?

No. Staff do not search records, help prepare a document or provide recording forms. A title company or attorney should handle the drafting.

How do I get an alert if a document is filed on my Vinton County property?

Enroll in the free fraud alert, either online at propertyfraudalert.com or by phone at 1-800-728-3858. It comes with the recorder's current recording provider.

Where to record a deed in Warren County

Warren County deeds go to the recorder at 406 Justice Drive, Lebanon, OH 45036, on the same campus as the auditor. Call 513-695-1382 or 513-695-1383. The fax line is 513-695-2949.

Make checks payable to the Warren County Recorder. The counter wants the exact amount and returns any short payment without recording it. Frequent filers are encouraged to open an escrow account so an over or under payment does not hold up a same-day recording. A typical filing is turned around in 24 hours.

Recording fees

The recorder's fee schedule is dated October 17, 2019 and tracks the amounts in Revised Code 317.32.

Selected Warren County recording fees
Document or serviceFee
First two pages$34.00
Each additional page$8.00
Copies made by staff$2.00
Subdivision plat, 24 by 36 inches$86.40 per page
Federal lien$5.00
Federal release$3.00
Zoning resolution$50.00
Zoning amendment$20.00
Financing statement (real estate only)$12.00
Each name indexed on a financing statement$4.00

The office does not charge the optional $5 digital preservation fee. If a filer sends the extra $5 anyway, the office keeps it instead of rejecting the paper for incorrect fees. Marginal notations that index earlier instruments carry no charge. Members of the public who copy documents themselves pay 25 cents per page.

Searching land records online

Most documents have been online since April 20, 2016, and all deeds are indexed and viewable back to 1797. The search works best with the parcel number. The 10-digit parcel number appears in the upper left corner of an address or name search on the auditor's property site.

To save a copy, scroll to the bottom of the open document, click the print icon and use the PDF that opens. More than 5 million documents have been recorded in the county, and staff will help by phone at 513-695-1382.

  • E-recording works for every document type except plats.
  • Every land record must include a legal description.
  • A transfer document that needs to be re-recorded must be redone with new notarized signatures, a rule shared by the recorder and the auditor.
  • A free property fraud alert sends an email, text or phone message when a document is filed on a parcel you own. If you do not use a computer, call the office to sign up.
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Warren County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What the auditor requires before the recorder

Ohio makes the auditor transfer the deed first. The auditor's transfer page lists what must be in order, and a deed missing any item comes back to you.

  • A properly completed Statement of Value and Receipt (DTE Form 100), or a Statement of Reason for Exemption (DTE Form 100 EX), plus the fees payable to the Warren County Auditor.
  • A grantor name that matches the way the grantor took title in the prior deed.
  • A reference to the previous deed of record, written on the new deed.
  • Approval and initials from the map department before the deed is presented to the auditor.
  • Form DTE 102 when the parcel is, or last year was, in the CAUV farm program.
  • The grantor's signature, notarized.

The charges: $1.00 per thousand dollars of price as the mandatory state conveyance fee, $2.00 per thousand as the county's transfer tax, for a combined $3.00 per thousand, with leftover pennies bumped up to the next dime, plus $0.50 per parcel for the transfer itself. The county commissioners adopted the $2.00 levy, which is a permissive one.

Transfers exempt from the conveyance fee

An exempt transfer uses form 100 EX, where the grantee checks one reason from a lettered list on the back. Reasons (b), (g) and (m) need a notarized affidavit explaining the facts, since the auditor wants to know why no money changed hands.

Under section 319.54 the exempt categories include:

  • Transfers to or from governments and their agencies.
  • Deeds that exist only to secure or release a debt.
  • Confirmation and correction deeds.
  • Gifts between spouses and between parents and children.
  • Sales for delinquent taxes or assessments.
  • Deeds that put property into, or take it out of, a trust the maker can revoke.
  • Transfers among heirs when no consideration is paid.

After closing

The recorder indexes each document so a title examiner can trace the chain of ownership and see any debt against the parcel. Recording right after closing puts your buyer's deed in that chain. The permanent record is what makes it possible to buy land with a clear title.

Every Ohio deed needs the grantor's signature with a notary's certificate. Warren County treats the signature and acknowledgment as a precondition and will not take the deed without them.

Here is what to have ready on recording day: the notarized original deed with the auditor's endorsement, the parcel number, a check for the exact amount made out to the Warren County Recorder, and a prepaid envelope if you are mailing it. If your lender is paying off an old mortgage, ask the title company to confirm that the release will be recorded too. An unreleased mortgage can show up in the next title search and cause trouble for your buyer later. Filings sent by e-recording skip the envelope and the trip.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Warren County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What the recorder keeps and what sits elsewhere

The county uses tract (geographical) indexing and has no registered land (Torrens) system. Staff do not sell blank forms. The office records military discharge papers (DD214). A mailed filing has to include return postage or a prepaid envelope.

People often arrive at this office for papers it does not hold. Vital records and court files sit with other departments:

  • Birth and death records: 513-695-1220.
  • Marriage licenses: 513-695-1183.
  • Divorce records: 513-695-1120.

Property tax on a home being sold

The county treasurer collects it, with office hours Monday through Friday from 7:30 am to 4:30 pm. Pay online through the myWarrenCountyOhio portal or by phone at 513-496-2931. Due dates are set each year, so ask the treasurer for the current ones.

If you have not paid, or your mortgage servicer pays from escrow, confirm the balance before closing day so the payoff and the deed fees can be settled together.

For a sale, plan the office stops in order: the treasurer for the tax balance, the map department and auditor for the transfer, then the recorder. A cash buyer skips the lender's paperwork, but the same deed steps apply, so bring the prior deed reference and a notary with you to avoid a return trip.

Frequently asked questions

How do I reach the Warren County recorder?

Call 513-695-1382 or 513-695-1383, or write to 406 Justice Drive, Lebanon, OH 45036. The fax line is 513-695-2949, and documents typically turn around in about a day.

What is the Warren County fee to record a deed?

The schedule shows $34.00 for the opening two pages and $8.00 per page beyond that. The office does not collect the optional $5 preservation fee.

Does Warren County accept e-recording?

Yes, for every document type except plats. Paper filings still go to the counter at 406 Justice Drive with exact fees.

What happens if my check for Warren County recording is the wrong amount?

The document comes back unrecorded. The recorder requires exact fees and returns shortages, and it recommends an escrow account for filers who want over or under payments handled the same day.

How much is the Warren County transfer fee on a house sale?

Washington County recorder's office

The Washington County recorder works from the courthouse at 205 Putnam Street, Marietta, OH 45750. Call 740-373-6623, extension 2223 or 2225, or fax 740-373-9643. Counter hours are 8:00 am to 4:30 pm, Monday to Friday, with legal holidays excluded.

Every document that conveys or burdens land in the county goes into the recorder's permanent archive, and the filing fees go to the county's general fund. A deed for any parcel, whether the owner lives in Marietta or in Belpre, Beverly or Waterford, ends up at this counter or in its e-recording queue.

Selling in Washington County

Washington County has 27,987 homes and apartments, and about three of every four occupied homes are lived in by their owners. Marietta is the county seat and largest city. River-valley houses in older neighborhoods and rural parcels outside town call for different paperwork, which is why the courthouse offices below matter. For a rural parcel, ask your title company to check the recorded survey and any easements before you list.

Before you sign a listing agreement, gather the previous deed, the parcel number and the most recent tax bill. Those three papers answer most of what the auditor, the recorder and a buyer's title agent will ask. If you inherited the house or took title through a trust, tell the title company at the start, since those transfers use the exempt-class paperwork described below. Allow a few days for recording once the deed is filed, and keep a copy of the recorded deed for your own files.

Which office does what in a sale

The auditor and recorder share the courthouse at 205 Putnam Street and the 740-373-6623 main line, so a seller can finish two stops in one visit.

Washington County courthouse extensions for deed-related tasks
TaskOfficeExtension
Real estate transfersAuditor2124
Property appraisal valueAuditor2141
Report new construction or demolitionAuditor2141
Homestead exemptionsAuditor2123
Tax mapAuditor2161
Recording a deed or mortgageRecorder2223 or 2225

The auditor's site also posts sales reports, and the auditor's counter keeps the same weekday hours as the recorder, 8:00 am to 4:30 pm.

How the recorder takes documents

Paper goes to the counter, and electronic filing runs through approved vendors. Corporation Service Company (866-652-0111) and eRecording Partners Network (888-325-3365) both take deeds. Simplifile is also listed, but it cannot be used for deeds.

Expect a document turnaround of three days. Payment errors are handled this way: filings that arrive under the correct fee are returned, and filings over by $5.00 or more are usually returned too, while an overage under $5.00 is sent back in cash. Mailing the exact amount avoids the delay.

For searching, the recorder links to an online records search and a second cloud-based search. A no-charge search is also available at uslandrecords.com.

Recording fees set by Ohio law

Ohio's section 317.32 builds each charge from two equal halves. The opening two pages cost $17 and $17, later pages cost $4 and $4 apiece, and a preservation surcharge is allowed up to $5. Ask the recorder which surcharge figure the county applies, since the statute sets only the cap.

  • A certified copy is $1 plus $1 a page, with the seal at 50 cents plus 50 cents.
  • Plats and maps are charged by the square inch, with a $20 plus $20 minimum.
  • Declarations under the living will and health care power of attorney statutes run $17 to $20 plus the same range again.
  • County land reutilization corporations are exempt from recorder fees.

Auditor charges on a transfer

The conveyance fee is $.40 per $100 of value. That rate fits the statute's two layers: ten cents per hundred under section 319.54 and up to thirty cents more where commissioners adopted a tax under section 322.02. The auditor's website has a conveyance calculator, and extension 2124 handles real estate transfers.

Transfers in an exempt class pay nothing, though the paperwork still names the class. The cases that come up most in family sales:

  • A gift from one spouse to the other, or from a parent to a child.
  • A deed that corrects an earlier one.
  • A transfer made only as security for a loan.
  • A distribution among heirs where no money is paid.
  • A deed placing the house in a trust the owner can revoke.

When a home carries the homestead reduction, the sale also calls for DTE Form 101, a Statement of Conveyance of Homestead Property.

Valuation, appeals and tax relief

Every parcel is revalued at market once in six years, and the Ohio Tax Commissioner typically orders a statistical adjustment three years later using actual county sales. Appraisal questions go to extension 2141, and the website has a tax estimator and a delinquency report.

Disputes over value go to the county Board of Revision, made up of a county commissioner, the treasurer and the auditor. The complaint form is due by March 31, and hearings usually fall in April and May. Bring an appraisal report or current sales of similar houses in your neighborhood.

  • Homestead. For seniors 65 and over and permanently and totally disabled owners, on form DTE 105A. It shields $25,000 of market value, and owners with a military service disability can shield $50,000.
  • Owner occupancy reduction. A 2 1/2 percent reduction for the home you own and live in, applied for between January 1 and December 31 at no cost.
  • CAUV. Farm value for at least 10 acres of crops, animals or commercial timber, with a one-time $25 filing fee and a yearly renewal. Missing a renewal costs the savings and brings a payback of the previous three years.

The treasurer, at the same courthouse, collects real estate and manufactured home tax. Call 740-373-6623 and choose option 3 and then 2, any weekday from 8:00 am to 4:30 pm. Manufactured and mobile homes must be registered with the auditor within 30 days of placement in the county, and moving one takes a $5 permit.

Steps from signed deed to recorded deed

The usual order for a Washington County seller looks like this.

  • Have the deed drafted by a title company or attorney and notarized.
  • Call extension 2124 and take the deed to the auditor for the statement of value, the conveyance fee and the endorsement.
  • Send the endorsed deed to the recorder with the exact fee, in person or through an approved e-recording vendor.
  • Ask the treasurer for the tax balance so it can be settled at closing.

A cash sale skips the lender's paperwork, but the deed steps are the same. Because the auditor and recorder share one courthouse, you can usually finish both in a single trip if the deed is ready.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Washington County recorder's phone number?

Call 740-373-6623 and ask for extension 2223 or 2225. Visit the courthouse at 205 Putnam Street in Marietta between 8:00 am and 4:30 pm on weekdays.

Can a deed be e-recorded in Washington County?

Yes, through Corporation Service Company or eRecording Partners Network. Simplifile cannot be used to record deeds.

How long does recording take in Washington County?

Plan on three days. Having the auditor's endorsement and the exact fee on the deed keeps the filing from being returned.

What happens if I send the wrong fee to the Washington County recorder?

A short payment is returned. A payment over by $5.00 or more is usually returned as well, and an overage under $5.00 comes back in cash.

Which Washington County office handles a real estate transfer before recording?

The auditor, at extension 2124 off 740-373-6623. The auditor takes the statement of value and the conveyance fee, endorses the deed, and passes it along to the recorder.

The Auditor, Treasurer, Board of Revision and Map Office occupy the same building, so most of a sale's paperwork can be done in one place.

The route is posted on the Auditor's real estate page, and a deed that skips a stop tends to come back unrecorded.

The value statement on a sale

The statute counts the full price paid or owed, mortgage and vendor's lien amounts included. A gift is valued at its likely open market price. Willfully misstating value is prohibited.

Two more questions ride along. One covers owner-occupied credit and homestead reductions. The other covers agricultural use valuation and any recoupment charge. A yes to either means both parties confirm the amount has been accounted for.

Tax due dates and your closing

Installment bills are issued in January or February and again in June or July. The last days at the Treasurer fall in late February and late July. A 10 percent penalty follows, and half is returned if the balance clears within 10 days.

If a deed records in the same week a bill comes due, put in writing who pays. Bank payments face earlier cutoffs than payments at the Treasurer. Partial payments are accepted and all go toward the upcoming bill.

Can a new owner file a value complaint after a sale?

Usually, yes. R.C. 5715.19 generally bars a second complaint on one parcel inside an interim period. A sale can therefore reopen the door for a parcel the seller already contested.

Filing opens each January 1, and for tax year 2026 the Auditor lists January 1 to March 31, 2027. Signatures must be notarized, which Auditor staff can usually do in person. The second half bill is held until the Board rules, and the first half stays payable on time.

Taxes after the deed is recorded

Assessed value is 35 percent of market value, multiplied by the district rate and trimmed by a reduction factor. The owner-occupied credit has its own application, form DTE 105C, in the Auditor's library. Rates differ by district, and the Treasurer's website charts them all.

Online tools to use before recording

  • Auditor: a parcel search and map, a conveyance calculator, a tax estimator, a levy estimator, sales reports and a delinquency report, plus downloadable forms.
  • Treasurer: payment through Autoagent online or at 1-844-615-1900, and monthly or semi-annual ACH direct debit for parcels that owe current taxes.
  • Recorder: a call to 330-287-5460 settles questions about what a particular paper needs.

Run the sales report and tax estimator first. They show what nearby parcels sold for and what the levies on your district would produce, which helps when you write the value into the statement.

Market context

Owners hold 76.6 percent of Wayne County homes, and the middle owner-held home is worth $222,100. About 59,000 parcels exist in the county, so most recorded deeds touch only a small slice of them in any year. If you are selling for cash, the same four steps apply: Map Office, Auditor, Recorder, and a tax payoff from the Treasurer.

Plan your trip in this order. First, confirm with the Treasurer that nothing is owed on the parcel. Second, have the deed drafted and take it to the Map Office. With the Recorder, 330-287-5460, in the Administration Building. Get the Auditor's endorsement first.

Before. The sequence is Map Office, Auditor, then Recorder.

Page layout rules

R.C. 317.114 gives every recorder the same standard so that recording stamps have room on the page. A deed that falls short is still recorded, with $20 more collected. Williams County's Recorder asks for the following.

  • Dark blue or black ink only, and no highlighter.
  • A font of 10 points or larger.
  • One inch of white space left, right and bottom.
  • Page one keeps 3 inches clear at the top, later pages 1.5 inches.
  • Paper from letter size (8.5 by 11) to legal length (8.5 by 14).

Four categories escape the rules: documents signed before July 1, 2009, papers from a court or taxing authority, state and federal forms with DD214 discharges, and plats.

Stamps a deed needs first

A conveyance can arrive by mail only after the Engineer and the Auditor have stamped it, a rule that covers deeds, land contracts, easements and affidavits. The County Engineer reviews the legal description, the Auditor then names the conveyance charge, and for many documents the Treasurer first confirms that taxes on the parcel are paid.

  • Engineer: clears the legal description.
  • Treasurer: validates payment of taxes.
  • Auditor, 419-636-5639: states the charge.
  • Recorder: records and indexes the stamped deed.

The Auditor's conveyance fee is $4 per $1,000 of price, with a transfer fee of $0.50 per parcel or deed. R.C. 319.202 assigns that fee to the grantor and requires the grantee's value statement. New conveyance standards started on January 1, 2026, and a link to them is on the Auditor's page.

The July 2025 population estimate is 36,549, a 1.5 percent drop from the April 2020 base. Of 16,659 housing units, 76.3 percent have owner occupants. Many sales here involve farm lots and older homes in small towns, which means legal descriptions deserve a careful look. Raise any boundary question with your title company well before closing, not at the counter on the day you file.

Walk in, and the counter copy of a public record, a deed among them, is $0.25 per page, with staff glad to help find it. Written requests run $2.00 per page and need the volume and page from the Ohio Land Records index, a check or money order, and a stamped envelope addressed to you. Phone and email requests are not filled.

That online index covers filings from October 25, 1999 forward and shows new entries within a day of recording. It names the owner, document type and property description without displaying the document itself. Certified copies exist, though in person a plain copy costs the same $0.25 per page, so request a certified one only when a lender or court insists on it.

Plats are searchable through the County Engineer's site. The Recorder holds records back to the start of land ownership in the county, and because the online index begins in 1999, older deeds need a trip to the courthouse.

Watch for a mailer called a "Deed Processing Notice" from a South Dakota company that asks homeowners for $83 to send a deed copy. Deeds are public records, so a friend can collect one for you at the courthouse.

Before you order a copy, write down the owner's name and the approximate filing date so you can find the volume and page in the index quickly. If the deed predates the online index, tell the clerk the parcel number and the names of earlier owners, and staff can point you to the right book.

  • Records Center is the county repository for both public and confidential county records.
  • Clerk of Courts takes passports, divorce records and common pleas cases.
  • Property Fraud Alert: guidance for owners who worry about forged filings.

The Auditor, Engineer and Treasurer sit alongside these offices on the same courthouse square, and the Recorder is the last stop for a deed.

Steps from signed deed to recorded deed

A seller's route through the courthouse goes like this.

  • Have an attorney or title company draft the deed to the layout rules above.
  • Take the legal description to the Engineer for review.
  • Ask the Treasurer to confirm the parcel's taxes are paid.

A cash sale skips the lender's paperwork, but the stamps and the recording fee stay the same. If an inherited house is involved, check with the Probate Court first so the deed comes from the right party. Call 419-636-3259 if you are unsure what a particular paper needs.

Keep the recorded deed and the receipt once you have them. Your buyer's lender may ask for proof of recording, and so may you if a later tax or title question comes up. If anything was refused at the counter, the clerk can tell you which stamp or correction is missing so you can fix it and return the same day.

What time does the Williams County Recorder stop taking deeds?

At 4:00 p.m., half an hour before the office closes. The counter is upstairs in the Bryan courthouse and opens at 8:30 a.m. on weekdays.

Expect $39.00 for a deed of up to two pages, then $8.00 for every page beyond that. Reference fees of $4.00 may be added, and sloppy formatting brings a $20.00 penalty.

The Auditor charges $4 per $1,000 of the purchase price, with $0.50 for each parcel or deed as the transfer fee. Ask the Auditor for the total on your price.

Does the Williams County Recorder accept deeds by mail?

Only when the Engineer and the Auditor have stamped the document beforehand. The same goes for land contracts, easements and affidavits.

Recording fees

Revised Code 317.32 splits each recording charge into two equal halves, a base fee and a housing trust fund fee. A half costs $17 for pages one and two and $4 for every further page. Counties can tack on a preservation surcharge of up to $5. The Recorder's site includes an estimator that totals the fees for your paperwork.

Pages are eight and a half by fourteen inches, and a partial page is charged in full. A long exhibit therefore costs more.

Recording charges a home seller is most likely to meet
ChargeAmount
Pages one and twoTwo halves of $17 each
Each added pageTwo halves of $4 each
County preservation surchargeCapped at $5
Reference entered by a separate instrumentTwo halves of $2 each, per reference
Copy of a recorded page$2.00 each
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Wood County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Why the Auditor sees the deed first

The transfer is arranged with the Auditor at 419-354-9150. A value statement comes from the buyer, the Auditor marks the fee on the deed, and the stamped paper then goes to the Recorder. The fee under Revised Code 319.54 is one dollar or ten cents per hundred dollars of value, whichever is larger. The seller pays. The Auditor shares the Recorder's floor in the County Office Building, so a deed moves between counters without anyone leaving the building.

A board of commissioners can levy its own transfer tax, up to thirty cents per hundred dollars (Revised Code 322.02). Phone the Auditor to learn if one applies, then fold that into your closing estimate.

How to search records or order a copy

The office website has three ways to search.

  • Adaptable Visual Access covers the index from 1980 forward, a day or so after each filing.
  • A Laredo Anywhere account shows images of documents. It is built for heavy professional use, and you must send in an account request form.
  • AmeriScan's Documents-On-Demand shows the old physical book indexes.

Under Revised Code 317.13, every county recorder must post indexes and images of instruments from 1980 onward and accept conveyances electronically. A recorder may not charge a fee just to open a login.

Each copied page is $2.00. Every request needs an instrument number or a book and page, because staff will not dig through a document to find a legal description for you. A typical order runs like this:

  1. Search the index by name and write down the instrument number.
  2. Decide whether you want the whole document or only certain pages. The first or last page needs no extra identification.
  3. Send the number and page choice by email or phone.

From signing to a recorded deed

Skip a stop and the deed comes back to you. This is the usual route.

  1. You sign before a notary, who completes the acknowledgment.
  2. The buyer hands the Auditor a value statement. The Auditor takes the conveyance fee and stamps the front of the deed.
  3. The stamped deed reaches the Recorder along with payment for all pages. It is logged and appears in the index roughly a day later.
  4. The recorded deed is returned, and the Auditor updates the tax rolls to the buyer's name.

A title company normally runs this chain. If you are doing it yourself, phone the Recorder first and confirm the page count and total.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Wood County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What to bring to the counter

Carry the original signed deed rather than a copy, plus the legal description from your last recorded deed. Should the deed mention an older mortgage, land contract or life estate, have its instrument number or volume and page handy so the reference is indexed properly. Payment must cover every page, caption page included. Run the estimator first so you know the amount, and keep your receipt and the instrument number the office gives you, since you will need that number for any later copy.

For paper format, call the Recorder at 419-354-9140. For the fee stamped on the deed, call the Auditor.

Selling with an old mortgage or lien

Did you pay off a mortgage that never got a recorded release? Request one from the lender and record it with a marginal reference to the original. After that, ask the Treasurer if any tax is still due.

A good habit before listing is to look yourself up in the Recorder's online index and read the instrument that put the house in your name. Compare its legal description with your survey or tax bill. If a name is misspelled or a mortgage release is missing, you will want to learn that now, while there is time to record a correction, and not on the week of closing when a buyer's title agent flags it.

Settle these before listing. Any buyer's title company will turn them up, and each can hold a closing back. A cash purchase has no lender underwriting, yet the title search still happens, so loose mortgages and unpaid taxes need fixing in every case.

Fifteen school systems draw from Wood County, so be ready to say which one serves your address. A parcel near a county line is recorded wherever the land actually sits.

Frequently asked questions

How much is the recording fee for a Wood County deed?

For two pages you pay $17 plus a matching $17 housing trust fund fee. Each extra page adds $4 and $4, and a preservation surcharge of up to $5 may apply. Use the estimator on the Recorder's website for your exact total.

Does Wood County charge a transfer tax on a sale?

Most sales owe the Auditor's conveyance fee, paid by the seller. A separate county transfer tax applies only if commissioners enacted one, so ask the Auditor at 419-354-9150.

Can I order my recorded deed by phone?

Yes. Find the instrument number in the online index and call or email it to the office. Pages are $2.00 apiece.

Do Wood County's online records include old deeds?

The index starts in 1980 and runs about a day behind. Older records are in book indexes served through AmeriScan.

What happens if a signed deed is never recorded?

The buyer carries the risk, because a later good faith purchaser can beat an unrecorded deed. Filing right after closing closes that gap.
